cases.n: Redeemed Christian Church pastor served as Nigeria's vice-president
cases.d: Yemi Osinbajo, a senior pastor in the Redeemed Christian Church of God (RCCG), was Vice President of Nigeria from 2015 to 2023 and acting president twice in 2017. The RCCG is a Nigerian Pentecostal church with branches in many countries; Osinbajo is senior pastor of its Lagos Province 48.
cases.cite: BusinessDay (Lagos), 12 Apr 2022; Wikipedia biography
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: A vice-president being a pastor of a church that does not work to place members in office is membership trivia with no consequence described.

cases.n: Unification Church gives Senegal's sitting president $1m prize
cases.d: The Unification Church, a Korean-founded religious movement, gave Senegal's serving president, Macky Sall, a share of a US$1 million award by naming him a laureate of its Sunhak Peace Prize in February 2020. The church funds the prize in memory of its founder Sun Myung Moon. Sall shared the award with Lutheran bishop Munib Younan, so church money went to a head of state while he held office. Former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon was given a separate Founders' Centenary Award. The prize was announced publicly by the church's prize committee and reported by AllAfrica.
cases.cite: AllAfrica, 5 Feb 2020; Sunhak Peace Prize Committee
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: A publicly announced religious peace prize awarded to Senegal's president is not someone getting inside a government to steer its decisions.

cases.n: Unification Church arm courted Cambodia's Hun Sen with summit and prizes
cases.d: The Unification Church, a Korean-founded religious movement, used its political outreach body, the Universal Peace Federation (UPF), to build ties with Cambodia's prime minister, Hun Sen. In November 2019 the UPF held its Asia-Pacific Summit at Cambodia's Peace Palace in Phnom Penh, where church leader Hak Ja Han presented Hun Sen with a 'Leadership and Good Governance Award'. In early 2022, still in office, Hun Sen received the church's Sunhak Peace Prize Founders' Award. Both events were reported in the Cambodian press. The record shows the church courting a sitting head of government with honours, not decisions he took for it.
cases.cite: Phnom Penh Post / Open Development Cambodia, 20 Nov 2019; Khmer Times, 31 Jan 2022
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: The church giving a head of government awards and hosting a summit; the record itself says no decisions were taken for it.

cases.n: Unification Church arm paid Trump millions between his presidencies
cases.rank: former and current President of the United States
cases.d: The Universal Peace Federation, the outreach arm of the Unification Church, paid Donald Trump for video speeches to its summits between his two presidencies, as listed in his revised 2023 financial disclosure. CNN counted $2 million for two UPF World Summits; Korean outlet Asia Economy tallied $2.5 million for three speeches: $500,000 for a September 2021 rally and $1 million each for two 2022 Seoul summits. He returned to the presidency in January 2025.
cases.cite: US Office of Government Ethics financial disclosure, July 2023, via CNN (13 Jul 2023) and Asia Economy (25 Oct 2023)
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: The main subject is speaking fees, declared in a financial disclosure, paid to Trump while he held no office; no one inside an institution is shown serving the church.

cases.n: Sufi shrine custodian family's Qureshi as Pakistan's foreign minister
cases.d: In Pakistan, families who hold hereditary custody of Sufi shrines ('makhdooms' or 'pirs') draw income and votes from devotees and use them to win office. Shah Mahmood Qureshi's family are custodians of the Shrine of Bahauddin Zakariya in Multan. He was foreign minister in 2008–11 and again under Imran Khan in 2018–22. In 2014 his brother accused him of using the saints' names for politics, which Qureshi denied.
cases.cite: Wikipedia biography, citing Dawn and Pakistani press
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: A shrine-custodian family winning office through devotees' votes is the family's own politics, not an outside party getting inside an institution.

cases.n: Knights of Columbus member confirmed as US federal judge
cases.rank: US District Judge, District of Nebraska
cases.d: Brian Buescher, a member of the Knights of Columbus, a Catholic men's fraternal order founded in the United States, was confirmed as a federal district judge in Nebraska. During his 2018 confirmation process, Senators Kamala Harris and Mazie Hirono asked about his membership, saying the order had taken 'extreme positions'; Republican senators called this a religious test barred by Article VI of the Constitution. The Senate confirmed him 51–40 on 24 July 2019 and he sits on the bench today.
cases.cite: Senate Judiciary Committee written questions, Nov–Dec 2018; AP, 30 Dec 2018; Senate roll call, 24 Jul 2019
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: The main subject is a confirmation-hearing dispute over a judge's religious membership; the order is not shown placing members or steering decisions.

cases.n: Chinese state-owned Sinochem's control of Pirelli curbed by Italy
cases.rank: board control of the tyre maker
cases.d: Chinese state-owned ChemChina, later merged into Sinochem, took control of the Italian tyre maker Pirelli in 2015, and still held about 37% in 2025, which put a foreign state company in charge of a major Italian firm. In 2023 the Italian government used its 'golden power' national-security powers, which let it block or limit foreign control of strategic companies, to limit Sinochem's say over Pirelli (decree of 4 August 2023). In April 2025 Pirelli's board ruled that Sinochem's control had ended, citing that decree.
cases.cite: Italian Prime Minister's decree (DPCM) of 4 Aug 2023; Pirelli board decision Apr 2025
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: An open, declared acquisition of a company and the government's curbing of it, not hidden control.

cases.n: Criminals bribed Coinbase support agents to copy customer data
cases.rank: customer-support agents at an outsourcing contractor
cases.d: Criminals bribed support agents working for Coinbase, the largest US cryptocurrency exchange, at its Indian contractor TaskUs, to copy customer data, then demanded US$20 million not to publish it. Coinbase disclosed this in May 2025; about 69,500 customers were affected. TaskUs said two people were involved and closed a 226-person team, and a former agent was arrested in Hyderabad in late 2025.
cases.cite: Coinbase SEC filing and statements, May 2025; Indian police arrest, Dec 2025
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: The main subject is a data theft and ransom demand by criminals against Coinbase customers, not an outside party steering decisions inside the company.

cases.n: Rio office-holders tied to militia land interests ordered a killing
cases.rank: federal deputy and State Audit Court counsellor
cases.d: Two office-holders in Rio de Janeiro, federal deputy Chiquinho Brazão and his brother Domingos Brazão, a counsellor of Rio's State Audit Court, ordered the 2018 killing of city councillor Marielle Franco, Brazil's Supreme Federal Court found; investigators linked the motive to land interests in west Rio areas controlled by militias, armed groups made up largely of former and serving police. Franco and her driver Anderson Gomes were shot dead on 14 March 2018. Former military police officers Ronnie Lessa and Élcio de Queiroz confessed and were convicted by a jury in October 2024. Federal Police named police chief Rivaldo Barbosa as having obstructed the investigation. On 25 February 2026 the court unanimously convicted the Brazão brothers and sentenced each to 76 years.
cases.cite: Supreme Federal Court (STF), judgment of 25 February 2026; Rio jury verdict, 31 October 2024
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: The case is primarily the murder of Marielle Franco; the militia link is a motive investigators drew, not a record of militias placing or controlling the office-holders.

cases.n: Gambian President Jammeh co-founded the rosewood export monopoly
cases.d: President Yahya Jammeh co-founded Westwood Company, which held The Gambia's exclusive licence to export rosewood, with Swiss national Nicolae Bogdan Buzaianu, according to the Swiss NGO TRIAL International. Between 2014 and 2017 The Gambia exported nearly $163 million of rosewood to China, although its own rosewood was almost gone by 2011; most came from Senegal's Casamance region, where logging funds armed groups. TRIAL International filed a criminal complaint for pillage, the war crime of looting resources, with the Swiss Attorney General in June 2019. The Environmental Investigation Agency's 2020 report 'Cashing in on Chaos' documented the trade.
cases.cite: TRIAL International complaint to the Swiss Office of the Attorney General (June 2019); Environmental Investigation Agency, 'Cashing in on Chaos' (2020)
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: The main subject is a head of state's own rosewood export business and resource looting, not an outside party getting inside the Gambian government.

cases.n: Kabul Bank: president's and vice-president's brothers among insiders
cases.rank: President's and First Vice-President's families; state salary payments
cases.d: Kabul Bank, Afghanistan's largest private bank, which paid the salaries of soldiers, police and civil servants, counted among its shareholders Mahmood Karzai, brother of President Hamid Karzai, and Abdul Haseen Fahim, brother of First Vice-President Mohammad Qasim Fahim, and gave millions to a presidential campaign against central bank advice. The Independent Joint Anti-Corruption Monitoring and Evaluation Committee, chaired by Drago Kos, reported in November 2012 that the bank had been run as a fraud: close to $900 million, later put at $935 million, was taken, most loans went to just 19 people and companies, and money went to more than two dozen countries. The bailout cost over 5% of GDP. Founder Sher Khan Farnood and chief executive Khalilullah Ferozi were jailed for five years; the two brothers were not charged. In October 2014 President Ashraf Ghani reopened the case.
cases.cite: Independent Joint Anti-Corruption Monitoring and Evaluation Committee report (28 Nov 2012); RFE/RL; Al Jazeera, 1 Dec 2012; The Peninsula, 2 Oct 2014
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: The record is about Kabul Bank being looted by its own shareholders; the political families among them and the campaign money are side details.

cases.n: Lamine Diack — IAAF president convicted of selling cover-ups to Russia
cases.rank: president of world athletics' governing body
cases.d: Russian sports officials paid Lamine Diack, president of the IAAF, so that the body that runs world athletics would hide Russian athletes' doping. Diack led the IAAF (now World Athletics, based in Monaco) from 1999 to 2015 and sat on the International Olympic Committee (IOC). About €3.2m was extorted from at least 23 suspected dopers so they could compete at London 2012. Investigators found he agreed a $1.5m deal with Russian sports officials to fund Macky Sall's 2012 presidential campaign in Senegal in exchange for delaying anti-doping cases. On 16 September 2020 a Paris court convicted him of corruption. His son Papa Massata Diack got five years in absentia. Lamine Diack died in 2021 with appeals pending.
cases.cite: Paris Criminal Court judgment, 16 Sept 2020
cases.org_note: org = target body; infiltrator is Russian state sport officials
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: The case is mainly corruption and extortion inside world athletics' own ranks over doping cover-ups, like the FIFA bribery case.

cases.n: Bukele officials gave MS-13 prison benefits for votes, US indictment says
cases.rank: prisons director and Social Fabric director
cases.d: El Salvador's government and prison officials gave leaders of the MS-13 gang benefits and released one wanted by the US, in return for the gang cutting public killings and backing President Nayib Bukele's party, Nuevas Ideas, in the 2021 election, according to a US indictment of 13 MS-13 leaders unsealed on 23 February 2023. MS-13 is a transnational gang. The indictment says the meetings 'were organized by the government of El Salvador and prison officials'. The US sanctioned prisons director Osiris Luna and Carlos Marroquín in December 2021 for these talks. Bukele's government denies any pact.
cases.cite: US District Court (E.D.N.Y.) indictment unsealed 23 Feb 2023; US Treasury Global Magnitsky designations, Dec 2021; El Faro
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: The record is a negotiated pact between El Salvador's government and a gang, not a gang getting its people or money inside an institution.

cases.n: Marengo trial: lawyer and police employee leaked to Taghi's network
cases.d: A trafficking network led by Ridouan Taghi got a lawyer and a police employee to pass it protected information, and both were prosecuted during the Marengo trial in Amsterdam, the largest criminal trial in Dutch history. During the proceedings the brother of the crown witness, a former member who testified, was murdered in March 2018, and the witness's lawyer, Derk Wiersum, was shot dead outside his home on 18 September 2019. On 27 February 2024 the court sentenced Taghi to life imprisonment.
cases.cite: Amsterdam District Court, Marengo proceedings, 2018–2024; Wikipedia, 'Marengo trial' (Wiersum murder 18 Sept 2019; judgment 27 Feb 2024)
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: The Marengo case is primarily a drug-trafficking and murder trial; the leaks from a lawyer and a police employee are a side detail.

cases.n: Taghi's lawyer carried messages out of a maximum-security prison
cases.d: The Marengo organisation of Ridouan Taghi, a Dutch drug trafficker on trial for murders, used his lawyer Inez Weski to pass messages between him in a maximum-security prison and his organisation outside. She used the confidential channel lawyers have with detainees. She was arrested in April 2023, ten days after selling her law office to her son and formally retiring. In May 2026 the Rotterdam District Court convicted her of taking part in the organisation and set her sentence at the 42 days she had already spent in pre-trial detention. Taghi was sentenced to life in February 2024.
cases.cite: Rechtbank Rotterdam, conviction May 2026; Openbaar Ministerie arrest April 2023; Taghi life sentence, February 2024
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: Main subject is a private defence lawyer passing a jailed trafficker's messages; no government body, international body or company was infiltrated.

cases.n: Wagner remnants supply tramadol to Central African presidential guard
cases.rank: presidential guard and senior security officials
cases.d: Remnants of the Wagner organisation, the Russian private military group that has fought for the Central African Republic's government, are reported to supply tramadol, an opioid painkiller, to members of the presidential guard and to a youth militia, while senior security officials are alleged to control the market. Wall Street Journal reporting from Bangui in July 2026, drawing on researchers, dealers and a former Wagner employee, found that a consignment worth about $7,000 locally fetches up to $21,000 in Cameroon after roughly $4,000 is paid to Wagner and allied armed groups en route. The Africa Center for Strategic Studies, a US-sponsored research centre, assesses that the old Wagner has in effect taken over the state. Nothing has been charged, and there is no update on an earlier case against a customs agent.
cases.cite: Wall Street Journal reporting from Bangui, 12 July 2026; GI-TOC Central Africa Observatory report, June 2026; Africa Center for Strategic Studies assessment; US State Department Trafficking in Persons Report, 2025
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: The main subject is a drug-supply trade to security forces, not an outside party getting inside the state to steer decisions.

cases.n: Cachiros traffickers laundered through Honduran bank of a political family
cases.d: The Cachiros, a Honduran drug-trafficking organisation, used Banco Continental, a bank owned by the family of a former Honduran vice-president, to launder their money, according to the US Treasury. In October 2015 OFAC, the Treasury's sanctions office, designated the bank and its owners under the Kingpin Act, a law that freezes alleged traffickers' assets and bars US dealings with them. Honduran banking regulators put the bank into liquidation within days, and depositors were paid out over the following year. The designation is an executive finding, not a court verdict.
cases.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, October 2015; CNBS liquidation order, October 2015
cases.rank: Domestic bank — owner-controlled lending (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: The main subject is money laundering through a bank and its sanctioning; the record shows no crime group placing people in or controlling the bank.

cases.n: Zimbabwe gold brokers offered to launder cash via state refinery
cases.d: Gold brokers in Zimbabwe, one of them holding the government post of ambassador-at-large (a roving diplomatic envoy), offered to launder cash through the country's state gold refinery and export it as gold bullion. The offers were recorded by undercover reporters from Al Jazeera's Investigative Unit for its series Gold Mafia, broadcast in March 2023. The method works because gold turns cash into a commodity that is sold abroad with an invoice, so the money arrives looking like the proceeds of a gold sale. After the broadcast the Zimbabwean government appointed a commission to look into the claims and the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe issued statements, but the practice continued.
cases.cite: Al Jazeera Investigative Unit, Gold Mafia, March 2023; Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe statements
cases.rank: State refinery and licensed buyers (gold, commodities & agribusiness)
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: The main subject is gold-based money laundering offers caught on camera; one broker's envoy title is incidental.

cases.n: Bank manager advised drug-den family on moving proceeds
cases.d: The couple running the Shabu Tiangge, a drug market in Pasig City in the Philippines ('shabu' is slang for methamphetamine), had their personal banking manager advise them, after a police raid, on how to move the drug proceeds from their account to a relative's. On 20 September 2022 a Pasig City court convicted the operator's widow on six counts under the Anti-Money Laundering Act, sentencing her to seven to 13 years on each, with fines totalling 18 million pesos. The manager was convicted on two counts of facilitating and given four to six years; the court said she would not have made the transfers without his advice. The sums were about 1.44 million pesos, moved over three months in 2005 and 2006. He was the fifth Philippine bank employee convicted of laundering.
cases.cite: Pasig City Regional Trial Court Branch 167, joint decision of 20 September 2022, Judge Annielyn Medes-Cabelis; Anti-Money Laundering Council statement; prior convictions under RA 9165, Pasig RTC 2009, affirmed on appeal 2015
cases.rank: A savings bank branch and its personal banking manager (banks & money transmission)
cases.drop_reason: Infiltration is incidental, not the main subject: A money-laundering conviction of a drug family and their bank manager; no crime group placed or controlled anyone inside the bank.

cases.n: Ludwig Erhard — Mont Pelerin member as West German economics minister
cases.rank: Economics Minister (1949-63); Chancellor of West Germany (1963-66)
cases.d: Ludwig Erhard joined the Mont Pelerin Society in 1950 while he was West Germany's Economics Minister, and used its meetings to test his plans for the West German economy. The Mont Pelerin Society (MPS) is an international society of free-market economists and allies founded in 1947 by Friedrich Hayek, which works to spread free-market ideas into policy. Erhard stayed Economics Minister until 1963 and was Chancellor from 1963 to 1966. Membership and office are documented; no forum has found that the society directed the member's decisions.
cases.cite: Mont Pelerin Society Directory (2010) and published membership histories, as summarised in the Wikipedia article on the society (members who advanced to policy positions)
cases.drop_reason: Membership of the Mont Pelerin Society only; dropped with the other membership-only Mont Pelerin entries for consistency.

cases.n: Antonio Martino — Mont Pelerin president, then Italian minister
cases.d: Antonio Martino, a University of Chicago-trained economist, was president of the Mont Pelerin Society from 1988 to 1990 and then entered Italian government. The Mont Pelerin Society (MPS) is an international society of free-market economists and allies founded in 1947 by Friedrich Hayek, which works to spread free-market ideas into policy. After leading the society, Martino co-founded the Forza Italia party and was Foreign Minister in Silvio Berlusconi's first government (1994-95) and Defence Minister in his second (2001-06). Membership and office are documented; no forum has found that the society directed the member's decisions.
cases.cite: Mont Pelerin Society Directory (2010) and published membership histories, as summarised in the Wikipedia article on the society (members who advanced to policy positions)
cases.drop_reason: Membership of the Mont Pelerin Society only; dropped with the other membership-only Mont Pelerin entries for consistency.

cases.n: Geoffrey Howe — Mont Pelerin member as Thatcher's Chancellor
cases.rank: Chancellor of the Exchequer (1979-83); Foreign Secretary (1983-89)
cases.d: Geoffrey Howe, listed among Mont Pelerin Society members who held office, ran Britain's Treasury under Margaret Thatcher. The Mont Pelerin Society (MPS) is an international society of free-market economists and allies founded in 1947 by Friedrich Hayek, which works to spread free-market ideas into policy. Howe was Thatcher's first Chancellor of the Exchequer, the minister in charge of tax and public spending, from 1979 to 1983, and then Foreign Secretary from 1983 to 1989. Membership and office are documented; no forum has found that the society directed the member's decisions.
cases.cite: Mont Pelerin Society Directory (2010) and published membership histories, as summarised in the Wikipedia article on the society (members who advanced to policy positions)
cases.drop_reason: Membership of the Mont Pelerin Society only; dropped with the other membership-only Mont Pelerin entries for consistency.

cases.n: Ruth Richardson — Mont Pelerin member as NZ finance minister
cases.d: The Mont Pelerin Society (MPS), an international society of free-market economists and allies founded in 1947 by Friedrich Hayek to spread free-market ideas into policy, had a listed member as New Zealand's Finance Minister. Ruth Richardson held that post from November 1990 to 1993, and later sat on the society's board in 2018–20. Her membership appears in the society's 2010 directory and in published membership histories. Membership and office are documented; no forum has found that the society directed the member's decisions.
cases.cite: Mont Pelerin Society Directory (2010) and published membership histories, as summarised in the Wikipedia article on the society (members who advanced to policy positions)
cases.drop_reason: Membership of the Mont Pelerin Society only; dropped with the other membership-only Mont Pelerin entries for consistency.

cases.n: Hojjatieh Society purged from Iranian state bodies
cases.org_note: Hojjatieh (Anjoman-e Imam-e Zaman), Shi'a society founded 1953 by Sheikh Mahmoud Halabi
cases.rank: officials in government, judiciary and education bodies
cases.d: The Hojjatieh Society, a Shia religious association in Iran founded by Mahmoud Halabi, had affiliates in decision-making, academic and educational bodies after the 1979 revolution. In a speech on 12 July 1983 Ayatollah Khomeini, Iran's supreme leader, attacked the society. Halabi announced its suspension the same day, and its affiliates were then purged from those bodies. Former members are reported to have later held posts in the judiciary, the security system and government staffing offices. Claims that senior figures were members, and that the society had influence under President Ahmadinejad, are contested.
cases.cite: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah (1999); RFE/RL reporting 2006
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Shows affiliates held posts, with no record of the society placing them or steering decisions.

cases.n: Iran's Grand Master Sharif-Emami twice served as prime minister
cases.d: Jafar Sharif-Emami was Grand Master, the head, of the Grand Lodge of Iran, the country's main Freemason body, for several years. Freemasonry is a fraternal society organised in lodges, whose members swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. He was also the Shah's prime minister, first from 31 August 1960 to 5 May 1961, and again from 27 August to early November 1978, in the last months before the revolution that ended the monarchy. The head of the lodge therefore also ran the government.
cases.cite: Biographical and historical accounts of Iranian Freemasonry
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Only shows the Grand Master was also prime minister; nothing shows the lodge steered his government.

cases.n: Gabon's President Omar Bongo founded and led its Masonic lodges
cases.d: Omar Bongo, president of Gabon from 28 November 1967 until his death on 8 June 2009, was also the head of the country's Freemasonry for decades. Freemasonry is a fraternal society organised in lodges, whose members swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. Initiated in 1953, he founded two Masonic bodies: the Grand Rite Equatorial, affiliated with the Grand Orient de France, and the Grand Lodge of Gabon, linked to the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise (GLNF). He held the grand mastership until his death, tying Gabon's ruling elite to French lodges.
cases.cite: Afrik-News, 'Freemason Presidents in Africa: Ali Bongo ordained Grand Master of Gabon', 2009; Nicholas Shaxson, Poisoned Wells (2007)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Only shows the president headed the lodges; nothing shows them steering state decisions.

cases.n: French lodge installs Gabon's Ali Bongo as Grand Master
cases.d: In 2009 Francois Stifani, Grand Master of the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise (GLNF), a French Freemason body, installed Ali Bongo as Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Gabon and the Grand Equatorial Rite, succeeding his father Omar Bongo. Ali Bongo became president of Gabon the same year, so the head of state again also led the country's lodges. Freemasonry is a fraternal society organised in lodges, whose members swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. He kept the grand mastership until after his overthrow in the August 2023 coup.
cases.cite: Afrik-News, 2009; Africa Intelligence, October 2023
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): About a lodge post given to the president, not the lodge getting inside the state or steering it.

cases.n: Gabon's Freemasons keep a state official as Grand Master after 2023 coup
cases.d: Gabon's main Freemason body, the Grand Lodge of Gabon, has kept a serving state official at its head. Freemasonry is a fraternal society organised in lodges, whose members swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. The grand mastership had traditionally gone to the head of state, and President Ali Bongo held it until the coup that removed him. In October 2023 the lodge replaced him with Jacques Denis Tsanga, governor of Haut-Ogooue province and minister of water and forests in 2018-19. Transitional president Brice Oligui Nguema reportedly declined the post. Africa Intelligence reported the change.
cases.cite: Africa Intelligence, 20 October 2023, as reported by Connection Ivoirienne
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Only shows an official leads the lodge; nothing shows the lodge steering government.

cases.n: Congo's President Sassou-Nguesso reported as Grand Master
cases.d: Denis Sassou-Nguesso, president of the Republic of Congo, is reported to be Grand Master, the head, of the Grand Lodge of Congo-Brazzaville, which is linked to the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise, a French Freemason body. Freemasonry is a fraternal society organised in lodges, whose members swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. The reports appeared in Afrik-News in 2009 and in a 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier on African heads of state in lodges. A 2013 report also said he sponsored the initiation of the Central African Republic's president, Francois Bozize.
cases.cite: Afrik-News, 2009; Jeune Afrique dossier as republished by L'Hebdo Ivoirien, May 2013
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Press report of lodge membership only; no steering of decisions shown.

cases.n: Niger's President Mamadou Tandja reported as a Freemason
cases.d: Mamadou Tandja, president of Niger from 1999 to 2010, was named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting by Afrik-News on African heads of state who belong to Masonic lodges. Freemasonry is a fraternal society organised in lodges, whose members swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. Several presidents of former French colonies in West and Central Africa were named in the same reporting. No lodge is named for Tandja, and the record is press reporting, not an official finding.
cases.cite: Afrik-News, 'Freemason Presidents in Africa', 2009
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Press report of membership only, with no lodge named and no steering shown.

cases.n: CAR's President Bozize initiated under Sassou-Nguesso's sponsorship
cases.d: Francois Bozize, president of the Central African Republic from 2003 to 2013, was named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting by Afrik-News on African heads of state in Masonic lodges. Freemasonry is a fraternal society organised in lodges, whose members swear oaths of mutual support and are often drawn from political and business elites. A 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier said he joined under the sponsorship of the Republic of Congo's president Denis Sassou-Nguesso, who is reported to lead the Grand Lodge of Congo-Brazzaville. The record is press reporting, not an official finding.
cases.cite: Afrik-News, 2009; Jeune Afrique dossier as republished by L'Hebdo Ivoirien, 29 May 2013
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Press report of membership and sponsorship only; no steering shown.

cases.n: Cameroon's Biya paid state oil money to a Templar order
cases.org_note: Ordre Souverain du Temple Initiatique (OSTI) and its charity CIRCES, esoteric Templar order founded by Raymond Bernard, former head of AMORC (Rosicrucians) in France
cases.d: President Paul Biya of Cameroon passed state money to OSTI and CIRCES, esoteric Templar orders led by Frenchman Raymond Bernard, Le Monde reported in December 1999. The paper said Biya gave them tens of millions of francs between 1988 and 1992, including 40 million francs personally, and that 11.2 million francs moved from Cameroon's state oil company SNH to Bernard's personal account. The presidency called Bernard an 'old friend' and would not comment on the payments. Bernard was questioned in the inquiry into the Solar Temple, a separate order whose members died in mass killings and suicides in the 1990s, but was not charged.
cases.cite: Le Monde, 'L'argent africain des Templiers', 24 December 1999; Le Monde, 17 August 2000
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Shows the president paying state money to an order, not the order placing people or control inside.

cases.n: Liberia: Masonic lodge membership needed to lead the ruling party
cases.d: In Liberia, membership of the Masonic Order, the country's Freemason lodge, was widely seen as a requirement for leadership in the ruling True Whig Party, and by the 1970s most high officials were Masons. William Tolbert, vice-president from 1952 to 1971 and president from 1971 to 1980, was the order's Grand Master, its head. Tolbert was killed on 12 April 1980 in Samuel Doe's coup, and much of the Masonic leadership was killed with him.
cases.cite: Histories of the Masonic Order of Liberia
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Officials' membership was common, but the record does not show the lodge placing them or steering policy.

cases.n: Liberia's Samuel Doe banned Freemasonry, then joined it
cases.d: Liberia's Masonic Order, its Freemason body, had long supplied the country's rulers; most high officials were members before 1980. After the April 1980 coup in which President William Tolbert, the order's Grand Master, was killed, the new ruler Samuel Doe banned Freemasonry. He later lifted the ban. The order was formally reinstated in 1988, and Doe himself was initiated in 1989 while head of state, bringing the lodge back into the presidency.
cases.cite: Histories of the Masonic Order of Liberia
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Membership of the head of state only; no steering shown.

cases.n: Unification Church tied to 179 of 379 ruling-party lawmakers
cases.rank: ruling-party members of the National Diet
cases.d: The Unification Church, a Korean-founded religious movement, built ties with lawmakers of Japan's governing Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) by supplying money, events and campaign volunteers. On 8 September 2022 LDP secretary-general Toshimitsu Motegi released the party's own survey of its 379 members of the Diet, Japan's parliament: 179 reported ties to the church or affiliated groups. Of these, 96 had attended church or affiliated events, 20 gave speeches, nearly 50 paid money at events, 29 accepted donations and 17 used church followers as campaign volunteers. The survey relied on lawmakers reporting on themselves, and left out former prime minister Shinzo Abe because he had been killed that July.
cases.cite: Liberal Democratic Party internal survey, 8 September 2022 (AP report)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Shows ties, money and volunteers to lawmakers, but no decisions served the church or stated aim.

cases.n: Japan's defence minister used Unification Church campaign helpers
cases.d: Unification Church members worked on the election campaigns of Nobuo Kishi, Japan's defence minister and younger brother of former prime minister Shinzo Abe. The Unification Church is a Korean-founded religious movement. Kishi said so himself in July 2022, after Abe's killing put the church's political ties under scrutiny. In the governing Liberal Democratic Party's own survey of 8 September 2022 he was named among the 17 lawmakers who had accepted church followers as campaign volunteers.
cases.cite: Statement by Defense Minister Kishi, July 2022 (The Diplomat); LDP survey 8 September 2022 (AP)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Campaign volunteers for one minister; no decision shown serving the church.

cases.n: Ex-minister Koichi Hagiuda used Unification Church campaign helpers
cases.rank: former economy and industry minister, senior LDP lawmaker
cases.d: Followers of the Unification Church, a Korean-founded religious movement, worked as volunteers on the election campaigns of Koichi Hagiuda, a former Japanese Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry. He was named in the governing Liberal Democratic Party's survey of 8 September 2022 among the 17 lawmakers who had accepted church followers as campaign volunteers. The party ran the survey after the killing of former prime minister Shinzo Abe in July 2022 exposed the church's ties to politicians; it relied on lawmakers reporting on themselves.
cases.cite: Liberal Democratic Party internal survey, 8 September 2022 (AP report)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Campaign volunteers for one ex-minister; no decision shown serving the church.

cases.n: Minister Daishiro Yamagiwa resigns over Unification Church ties
cases.d: The Unification Church, a Korean-founded religious movement, built ties with lawmakers of Japan's governing Liberal Democratic Party, and one of them, Daishiro Yamagiwa, sat in the cabinet as economic revitalisation minister. Yamagiwa confirmed he appeared in a 2019 group photo with church leader Hak Ja Han and had attended a church-organised event in 2018. He said he regretted that his attendance at several of the group's meetings had given it credit. He resigned on 24 October 2022 and Prime Minister Fumio Kishida accepted the resignation; the week before, Kishida had ordered a government probe into the church.
cases.cite: Resignation accepted by Prime Minister Kishida, 24 October 2022 (AFP via Philstar)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Event attendance by a minister; no decision shown serving the church.

cases.n: Ex-PM Nobusuke Kishi co-founded Unification Church's political arm
cases.d: Former Japanese prime minister Nobusuke Kishi, Shinzo Abe's grandfather, helped the Unification Church, a Korean-founded religious movement, set up its political operation in Japan. In 1968 he founded the International Federation for Victory over Communism (Shokyo Rengo) with Ryoichi Sasakawa and Yoshio Kodama; it handled the church's political work in Japan. A 1975 FBI report named Kishi and Sasakawa as heads of its Japanese branch. The church built its Tokyo headquarters next to Kishi's former residence in Shibuya, and Kishi gave speeches to followers there in 1970, 1971 and 1973. These ties came back into view after Abe's killing in 2022.
cases.cite: The Diplomat, July 2022 (citing 1975 FBI report); Tansa investigative series 'The True Mother Files' (citing Kishi's memoirs and Arita 2024)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An ex-PM openly helped found the church's political arm; nothing shows the church inside his government.

cases.n: Shinto lobby's Diet league counted 16 of 19 Abe cabinet members
cases.org_note: New key: Shinto Seiji Renmei (Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership), the political arm of the Association of Shinto Shrines; works closely with Nippon Kaigi.
cases.d: Shinto Seiji Renmei, the political arm of Japan's Shinto shrine association, had most of Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's cabinet in its league of supporters in the Diet, Japan's parliament. The league is made up of Diet members who back the shrine association's aims. Researcher Ernils Larsson of Uppsala University reported in December 2014 that 296 Diet members were listed supporters of the league, including 16 of the 19 members of Abe's cabinet at the time. He also wrote that a majority of cabinet ministers belonged to Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby. Membership of the league was listed, not secret.
cases.cite: Ernils Larsson, 'Abe's cabinet reshuffle reflects growing influence of the religious right', East Asia Forum, 3 December 2014
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Openly listed membership of a supporters' league; no steering of decisions shown.

cases.n: Australia expels donor Huang Xiangmo over foreign interference
cases.rank: major donor to both main parties
cases.d: Huang Xiangmo, a property developer, gave about AU$2 million with associates to Australia's Labor Party and over AU$1 million to the Liberal Party, while chairing groups linked to the United Front, the Chinese Communist Party's network for building influence abroad. In February 2019 the Australian government cancelled his permanent residency and rejected his citizenship application. ASIO, Australia's domestic intelligence agency, judged him 'amenable to conducting acts of foreign interference', citing his roles chairing the Australian Council for the Promotion of Peaceful Reunification of China (2014-17) and the Oceanic Alliance of the Promotion of Peaceful Reunification of China.
cases.cite: Australian Department of Home Affairs decision on ASIO advice, February 2019 (The Diplomat)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open donations and an expulsion; no official shown acting for him.

cases.n: Banned donor Huang Xiangmo's $100,000 cash hidden in NSW Labor funds
cases.rank: state parliament member and party head office
cases.d: Huang Xiangmo, a property developer barred from donating in New South Wales, supplied $100,000 in cash delivered to NSW Labor's offices in 2015, disguised as donations from restaurant staff at a Chinese Friends of Labor dinner. The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), the state's anti-corruption body, reported this on 28 February 2022. ICAC found former NSW Labor MP Ernest Wong engaged in corrupt conduct by concealing illegal donations and trying to get a donor to give false testimony. ICAC made no finding about the United Front, the Chinese Communist Party's influence network abroad; the link is through Huang's roles chairing a reunification council linked to it.
cases.cite: NSW ICAC, Operation Aero report, 28 February 2022 (AAP)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A banned donor's cash hidden in party funds; the story is illegal party donations, not someone placed inside an institution.

cases.n: Melbourne community leader first convicted of foreign interference
cases.rank: acting federal immigration and multicultural affairs minister (target)
cases.d: Di Sanh Duong, a Melbourne community leader, prepared to use his standing to reach Alan Tudge, then Australia's acting immigration minister, on behalf of China, a jury found. The Crown said he used roles in groups such as the Oceania Federation of Chinese Organisations for Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos, and hid links to the United Front Work Department (the Chinese Communist Party's influence body), the Ministry of State Security (China's spy agency) and the Chinese consulate. On 19 December 2023 a County Court of Victoria jury found him guilty of preparing a foreign interference offence, the first conviction under Australia's 2018 law. He was sentenced on 29 February 2024 to 2 years 9 months.
cases.cite: Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions case report; County Court of Victoria, verdict 19 December 2023, sentence 29 February 2024
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An outside attempt to reach a minister; no one inside was recruited.

cases.n: Taiwan ex-official Chang Hsien-yao indicted for Beijing election plan
cases.org_note: Prosecutors say Chang met Wang Huning, chairman of the CPPCC National Committee, the top body of China's united front system; the indictment speaks of 'sources of infiltration'. Country field: canonical list has no Taiwan entry — caller should decide placement.
cases.rank: former legislator; former deputy head of the Mainland Affairs Council (2013–14)
cases.d: Taiwanese prosecutors allege that Chang Hsien-yao, a former People First Party legislator for Kaohsiung (2005-08) and special deputy head of the Mainland Affairs Council, Taiwan's agency for policy on China, worked on Beijing's instructions in the 2024 presidential election. They say that from June 2023 he took instructions from people linked to the Chinese government to promote Terry Gou's presidential bid, gave Chinese officials a document on the election on 6 September 2023, and met senior Chinese leader Wang Huning in Beijing on 11 September 2023 to confirm the plan. He was indicted on 12 February 2025 under Article 4 of the Anti-Infiltration Act and the presidential election law.
cases.cite: Taiwan prosecutors' indictment, 12 February 2025 (Central News Agency)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A former official acting in an election campaign, not inside a government body.

cases.n: Taiwan's Gong He Party leader jailed for Beijing-funded campaigns
cases.org_note: Funding came through officials of the Putian Taiwan Affairs Office in Fujian; the court called it 'united front' activity. Country field: canonical list has no Taiwan entry — caller should decide placement.
cases.rank: registered political party and its 2022 local-election candidates
cases.d: Money from Fujian, the Chinese province facing Taiwan, funded the Gong He Party's November 2022 election campaigns in Taiwan, prosecutors said, including a Taipei mayoral candidate who got 316 votes. Taiwan's Ministry of Justice indicted party chairman Chou Ke-chi and Taipei Puxian Association board members Pan Jindong and Chu Chun-yuan on 9 August 2023 under the Anti-Infiltration Act, which bars taking money or instructions from China for political activity. In late June 2025 the Taipei District Court sentenced Chou to two years, Pan to 18 months and Chu to one year, finding they took Beijing funds for united front activity, the Chinese Communist Party's work to build influence abroad. The sentences can be appealed.
cases.cite: Taipei District Court verdict, June 2025 (Taipei Times via ANI); indictment 9 August 2023 (UCA News)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Outside funding of a fringe party's campaigns; no one got inside a government body.

cases.n: Beijing-directed money for a New Taipei council candidate
cases.org_note: Prosecutors allege the Federation of Hong Kong Jiangsu Youth took assignments from the United Front Work Department of the CCP Jiangsu Provincial Committee. Country field: canonical list has no Taiwan entry — caller should decide placement.
cases.d: Prosecutors allege that 100,000 yuan was sent on Beijing's instructions to fund Labor Party candidate Wang Cheng in the 2022 New Taipei City Council election in Taiwan. On 26 February 2024 New Taipei prosecutors indicted Sun Chih-chuan of the Chinese Youth Development Union and a Chinese woman surnamed Da, director of the Federation of Hong Kong Jiangsu Youth, under the Anti-Infiltration Act and the Political Donations Act. They say the money moved via a US$10,000 transfer from Da's Hong Kong account, and that Wang received NT$435,000. Both defendants deny ties to Beijing.
cases.cite: New Taipei District Prosecutors Office indictment, 26 February 2024 (Central News Agency)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Money for a candidate's campaign; the story does not put anyone inside an institution.

cases.n: Taiwan raids pro-China party founded by Bamboo Union gang leader
cases.org_note: Party founded by Chang An-le ('White Wolf'), former Bamboo Union gang leader. Prosecutors were examining China-sourced funding; no united-front finding by a court is recorded here. Country field: canonical list has no Taiwan entry — caller should decide placement.
cases.d: Taiwanese legislators alleged that money from Chinese officials and state-linked firms was moved through the Taolue Group, a company of Chang An-le, to his Chinese Unity Promotion Party, which campaigns for unification with China. Chang is a former leader of the Bamboo Union, a Taiwanese organised crime gang. In August 2018 Taipei prosecutors raided the party's head office and its leaders' homes, citing possible breaches of the National Security Act, the Political Donations Act and the Organized Crime Prevention Act. Chang said the party received money from China but that it came from his company's profits there.
cases.cite: Taipei District Prosecutors Office search operation, August 2018 (Taipei Times)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Outside money for a party's campaigning; the story does not put anyone inside a government body.

cases.n: Anti-communist league's Latin American chair led Argentina's military
cases.rank: army general; chairman, Joint Military Chiefs
cases.d: The World Anti-Communist League, an international network of governments, parties and militant groups set up to fight communism, had its Latin American chairman at the head of Argentina's armed forces. Carlos Guillermo Suárez Mason chaired the league's Latin American chapter while serving as a senior Argentine army general. In 1980 he moved from command of the First Army Corps, which garrisoned Buenos Aires, to chairman of the Joint Military Chiefs, the top command over the armed forces. He also financed and relaunched the far-right magazine Cabildo.
cases.cite: Biographical record of Carlos Guillermo Suárez Mason (academic and press histories of the Argentine dictatorship)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Only shows a general led an open anti-communist network; no decisions served it.

cases.n: P2-listed diplomat Federico Barttfeld removed as under-secretary
cases.d: Federico Carlos Barttfeld is named on the membership lists of P2 (Propaganda Due), a secret Masonic lodge run by Italian businessman Licio Gelli, seized in Italy in March 1981. He went on to serve as Argentina's ambassador to Yugoslavia (1991-95) and China (1998-2001), and later as an under-secretary of state under Néstor Kirchner. He was relieved of his functions in 2003 over alleged involvement in the Dirty War, the military regime's campaign of kidnapping and killing of opponents.
cases.cite: P2 membership lists seized at Castiglion Fibocchi, March 1981, published by the Italian government May 1981; Italian Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the P2 Lodge (Anselmi Commission), 1984

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Listed as a P2 member but served in later decades; nothing ties P2 to his posts or his removal.

cases.n: Opus Dei member Joaquín Lavín as Chile's education minister
cases.rank: minister of education; minister of social development
cases.d: Joaquín Lavín, a supernumerary member of Opus Dei, served as a Chilean government minister twice under President Sebastián Piñera. Opus Dei is a Catholic organisation of priests and lay members that encourages its members to carry their faith into their professional and public lives. A supernumerary is a member who lives an ordinary family life while following the group's rules. Lavín was minister of education from 11 March 2010 to 18 July 2011, in charge of the country's school system, and minister of social development from October 2011 to June 2013.
cases.cite: Biographical record; press reporting
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Opus Dei membership of a minister only; no steering shown.

cases.n: Opus Dei numerary Rafael Rey as Peru's production and defence minister
cases.rank: minister of production; minister of defence
cases.d: Rafael Rey, a numerary member of Opus Dei, held two cabinet posts in Peru under President Alan García. Opus Dei is a Catholic organisation of priests and lay members that encourages its members to carry their faith into their professional and public lives. A numerary is a celibate member who commits fully to the organisation, usually living in its centres. Rey was minister of production from 28 July 2006 to 14 October 2008 and minister of defence, in charge of the armed forces, from 11 July 2009 to 14 September 2010.
cases.cite: Biographical record; press reporting
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Opus Dei membership of a minister only; no steering shown.

cases.n: BCCI paid off the mortgage of Panama's future president Barletta
cases.d: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), a bank later closed worldwide for fraud, paid off the mortgage of Nicolás Ardito Barletta on the instructions of General Manuel Noriega, Panama's military ruler, the US Senate's 1992 BCCI report found. Barletta was Noriega's chosen presidential candidate and became president of Panama in 1984. The payment put BCCI money behind the man Noriega placed at the head of government, while BCCI was also handling Noriega's own accounts.
cases.cite: US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry-Brown report), Dec 1992, ch. 5

arch.t: Bank of Credit and Commerce International — Abedi and Iqbal: BCCI Was the Largest Bank Fraud in History; CIA Used It for Covert Operations; 62 Countries Affected

cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): BCCI paid a candidate's mortgage on Noriega's orders; no decision shown serving BCCI.

cases.n: World Anti-Communist League leader as Guatemala's vice-president
cases.d: Mario Sandoval Alarcón, a leader of the World Anti-Communist League (WACL), was vice-president of Guatemala from 1 July 1974 to 1 July 1978. The WACL was an international network of right-wing parties, governments and militants that pushed anti-communist policy in member countries. Sandoval had founded Guatemala's National Liberation Movement (MLN) in 1960. Historians link the MLN to killings by the Mano Blanca death squad.
cases.cite: Academic histories of WACL and Guatemala
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Leadership of an open network by a vice-president; no steering shown.

cases.n: Scientology took files from the Justice Department and prosecutors
cases.rank: Department of Justice and U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C.
cases.d: Under Operation Snow White, the Church of Scientology's Guardian's Office broke into or copied documents from the US Justice Department and from the office of Assistant U.S. Attorney Nathan Dodell, a federal prosecutor handling Scientology litigation. Documents were also taken from the D.C. Metropolitan Police, the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Treasury. The aim was to see what the government knew about the church. Mary Sue Hubbard, wife of founder L. Ron Hubbard and head of the Guardian's Office, was sentenced to five years and a $10,000 fine. Jane Kember and Mo Budlong were convicted at trial in 1980 after fighting extradition from the UK.
cases.cite: United States v. Mary Sue Hubbard et al., U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, 1979; Kember and Budlong convicted 1980

arch.t: Scientology — Operation Snow White: Church Infiltrated 136 Government Agencies in 30 Countries; 11 Senior Officials Including Founder's Wife Convicted of Federal Crimes (PROVEN)

cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Break-ins and copying from outside; the record does not show members placed in these offices.

cases.n: The Fellowship housed members of Congress at its C Street townhouse
cases.d: The Fellowship, also called the Family, a private Christian network that runs the National Prayer Breakfast in Washington, gave members of Congress subsidised lodging. A group affiliated with it owns a townhouse on C Street where lawmakers lived for about $950 a month including housekeeping. Mother Jones named eight residents: Senators Sam Brownback, Tom Coburn, Jim DeMint and John Ensign, and Representatives Mike Doyle, Heath Shuler, Bart Stupak and Zach Wamp. Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a watchdog group, filed ethics complaints arguing that the lodging was an undeclared gift that broke House and Senate rules, and the Office of Congressional Ethics reviewed it in 2010.
cases.cite: Mother Jones reporting (2010); CREW ethics complaints; Office of Congressional Ethics review reported by Roll Call, June 2010
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Subsidised lodging for lawmakers; no decision shown serving the Fellowship.

cases.n: Russian agent Maria Butina worked her way into US political circles
cases.rank: National Prayer Breakfast (event attended by the sitting president)
cases.d: Maria Butina, working under Russian official Alexander Torshin, built back channels for Russia into Republican circles in the United States. She worked through the National Rifle Association (NRA) and helped arrange for Russians to attend the February 2017 National Prayer Breakfast, an event run by the religious network the Fellowship and attended by the president. A planned private meeting between Torshin and President Trump was cancelled after a national security aide flagged him. Butina pleaded guilty on 13 December 2018 to conspiracy to act as an agent of a foreign government and was sentenced on 26 April 2019 to 18 months. The FBI interviewed Fellowship organiser Doug Burleigh about his ties to her.
cases.cite: United States v. Maria Butina, U.S. District Court for D.C., plea 13 Dec 2018, sentence 26 Apr 2019
cases.org_note: The Fellowship was the host of the event she used, not the agent; the vehicle was a Russian state-directed network.
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Networking from outside via the NRA and an event; no official recruited inside.

cases.n: Skull and Bones member George H. W. Bush as CIA director and president
cases.rank: Director of Central Intelligence; later President
cases.d: Skull and Bones, a secret society at Yale University that picks 15 students a year, has had its members in top US government posts. One of them, George H. W. Bush (Skull and Bones 1948), served as the 11th Director of Central Intelligence, head of the CIA, in 1976–77 and as the 41st President in 1989–93. His father, Prescott Bush (Bones 1917), was a US Senator from Connecticut. Membership comes from published Skull and Bones rosters; no forum has found the society directed his official acts.
cases.cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official CIA and White House records of office

arch.t: Skull and Bones — Systematic CIA / Government Placement Network

cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Society membership only; the record says no forum found the society directed his acts.

cases.n: Both 2004 US presidential nominees were Skull and Bones members
cases.rank: President (George W. Bush) and Secretary of State (John Kerry)
cases.d: Skull and Bones, a secret society at Yale University that picks 15 students a year, has had its members fill top US government posts, and in 2004 both major-party presidential nominees came from it: George W. Bush (Bones 1968) and John Kerry (Bones 1966). Bush served as the 43rd President; Kerry later became the 68th Secretary of State (2013–17), the government's chief diplomat. Both confirmed their membership publicly while declining to discuss the society.
cases.cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official records of office
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Society membership only; nothing shows the society steered them.

cases.n: Skull and Bones member Stimson ran the War and State departments
cases.rank: Secretary of War (twice) and Secretary of State
cases.d: Two members of Skull and Bones, a secret society at Yale University that picks 15 students a year, ran the US War Department together during the Second World War. Henry L. Stimson (Bones 1888) was Secretary of War under Roosevelt and Truman from 1940 to 1945, having earlier been Secretary of War under Taft and Secretary of State under Hoover. Robert A. Lovett (Bones 1918) worked under him as Assistant Secretary of War for Air and later became Secretary of Defense. Other members of the society have also gone on to fill top US government posts. The link rests on published membership rosters set against official records of office.
cases.cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official records of office
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Society membership only; nothing shows the society steered them.

cases.n: Skull and Bones members in US national security posts
cases.d: Skull and Bones, a secret society at Yale University that picks 15 students a year, had its members in top US national-security posts. McGeorge Bundy (Bones 1940) was National Security Adviser, the president's chief aide on defence and foreign policy, to Presidents Kennedy and Johnson from 1961 to 1966. Other Bonesmen in national security posts include CIA officers Charles S. Whitehouse (1947) and William Sloane Coffin (1949), and F. Trubee Davison (1918), the CIA's Director of Personnel, who oversaw hiring. The record comes from published membership rosters and official records of office; it shows members in posts, not decisions taken for the society.
cases.cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official records of office
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Society membership only; the record says it shows posts, not decisions for the society.

cases.n: Skull and Bones member Steven Mnuchin as Treasury Secretary
cases.d: Skull and Bones, a secret society at Yale University, had one of its members, Steven Mnuchin (Bones 1985), at the head of the US Treasury, the department in charge of US government finances. Skull and Bones picks 15 students a year, and its members have gone on to fill top US government posts. Mnuchin served as the 77th Secretary of the Treasury from 2017 to 2021. An earlier member, Franklin MacVeagh (Bones 1862), held the same post under President Taft.
cases.cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official records of office
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Society membership only; nothing shows the society steered the Treasury.

cases.n: Trilateral Commission members Carter, Mondale and 19 others in office
cases.d: Members of the Trilateral Commission, a private policy network of business, political and academic figures from North America, Western Europe and Japan, took the top posts in Jimmy Carter's administration. Banker David Rockefeller founded the commission in July 1973, with Zbigniew Brzezinski as organiser. Carter and Walter Mondale were members before taking office as President and Vice President in 1977. Brzezinski and Harold Brown also served in the administration, and the Christian Science Monitor reported in 1980 that 17 other former commission members did too.
cases.cite: Christian Science Monitor, 'The trilateral controversy', 17 Apr 1980; Trilateral Commission membership lists

arch.t: Trilateral Commission — 19/20 Carter Senior Appointments Were Members

cases.n: Trilateral members Brzezinski, Vance and Brown in Carter cabinet
cases.rank: National Security Adviser, Secretary of State, Secretary of Defense
cases.d: Three members of the Trilateral Commission, a private policy network founded by David Rockefeller, took the top foreign and defence posts under President Jimmy Carter. Zbigniew Brzezinski, the commission's founding director, became National Security Adviser. Cyrus Vance became Secretary of State, and Harold Brown became Secretary of Defense. The appointments were raised during the 1980 campaign as evidence of the commission's reach.
cases.cite: Christian Science Monitor, 17 Apr 1980; Trilateral Commission membership lists

cases.n: Gülen movement groups paid for about 200 congressional trips
cases.rank: Members of Congress and their staff
cases.d: Groups tied to the movement of Turkish cleric Fethullah Gülen paid for about 200 trips to Turkey for members of the US Congress and their staff since 2008, a USA Today investigation found. It identified 214 trips that appeared improperly disclosed, meaning Congress was not told who really paid. Some sponsors claimed nonprofit status that state and IRS records did not show, and five admitted a Gülen group in Turkey paid in-country costs. In July 2015 the House Ethics Committee, reviewing a related trip, found outside parties may have lied to it and referred the matter to the Justice Department.
cases.cite: USA Today investigation, October 2015; House Committee on Ethics review, July 2015
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Paid congressional trips, improperly disclosed; no decision shown serving the movement.

cases.n: Gülen-linked charter school staff gave clustered campaign donations
cases.d: USA Today found clusters of campaign donations to members of the US Congress from Turkish Americans linked to the US charter schools of the movement of cleric Fethullah Gülen, which number over 100. Charter schools are publicly funded but privately run. The pattern suggested money was being channelled through individuals. Sen. Kelly Ayotte refunded $43,100 given on a single day by 19 out-of-state donors, five of whom could not be located. Rep. Henry Cuellar received nine $2,500 donations on one day, including one from a Toledo charter school teacher earning about $37,000 a year.
cases.cite: USA Today investigation, November 2015 (via Religion News Service)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Clustered campaign donations; no one inside and no decision shown.

cases.n: Han Dong's 2019 nomination and suspected Chinese consulate role
cases.d: China's consulate in Toronto was suspected of helping steer the 2019 Liberal nomination of Han Dong in the Toronto riding of Don Valley North. Canada's Special Rapporteur David Johnston found 'irregularities' in the nomination and a 'well-grounded suspicion' that they were tied to the consulate of the People's Republic of China, but no evidence Dong knew. Intelligence said international students were bused to the vote; Dong said a school arranged the bus. Dong left the Liberal caucus in March 2023. Johnston found false the claim that Dong urged China to delay freeing Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor; the Hogue Commission report corroborated Dong's denial, and in August 2025 the Commissioner of Canada Elections found no breach of election law in the nomination.
cases.cite: Independent Special Rapporteur on Foreign Interference (Johnston), first report, May 2023; Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference (Hogue Commission), 2024–25; Commissioner of Canada Elections, Aug 2025
cases.org_note: prc_state = PRC government officials or intelligence acting through local proxies, where the forum did not name the United Front Work Department
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Even as alleged, the consulate acted on a party nomination from outside, and the record says the MP did not know.

cases.n: Klan member Hugo Black reached the Supreme Court undisclosed
cases.rank: Associate Justice of the U.S. Supreme Court
cases.d: The Ku Klux Klan, a white-supremacist secret order, had a life member reach the US Supreme Court without the public knowing. Hugo Black joined the Klan in September 1923, resigned in July 1925 as he began his Senate run, and was welcomed back with a life membership in September 1926 during the campaign. The membership was not public when he was confirmed to the Court in 1937. Weeks later Ray Sprigle of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette exposed it and won a Pulitzer Prize. In a radio address on 1 October 1937 Black said: 'I did join the Klan. I later resigned. I never rejoined.' He served on the Court until 1971.
cases.cite: Pittsburgh Post-Gazette (Ray Sprigle), Sept 1937; Black's radio address, 1 Oct 1937

cases.n: Klan chapter leader Robert Byrd entered office and the Senate
cases.rank: U.S. Senator (West Virginia); West Virginia House of Delegates
cases.d: Robert Byrd organised and led a 150-member Ku Klux Klan chapter in West Virginia in the early 1940s as its 'Exalted Cyclops', the chapter head, and was a recruiter ('Kleagle') until early 1943. A 1946 letter shows his continued involvement in the year he was elected to the West Virginia House of Delegates. He went on to the U.S. House in 1952 and the Senate in 1958, and when he died in 2010 he had served in the Senate longer than anyone. He called the membership a 'sad mistake'.
cases.cite: Byrd's own statements and 2005 memoir; PolitiFact review of the record, 2019

cases.n: Oregon Klan backed Governor Pierce in return for its school law
cases.d: In 1922 the Ku Klux Klan in Oregon backed Democrat Walter M. Pierce for governor after its own candidate lost the Republican primary. In return Pierce agreed to support the Klan's Compulsory Education Act, and he won with 57% of the vote. The act, passed by voters the same year, would have forced children into public schools and was aimed at Catholic schools. The U.S. Supreme Court struck it down in Pierce v. Society of Sisters (1925).
cases.cite: Oregon election records, 1922; Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U.S. 510 (1925)
cases.org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (secret fraternal order with state-office reach in the 1920s)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An open electoral bargain with a non-member candidate; the law went to voters.

cases.n: Klan members inside Fruitland Park, Florida police
cases.rank: Deputy police chief and police officer
cases.d: Deputy Chief David Borst and Officer George Hunnewell of the police department in Fruitland Park, Florida, had been involved with the Ku Klux Klan between 2005 and 2009, an unrelated FBI investigation found; three informants linked Hunnewell. The FBI told the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, which informed the police chief in 2014. Borst resigned and Hunnewell was fired. The Lake County State Attorney's office, which prosecutes cases in the county, began reviewing their arrests for racial profiling, meaning targeting people because of their race.
cases.cite: Florida Department of Law Enforcement report based on FBI information, July 2014

cases.n: FBI warned white supremacists were placing 'ghost skins' in police
cases.d: An October 2006 FBI intelligence assessment warned that white supremacist groups had a 'historical' interest in infiltrating or recruiting police, and that this 'can lead to investigative breaches', such as leaks about inquiries. It described 'ghost skins', members who hide their beliefs to blend in, and at least one skinhead group urging them to seek police jobs. An April 2015 FBI counterterrorism policy guide said investigations of militia, white supremacist and sovereign citizen extremists had often found active links to law enforcement officers.
cases.cite: FBI Intelligence Assessment, 'White Supremacist Infiltration of Law Enforcement', 17 Oct 2006; FBI Counterterrorism Policy Guide, April 2015 (published by The Intercept, 2017)
cases.org_note: white_supremacist = organised white supremacist groups (Klan, skinhead and similar), as named by the FBI
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A general FBI warning; does not say who got inside which institution.

cases.n: Commons committee urged Freemasons in police and courts to register
cases.rank: judges, magistrates, police officers, Crown prosecutors
cases.d: Freemasons hold posts across the police and courts of England and Wales, and in March 1997 the House of Commons Home Affairs Committee published 'Freemasonry in the Police and the Judiciary'. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet in private lodges. The report counted nearly 350,000 masons in 7,835 lodges in England and Wales under the United Grand Lodge of England. It recommended that police officers, judges, magistrates and Crown prosecutors register membership of the Freemasons or any other secret society, stating that 'nothing so much undermines public confidence in public institutions' as public servants belonging to one. The Association of Chief Police Officers refused to back a register; Lord Chancellor Lord Mackay opposed compulsory disclosure for judges.
cases.cite: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee, 'Freemasonry in the Police and the Judiciary', Third Report 1996–97 (March 1997)

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

cases.n: Freemasons among judges; Grand Lodge stalled on police squad list
cases.rank: detectives of the West Midlands Serious Crime Squad
cases.d: Freemasons made up an estimated 5–10% of professional judges and 5–20% of magistrates in England and Wales, the House of Commons Home Affairs Committee said in its second report on Freemasonry (May 1999). Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges and swear oaths of mutual support. The Committee said it obtained the cooperation of the United Grand Lodge of England, the masons' governing body, only 'through compulsion' after 'months of prevarication and obfuscation'. The Grand Lodge needed five attempts to produce a list of masons in the West Midlands Serious Crime Squad, a police unit disbanded in 1989, and the Committee doubted the final list was complete. It called the government's voluntary police register inadequate.
cases.cite: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee, Freemasonry in Public Life, Second Report 1998–99 (May 1999), as reported by SQUALL magazine

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Membership estimates and disclosure disputes; no steering shown.

cases.n: 205 judges and 1,900 magistrates were masons when declaration ended
cases.d: Freemasons, members of a fraternal society organised in lodges whose members pledge mutual help, held 205 of the 3,808 judges' posts in England and Wales (5.4%) and 1,900 of the 29,702 magistrates' posts (6.4%), Ministry of Justice figures showed in 2009. Since 1998 applicants for judicial office had had to declare Masonic membership. The United Grand Lodge of England made representations against the rule in May 2009, citing the European Court of Human Rights cases Grande Oriente d'Italia di Palazzo Giustiniani v Italy (no. 1 and no. 2), and on 5 November 2009 Justice Secretary Jack Straw ended it. The review found no evidence of impropriety arising from judges being masons.
cases.cite: Written ministerial statement, Secretary of State for Justice, 5 November 2009
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Membership figures; the review found no impropriety.

cases.n: 397 Met Police officers and staff declare they are Freemasons
cases.d: Freemasons hold posts inside London's Metropolitan Police: 397 officers and staff declared membership of the Freemasons or similar hierarchical organisations by February 2026, once the force required it. The Met decided on 18 November 2025, and announced on 11 December 2025, that such membership would be a declarable association for its officers and staff; most of those who declared were Freemasons. The United Grand Lodge of England, the governing body of English Freemasonry, sought judicial review, a court challenge to the decision. On 17 February 2026 Mr Justice Chamberlain refused permission on all grounds, finding the requirement a proportionate way to maintain public trust in policing.
cases.cite: R (United Grand Lodge of England) v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis [2026] EWHC 330 (Admin); Judiciary press summary, 17 February 2026
