cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Membership declarations only; no steering shown.

cases.n: China's Communist Party reached the royal circle through Yang Tengbo
cases.rank: Duke of York (member of the royal family)
cases.d: The Chinese Communist Party reached into the British royal circle through businessman Yang Tengbo, the UK Home Office concluded. The Home Office believed he may have worked for the United Front Work Department, the party body that builds influence abroad. Through Prince Andrew he had been a guest at royal residences, and he had met former prime ministers David Cameron and Theresa May. In March 2023 Home Secretary Suella Braverman barred him from the UK for 'covert and deceptive activity' on behalf of the party. In December 2024 the Special Immigration Appeals Commission upheld the exclusion; its judges said there was 'not an abundance of evidence' of United Front links but found he had played down his ties to the party.
cases.cite: Home Office exclusion order, March 2023; Special Immigration Appeals Commission judgment, December 2024
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Access to the royal circle, not a government body; no one placed inside.

cases.n: Le Cercle chaired by MPs sitting on the Foreign Affairs Committee
cases.rank: members of the Commons Foreign Affairs Committee
cases.d: Two MPs sitting on the House of Commons Foreign Affairs Select Committee, which scrutinises UK foreign policy, chaired Le Cercle, a private foreign-policy club, without declaring the role to Parliament, PoliticsHome reported in 2019. They were Rory Stewart (chair 2013–14) and Nadhim Zahawi (2015–18). Le Cercle, founded in 1952–53, brings politicians, intelligence figures and business people together in private. Its earlier UK chairs were also sitting politicians: Julian Amery (1985–93), Jonathan Aitken (1993–96), Norman Lamont (1996–2008) and Michael Ancram (2008–13). Because the chairmanships were not declared, MPs examining government foreign policy held a leading role in a private network that Parliament and the public did not know about.
cases.cite: PoliticsHome (John Johnston), 2019; David Teacher, Rogue Agents: The Cercle and the 6I in the Private Cold War (2003)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Undeclared chairmanship of a private club; no steering shown.

cases.n: Knights of St Columbanus members in Costello's Irish cabinet
cases.org_note: Knights of Saint Columbanus: Catholic fraternal order founded in Ireland in 1915, long described as secretive.
cases.d: Members of the Knights of Saint Columbanus, a Catholic fraternal order founded in Ireland in 1915 and long described as secretive, sat in Ireland's government from 1948. John A. Costello, Taoiseach (prime minister) of the first Inter-Party government from 1948, was a Knight, as were other members of his cabinet; that government gave Maynooth seminary a special annual grant. Labour parliamentary chairman William Davin TD, also a Knight, is reported to have countered support within government for the Mother and Child health scheme, a plan for free state care of mothers and children that Archbishop John Charles McQuaid opposed. These accounts rest chiefly on John Cooney's biography of McQuaid (1999) and Anthony Jordan's biography of Costello (2007).
cases.cite: John Cooney, John Charles McQuaid: Ruler of Catholic Ireland (1999); Anthony Jordan, John A. Costello 1891–1976 (2007)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Order members in cabinet; the policy link shown runs to the archbishop, not the order.

cases.n: Manuel Valls, later Prime Minister, was a Grand Orient lodge member
cases.rank: mayor of Évry and National Assembly deputy (later Interior Minister and Prime Minister)
cases.d: Manuel Valls belonged to the Grand Orient de France, the country's largest Masonic body, while he rose into elected office. According to L'Express, he was initiated into the Grand Orient lodge 'Ni maîtres ni dieux' on 26 April 1989, moved in 1995 to 'L'Infini maçonnique', a lodge founded by Alain Bauer, and his resignation was recorded in 2005. During that period he became mayor of Évry (2001) and a National Assembly deputy (2002). After leaving he served as Interior Minister (2012) and Prime Minister (2014). Valls declined to answer L'Express's questions.
cases.cite: L'Express, reproduced by Seneweb
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Lodge membership of a politician only; no steering shown.

cases.n: British intelligence worked closely with Swiss secret army P-26
cases.d: British intelligence services worked closely with P-26, a secret Swiss resistance organisation inside the Swiss defence department that operated outside parliamentary and government control until 1990, although Switzerland is officially neutral and outside NATO. Judge Pierre Cornu's official report, of roughly 100 pages, found this extensive cooperation and also found that P-26 lacked political or legal legitimacy. Only a 17-page summary, titled 'P-26 not part of an international network', was published on 19 September 1991. Defence Minister Kaspar Villiger refused to release the full report, which remains sealed until 2041 despite parliamentary motions in 2005 and 2008, so the extent of British involvement is still not public.
cases.cite: Report of Judge Pierre Cornu to the Federal Council, 1991 (summary published 19 September 1991)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Cooperation with a Swiss body; the record does not show British people or control inside.

cases.n: Thule Society members Hess and Frank rose into the Nazi government
cases.rank: Deputy Führer (Hess); Reich minister and later Governor-General of occupied Poland (Frank)
cases.d: The Thule Society, a German nationalist and occultist lodge formed in Munich in 1918 around Rudolf von Sebottendorff's lodge, had members who later held top posts in Nazi Germany. Historian Nicholas Goodrick-Clarke states that Rudolf Hess and Hans Frank were members before they rose in the Nazi Party, while Alfred Rosenberg, Dietrich Eckart and Gottfried Feder attended only as guests. He calls longer membership lists that include Hitler and others 'spurious'. Hess became Deputy Führer, Hitler's deputy as party leader, in 1933; Frank became a Reich minister and, from 1939, Governor-General of occupied Poland.
cases.cite: Nicholas Goodrick-Clarke, The Occult Roots of Nazism (1985, later editions)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Lodge membership before rising in the Nazi party; no lodge steering shown.

cases.n: Sweden's secret IB spy bureau reported to the ruling party
cases.org_note: Informationsbyrån (IB): Swedish military intelligence unit with no official status, which registered and infiltrated the far left; directed by Birger Elmér.
cases.rank: military intelligence; Prime Minister and Social Democratic party secretary
cases.d: IB, a secret Swedish military intelligence bureau with no official status, was reported to answer to leaders of the governing Social Democratic Party as well as to the military. On 3 May 1973 journalists Jan Guillou and Peter Bratt revealed in Folket i Bild/Kulturfront that IB monitored and registered people with far-left views and infiltrated left-wing groups, including break-ins at the Communist Party's offices. Former security chief P.G. Vinge wrote that IB director Birger Elmér had regular contact with Prime Minister Olof Palme and reported to Social Democratic party secretary Sven Andersson; Palme denied any link. The journalists, not IB staff, were convicted of espionage on 4 January 1974. A 2002 public inquiry report, 'Rikets säkerhet och den personliga integriteten', set out IB's operations.
cases.cite: Swedish court verdict, 4 January 1974; Swedish government inquiry report 'Rikets säkerhet och den personliga integriteten' (2002)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): The ruling party and a state bureau reporting to its leaders, not an outside party getting inside.

cases.n: Ordo Iuris founder made Polish deputy foreign minister
cases.org_note: Ordo Iuris Institute for Legal Culture: Polish Catholic-conservative legal think tank founded in 2013 by the Christian Culture Association.
cases.d: Ordo Iuris, a Polish conservative Catholic legal think tank that drafts laws and campaigns to change policy, had its founder placed in government. Aleksander Stępkowski co-founded Ordo Iuris in 2013 and chaired its management board from 2013 to 2015. In November 2015 the new Law and Justice government of Beata Szydło appointed him deputy foreign minister for legal and treaty affairs, responsible for international agreements; he left the Ordo Iuris chair in December 2015. He was recalled in August 2016. In 2016 Ordo Iuris drafted a near-total abortion ban that the Sejm rejected on 6 October 2016 after nationwide protests.
cases.cite: Polish government appointment records; Forsal; Ruleoflaw.pl
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A think-tank founder took a post, but no decision he made served it; its bill was rejected.

cases.n: Ordo Iuris co-founder made acting head of Polish Supreme Court
cases.org_note: Ordo Iuris Institute for Legal Culture: Polish Catholic-conservative legal think tank founded in 2013.
cases.rank: acting First President of the Supreme Court
cases.d: Ordo Iuris, a Polish conservative Catholic legal think tank that campaigns to change law and policy, had its co-founder placed at the head of the country's highest court. Aleksander Stępkowski, Ordo Iuris co-founder and board president in 2013–2015 and 2016–2017, was nominated to the Supreme Court in 2018 by the reconstituted National Council of the Judiciary, the body that selects judges, whose overhaul by the Law and Justice government was contested. He was appointed in February 2019 with no prior judicial experience. On 15 May 2020, after Kamil Zaradkiewicz resigned, President Andrzej Duda entrusted him with the duties of acting First President of the Supreme Court.
cases.cite: Presidential decision of 15 May 2020; Ruleoflaw.pl
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Co-founder of a think tank appointed to the court by the government; nothing shows the think tank placed him or steered rulings.

cases.n: Secret Masonic lodge's leader became Russia's Prime Minister
cases.org_note: Lodge: Grand Orient of Russia's Peoples, an irregular Masonic body formed from Grand Orient de France lodges and openly separate from 1912.
cases.rank: Minister of Justice, Minister of War, then Prime Minister
cases.d: The Grand Orient of Russia's Peoples, a secret Masonic organisation, had its own leader at the head of Russia's government in 1917. Alexander Kerensky was its Secretary General from 1916 to mid-1917, succeeding Nikolai Nekrasov, who held the post in 1912–13 and 1914–16. After the February Revolution ended Tsarist rule, Kerensky served in the Provisional Government as Minister of Justice (March 1917), Minister for War (May) and Prime Minister (July). Historians describe most of the lodge's members as associated with the Provisional Government. The Bolsheviks overthrew that government in October 1917.
cases.cite: Academic histories of the Russian Revolution (Alpha History summary; Grand Orient of Russia's Peoples records as published by historians)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Shows lodge leaders held office but nothing showing the lodge steered decisions through them.

cases.n: P2 member Calvi convicted but kept control of Banco Ambrosiano
cases.d: Roberto Calvi, chairman of Banco Ambrosiano and a member of the secret P2 Masonic lodge, stayed in charge of the bank even after a criminal conviction. In 1981, months after his name appeared on the P2 membership list seized by police, Calvi was sentenced to four years (suspended) and fined US$19.8 million for moving US$27 million out of Italy illegally, in breach of Italy's currency-export rules. He was released pending appeal and kept his post as chairman of Banco Ambrosiano. The following year the bank collapsed with about US$1.3 billion unaccounted for, and P2 head Licio Gelli was later convicted of fraud over it.
cases.cite: Milan court, 1981 currency-export verdict

cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Calvi's own currency crime and staying in post; the lodge's role is incidental and covered by the Ambrosiano collapse case.

cases.n: P2 list brings down Prime Minister Forlani's government
cases.d: The secret P2 Masonic lodge had members close to Italy's Prime Minister, and the discovery of its membership list in 1981 ended his government. Prime Minister Arnaldo Forlani's chef de cabinet (chief of staff) was on the list, and Forlani was accused of delaying its publication. Justice Minister Adolfo Sarti, listed as a candidate for membership, resigned first; Forlani handed his resignation to President Sandro Pertini three days later, in May 1981, bringing down his government. The list also named ministers, members of parliament, military officers and the heads of the intelligence services.
cases.cite: Resignation of the Forlani government, May 1981; Time, 8 June 1981

cases.n: Former military intelligence (SID) chief Vito Miceli on P2 list
cases.d: The secret P2 Masonic lodge counted a former head of Italy's military intelligence among its members. General Vito Miceli led army counter-intelligence (SIOS) in 1969–70 and the SID, Italy's main intelligence service at the time, from 1970 to 1974, and appears on the P2 list (file 491). Padua judges arrested him on 31 October 1974 in the 'Rosa dei Venti' inquiry into a secret military structure suspected of planning a coup; he was acquitted in 1978, and the acquittal was upheld in 1984 and 1985. He sat in parliament as a deputy for the neo-fascist MSI party from 1976 to 1987.
cases.cite: Padua investigation 1974; acquittal 1978, Cassation 1985; P2 list

cases.n: Counter-intelligence chief Gianadelio Maletti on the P2 list
cases.d: The secret P2 Masonic lodge listed the head of Italian military counter-intelligence among its members. General Gianadelio Maletti headed counter-intelligence at the SID, Italy's main intelligence service, from 1971 to 1975 and appears on the P2 list (file 499), though he denied joining. On 23 February 1979 the Catanzaro Court of Assizes sentenced him to 4 years for shielding Guido Giannettini and Marco Pozzan in the case of the 1969 Piazza Fontana bombing in Milan; the sentence was cut to 2 years and made final in 1987. He moved to South Africa in 1980.
cases.cite: Catanzaro Court of Assizes, 23 Feb 1979; Bari Appeal Court of Assizes 1987

cases.n: Ex-financial police chief Giudice, P2 member, convicted of fuel fraud
cases.rank: commander-general of the Guardia di Finanza 1974–1978
cases.d: The secret P2 Masonic lodge counted a former commander of Italy's financial police among its members, and he was later convicted in a large tax-evasion case. General Raffaele Giudice commanded the Guardia di Finanza, which polices tax and customs, from 31 July 1974 to 20 November 1978 and appeared on the 1981 P2 list. In the 'oil scandal' (scandalo dei petroli), a scheme to evade taxes on fuel, the Turin Tribunal sentenced him on 30 April 1987 to 3 years 10 months at first instance; his case was separated on appeal.
cases.cite: Turin Tribunal, 30 April 1987 (first instance)

cases.n: P2's reach into the state led to Italy's 1982 ban on secret lodges
cases.d: P2 (Propaganda Due), a secret Masonic lodge, had enrolled members across Italy's government, armed forces and intelligence services, and police seized its membership list in 1981. Parliament responded by outlawing such groups. Law no. 17 of 25 January 1982, known as the 'Anselmi law', dissolved P2 and made illegal secret associations that seek to interfere with public bodies. The Grand Orient of Italy, the main Masonic body, had already withdrawn the lodge's charter in 1974, so P2 had no recognition from regular Freemasonry when the list was found. The same law was used in the 2010s prosecution of the 'P3' group.
cases.cite: Italian Law no. 17 of 25 January 1982

cases.n: P2 conspiracy trial ends with Gelli acquitted
cases.rank: prosecution for conspiracy against the state
cases.d: Rome prosecutors tried to prove in court that P2, the secret Masonic lodge whose members held posts across Italy's state, was a political conspiracy against the state. They charged lodge head Licio Gelli and others with that offence. The Rome court acquitted all defendants on 16 April 1994, and the Rome Court of Appeal confirmed the acquittal on 27 March 1996. Gelli was convicted in other cases, including the Banco Ambrosiano fraud and the cover-up of the Bologna bombing investigation, and the 1982 Anselmi law had already dissolved the lodge.
cases.cite: Rome Court of Assizes 16 April 1994; Rome Court of Appeal 27 March 1996

cases.n: P2 head Licio Gelli: Argentine post, prison escape, conviction
cases.d: Licio Gelli, head of the secret P2 Masonic lodge, had ties inside Argentina's state as well as Italy's: he held an Argentine honorary diplomatic post and is linked to Argentine P2 members Emilio Massera, a navy commander in the military junta, and José López Rega, a government minister. After the lodge was exposed, Gelli was arrested in Geneva in September 1982, escaped Champ-Dollon prison on 10 August 1983 and was extradited to Italy in February 1988. His 12-year sentence for the Banco Ambrosiano fraud was confirmed in April 1998; he vanished in May 1998 and was arrested in Cannes that September.
cases.cite: Court of Cassation, April 1998

cases.n: Andreotti reveals Gladio, a NATO-coordinated secret network
cases.d: Gladio, the Italian branch of the secret 'stay-behind' networks that NATO countries set up to resist a possible Soviet invasion, operated within Italy's intelligence services under NATO coordination and without public knowledge. On 24 October 1990 Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti told the Chamber of Deputies that a secret stay-behind 'structure of information, response and safeguard' had existed since the 1950s under NATO coordination. He gave the parliamentary massacres commission a list of 622 civilians, said 127 arms caches had been dismantled, and denied any role in bombings. On 22 November 1990 the European Parliament called on member states to dismantle such networks, and inquiries followed in Belgium, Switzerland and elsewhere.
cases.cite: Statement to the Chamber of Deputies 24 Oct 1990; European Parliament resolution 22 Nov 1990

cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Italy's own intelligence service ran the network within an alliance arrangement; no outside party shown placing people inside.

cases.n: NATO-linked secret Gladio network inside Italy's intelligence had 622 members
cases.d: A secret armed 'stay-behind' network called Gladio was run inside SISMI, Italy's military intelligence service, under NATO coordination, and was kept from parliament until Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti disclosed it in October 1990. A stay-behind network is a group of trained people meant to resist an occupying army. Parliament's commission on terrorism and massacres then questioned SISMI. On 29 November 1990 General Paolo Inzerilli, SISMI chief of staff, told it that 'the true number is 622': 215 active, 339 reserve, 65 dead and 3 'frozen' members of the network's units.
cases.cite: Parliamentary Commission on Terrorism and Massacres, hearing of 29 Nov 1990

cases.n: Mafia use of lodges: Anti-Mafia Commission seizes lodge lists
cases.d: Mafia groups in Sicily and Calabria were suspected of using Masonic lodges to reach officials and businesses, and Italy's parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission forced the lodges to reveal who belonged. On 1 March 2017 the Commission, chaired by Rosy Bindi, voted unanimously to seize membership lists of lodges in Sicily and Calabria from 1990 onward, after grand masters missed an 8 February deadline citing privacy. The Guardia di Finanza, Italy's financial police, searched the headquarters of the Grand Orient of Italy, the Regular Grand Lodge of Italy, the Serenissima Gran Loggia and the Gran Loggia d'Italia. In 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found the seizure breached Article 8 (the right to privacy); its Grand Chamber upheld that in July 2026.
cases.cite: Parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission decision of 1 March 2017; ECHR, Grande Oriente d'Italia v. Italy
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Describes a parliamentary seizure of lodge lists over suspicion; does not show who got inside what.

cases.n: Anti-Mafia report finds 193 lodge members in mafia cases
cases.d: Italy's parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission found people involved in mafia cases sitting in Masonic lodges in Sicily and Calabria, and proposed keeping judges, soldiers and police out of lodges. Its report on mafia and Freemasonry, presented by chair Rosy Bindi in December 2017 after the lodges' membership lists were seized, found that 193 people listed in lodges were recorded in organised-crime proceedings by the National Anti-Mafia Directorate, the national prosecutors' office for mafia cases. It recommended extending bans on lodge membership to magistrates, career military and police.
cases.cite: Parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission, report on mafia and Freemasonry, December 2017

cases.n: Castelvetrano: most of town executive were Freemasons
cases.rank: town executive and council (home town of Matteo Messina Denaro)
cases.d: Italy's Anti-Mafia Commission, investigating whether mafia groups used Masonic lodges to reach public bodies, found heavy Masonic membership in a Sicilian town government, a local bank and a Calabrian health authority. Its 2017 report found that in Castelvetrano, in Trapani province, in 2016, 4 of the 5 town assessors (members of the mayor's executive) and 7 of 30 councillors were Freemasons. It also found that 11 executives and staff of a Trapani-area cooperative bank belonged to a Grand Orient lodge, and a significant Masonic presence in senior posts at the Locri health authority in Calabria.
cases.cite: Parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission, report on mafia and Freemasonry, December 2017
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Freemasons sitting in a town government; nothing shows a lodge or mafia steering decisions.

cases.n: Communion and Liberation figure Formigoni led Lombardy for 18 years
cases.d: Comunione e Liberazione (Communion and Liberation, CL), an Italian Catholic lay movement, had its unofficial political spokesman at the head of Lombardy, Italy's richest region. Roberto Formigoni led Lombardy from 1995 to 2013. On 21 February 2019 the Court of Cassation confirmed his corruption conviction in the Maugeri health-care case, with a final sentence of 5 years 10 months. The court ruling concerned bribes, not the movement itself.
cases.cite: Italian Court of Cassation, 21 February 2019
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Movement figure's corruption conviction concerned bribes, not the movement.

cases.n: Opus Dei members enter Franco's cabinet and redirect the economy
cases.d: Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of lay people and priests, had members placed at the head of Spain's economic ministries under the dictator Francisco Franco. In February 1957 Franco appointed two Opus Dei members: Mariano Navarro Rubio as finance minister and Alberto Ullastres as trade minister. Both served until 1965 and drove the Stabilisation Plan that ended autarky, the policy of economic self-sufficiency, and opened Spain to foreign trade and investment. Historians count 8 Opus Dei members among Franco's 116 ministers, none before 1957. By 1969 eleven members of the cabinet had ties to the organisation.
cases.cite: Academic history (Preston; Crozier; Messori; John Allen)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Franco appointed Opus Dei members; nothing shows the organisation placed them or steered policy.

cases.n: Opus Dei member Navarro Rubio: finance minister, then central bank
cases.rank: Finance Minister 1957–65; Governor of the Bank of Spain 1965–70
cases.d: Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of lay people and priests, had one of its members run Spain's finances and then its central bank. Mariano Navarro Rubio, an Opus Dei member, was Franco's finance minister from 25 February 1957 to 8 July 1965 and helped drive the Stabilisation Plan that opened Spain's economy. He then became governor of the Banco de España, the central bank. He was accused in the 1969 MATESA scandal, over about 10 billion pesetas of state export credits to a textile-machinery firm, and left the central bank. Franco pardoned the accused former ministers before any verdict.
cases.cite: Spanish government records; academic history
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Individual member in office; nothing shows Opus Dei steering his decisions.

cases.n: Opus Dei member Ullastres: trade minister, then envoy to the EEC
cases.d: Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of lay people and priests, had one of its members in charge of Spain's trade policy and then its relations with Europe. Alberto Ullastres, one of the Opus Dei ministers known as 'Opusdeístas', was Franco's trade minister from 1957 to 1965 and led the Stabilisation Plan's opening of Spain's trade, ending the policy of self-sufficiency. From 1965 to 1976 he headed Spain's mission to the European Communities, the forerunner of the European Union. He was one of 8 Opus Dei members historians count among Franco's 116 ministers.
cases.cite: Academic history
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Individual member in office; nothing shows Opus Dei steering his decisions.

cases.n: Opus Dei member López Rodó ran Franco's development plans
cases.rank: Minister for Development Planning 1965–73; Foreign Minister 1973–74
cases.d: Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of lay people and priests, had one of its members direct Spain's economic planning for nearly two decades. Laureano López Rodó, an Opus Dei member close to Luis Carrero Blanco, Franco's chief aide and later Prime Minister, was technical secretary of the Presidency from 1956 to 1962 and Commissioner of the Development Plan from 1962 to 1965. He was then minister for development planning from 1965 to 1973, and foreign minister from 12 June 1973 to 4 January 1974. He was one of 8 Opus Dei members historians count among Franco's 116 ministers.
cases.cite: Spanish government records; academic history
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Individual member in office; nothing shows Opus Dei steering his decisions.

cases.n: Opus Dei member López-Bravo: Franco's industry and foreign minister
cases.d: Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of lay people and priests, had another member among Franco's senior ministers in Gregorio López-Bravo. He served as Franco's minister of industry and then foreign minister until 1973, and was part of the 1969 'monocolor' cabinet, in which eleven members had ties to Opus Dei. Historians count 8 Opus Dei members among Franco's 116 ministers, none before 1957. López-Bravo died in the Mount Oiz air crash in 1985.
cases.cite: Spanish government records; academic history
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Individual member in office; nothing shows Opus Dei steering his decisions.

cases.n: MATESA scandal and the 1969 Opus Dei-dominated cabinet
cases.rank: finance and trade ministers; state industrial bank
cases.d: By 1969 most of Franco's cabinet had ties to Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation of lay people and priests. The MATESA scandal broke on 23 July 1969: the textile-machinery firm MATESA owed about 10 billion pesetas in export credits from the state Banco de Crédito Industrial. Former ministers Mariano Navarro Rubio, an Opus Dei member, Juan José Espinosa San Martín (finance) and Faustino García-Moncó (trade) were charged, and Franco pardoned them before any verdict. Instead of reducing the movement's presence, the reshuffle of 29 October 1969 produced a 'monocolor' (single-colour) cabinet in which eleven members had ties to Opus Dei.
cases.cite: Spanish Supreme Court proceedings; Franco pardon 1971
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A state-credit scandal with members' ties to Opus Dei; nothing shows the organisation steering decisions.

cases.n: Narendra Modi, a career RSS organiser, became Prime Minister
cases.d: The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation that places its members in the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and other affiliated groups, had a long-serving organiser of its own become India's Prime Minister. Narendra Modi joined the RSS as a boy and served as a full-time organiser (pracharak) from the early 1970s, before the RSS seconded, or assigned, him to the BJP in 1985. He became Prime Minister in 2014. The RSS does not publish membership rolls; Modi's RSS career is set out in his official biographies and was acknowledged by the organisation.
cases.cite: Official PM biography; RSS statements; widely documented in Indian and international press
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Shows RSS career and secondment to a party, but no decision in office served the RSS.

cases.n: Iglesia ni Cristo head made a presidential special envoy
cases.rank: Special Envoy of the President for Overseas Filipinos' Concerns (Department of Foreign Affairs)
cases.d: The Iglesia ni Cristo (INC), a Philippine church that tells its members to vote as a bloc for the candidates it chooses, had its leader given a government post after backing the winning presidential candidate. The church backed Rodrigo Duterte in the 2016 election. Duterte then appointed Eduardo Villanueva Manalo, the INC's executive minister (head), as Special Envoy of the President for Overseas Filipinos' Concerns under the Department of Foreign Affairs. The appointment papers were dated 13 February 2018 and set a term from 30 January 2018 to 29 January 2019.
cases.cite: Presidential appointment papers dated 13 February 2018, reported by Philippine Daily Inquirer, 14 February 2018
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A church leader given a post after backing the winner; no decision shown serving the church.

cases.n: Iglesia ni Cristo rallies for its member-senator Marcoleta
cases.d: The Iglesia ni Cristo (INC), a Philippine church that tells its members to vote as a bloc, helped elect one of its own members to the Senate and then mobilised to defend him. Senator Rodante Marcoleta, an INC member elected in 2025 with the church's support, was set to be charged by Ombudsman Jesus Remulla, the official who investigates public officers, for failing to declare 75 million pesos in unused campaign contributions. On 30 June 2026 the church held a rally along EDSA, Manila's main highway, that police estimated at about 12,000; its spokesman called the case 'selective justice'. Marcoleta was expected to vote against convicting Vice-President Sara Duterte at her Senate impeachment trial.
cases.cite: Malay Mail (AFP), 30 June 2026; Wikipedia 'Iglesia ni Cristo' (2025 Senate support)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An open church rally for a member-senator; no decision shown serving the church.

cases.n: Moon's church acted as secret envoys for South Korea's government
cases.rank: South Korean defence industry and senior officials (Kim Jong-pil, Pak Chon-kyu)
cases.d: The Unification Church, the religious movement founded by Sun Myung Moon (the 'Moon Organization'), built close ties inside South Korea's government and worked on its behalf. In its 1978 final report the US House Subcommittee on International Organizations (the Fraser committee) named Kim Jong-pil, founder of the Korean Central Intelligence Agency (KCIA), and Pak Chon-kyu as the church's influential allies. It found that a Moon Organization business was an important Korean defence contractor making M-16 rifles, and that in late 1977 Moon representatives tried to renegotiate the Colt–ROK Government M-16 co-production agreement in circumstances suggesting they were secret envoys of the Korean government. It also found that the Moon-founded Korean Cultural and Freedom Foundation advanced the Seoul government's political interests.
cases.cite: US House Subcommittee on International Organizations, 'Investigation of Korean-American Relations', final report 1978 (excerpt on Wikisource)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Shows the church working for the South Korean government, not the church's people steering it from inside.

cases.n: Romania's interior minister and police chief named as undeclared Masons
cases.rank: interim interior minister and deputy prime minister; head of the Gendarmerie
cases.d: Newsweek România reported in September 2019, citing anonymous Masonic sources, that two men running Romania's security forces belonged to Masonic lodges without declaring it. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in local groups called lodges. The magazine said Mihai Fifor, then interim interior minister and deputy prime minister, joined in 2008 through Loja Armonia and later Loja Basarab, and that General Constantin Florea, head of the Gendarmerie (the militarised police), belonged to Loja Basarab. Neither had listed membership in his declaration of interests, which the magazine said the law required. Fifor neither confirmed nor denied. Costin Mihalache, head of the Government Chancellery and a former foreign-intelligence (SIE) officer, said he had been a Mason but no longer was. The claim rests on that one outlet.
cases.cite: Newsweek România investigation, republished by Alba24, 22 September 2019 (anonymous Masonic sources; the claim rests on that one outlet)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Undeclared lodge membership only; no decision shown for the lodge.

cases.n: Burkina Faso's President Compaoré reported as former Masonic grand master
cases.d: Freemasonry, a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges, had Burkina Faso's president and then his foreign minister at the head of the country's national lodge, Jeune Afrique reported in 2012. It said Blaise Compaoré, who ruled Burkina Faso from 1987 to 2014, was a former grand master of the Grande Loge du Burkina while he was president, and that his foreign minister, Djibrill Bassolé, had succeeded him as head of the lodge. A grand lodge is the national body over local lodges, and its elected head is the grand master. The source is a 2012 survey by Pascal Airault of Freemasonry among African leaders, based on Jeune Afrique's own reporting; it does not show particular decisions taken for the lodge.
cases.cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Membership report only; source says no decisions shown for the lodge.

cases.d: Freemasonry had its national leader in Burkina Faso's government: foreign minister Djibrill Bassolé was grand master of the Grande Loge du Burkina, having taken over the post from President Blaise Compaoré, Jeune Afrique reported in 2012. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges; a grand lodge is the national body over them, and its elected head is the grand master. The source is a 2012 Jeune Afrique survey by Pascal Airault of Freemasonry among African leaders, based on its own reporting; it does not show particular decisions taken for the lodge.

cases.n: Guinea's President Condé reported as overseeing the Grand Lodge
cases.d: Guinea's sitting president, Alpha Condé, was reported in 2012 to oversee ('chapeauter') the Grande Loge de Guinée, the country's national Masonic body, so the head of state also presided over a private society whose membership is not made public. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges; a grand lodge is the national body over them, and its elected head is the grand master. cases.n: Senegal's President Wade reported as an initiated Freemason
cases.d: Abdoulaye Wade, president of Senegal from 2000 to 2012, had been initiated into Freemasonry, the magazine Jeune Afrique reported in 2012. Freemasonry is a fraternal society whose members meet privately in lodges; a grand lodge is the national body over them, and its elected head is the grand master. Initiation is the ceremony by which a member joins. The report came from a survey by Pascal Airault of Freemasonry among African leaders, based on the magazine's own reporting; it does not show particular decisions taken for the lodge. After Wade lost power, his camp accused his successor Macky Sall of being a member too, which Sall denied.
cases.cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

cases.n: Côte d'Ivoire's prime minister and interior minister named as Masons
cases.rank: prime minister; minister of the interior
cases.d: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that two of Côte d'Ivoire's most senior office-holders, Prime Minister Jeannot Ahoussou-Kouadio and Interior Minister Hamed Bakayoko, were Freemasons, and that state prosecutor Simplice Koffi Kouadio had been received by the Grande Loge de Côte d'Ivoire. The source is a 2012 Jeune Afrique survey by Pascal Airault of Freemasonry among African leaders, based on its own reporting; it does not show particular decisions taken for the lodge.

cases.n: Gabon's police chief headed a Grand Lodge; ministers at Bongo's lodge
cases.d: Freemasonry had Gabon's police chief and its president at the head of the country's two grand lodges, Jeune Afrique reported in 2012. A grand lodge is the national body over local lodges, whose members meet privately; its elected head is the grand master. The report said Antoine Embinga, head of Gabon's police until his removal in January 2012, was grand master of the Grande Loge symbolique du Gabon. It said ministers Paul Toungui and Séraphin Moundounga and Léon Paul Ngoulakia, head of the National Security Council, attended the installation of President Ali Bongo as grand master of the Grande Loge du Gabon on 31 October 2009. The source, a survey by Pascal Airault based on Jeune Afrique's own reporting, does not show particular decisions taken for the lodges.

cases.n: Moon aide Bo Hi Pak and CAUSA tied to Bolivia's 1980 coup regime
cases.rank: de facto president Luis García Meza
cases.d: Journalist Robert Parry wrote that the Unification Church, Sun Myung Moon's religious movement, and its political arm CAUSA backed General Luis García Meza's government after his July 1980 coup in Bolivia, known as the 'cocaine coup'. Parry wrote that the church published a photo of Moon's aide Bo Hi Pak meeting García Meza, and quoted Pak saying 'I have erected a throne for Father Moon in the world's highest city'. He also wrote, without naming a source, that CAUSA ran joint operations with the junta and that later Bolivian investigations found Moon's group had invested about US$4 million in the coup. He cited Martin Andersen's 'Dossier Secreto' for García Meza attending a congress of the Latin American Anti-Communist Confederation (CAL), the regional branch of the World Anti-Communist League (WACL). This is a single-author account.
cases.cite: Robert Parry, The Consortium, 19 August 1998 (single-author account)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Single-author account of backing a coup regime; too vague on who got inside what.

cases.n: Honduran army chief's group took Unification Church front money
cases.rank: commander of the armed forces (Gen. Gustavo Álvarez Martínez)
cases.d: A front group for the Unification Church, Sun Myung Moon's religious movement, gave money to a political group headed by Honduras's top military officer. The Association for the Progress of Honduras (APROH), led by armed forces commander General Gustavo Álvarez Martínez, joined business leaders and officers; the Library of Congress country study says it received a US$50,000 contribution from the church front. The Christian Science Monitor reported in March 1984 that APROH and allied forces had taken control of university, professional, teacher, labour and peasant bodies. Fellow officers removed Álvarez on 31 March 1984, and APROH declined after that.
cases.cite: Library of Congress, 'Honduras: A Country Study' (1995); Christian Science Monitor, 21 March 1984
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A donation to a political group headed by the army chief; no decision shown serving the church.

cases.n: Ford-funded Berkeley economists took over Suharto's economic ministries
cases.rank: Head of BAPPENAS, finance minister and other economic ministries
cases.d: A group of University of Indonesia economists trained at the University of California, Berkeley on Ford Foundation money, later called the 'Berkeley Mafia', took over Indonesia's economic policy-making under Suharto. In the late 1950s the Ford Foundation paid for economists from dean Sumitro Djojohadikusumo's faculty to take graduate degrees at Berkeley. After Suharto took power in 1966 he made them his economic team: Widjojo Nitisastro headed the planning agency BAPPENAS (1967-83) and was Coordinating Minister for Economics, Finance and Industry (1973-83); Ali Wardhana was Finance Minister (1968-83); Emil Salim and Mohammad Sadli also held ministries. Their 1966 programme cut inflation from 650% to 13% by 1969 and opened the country to foreign investors.
cases.cite: Ford Foundation, 'Celebrating Indonesia'; Hal Hill and Thee Kian Wie, Bulletin of Indonesian Economic Studies (2008)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Foundation-funded training followed by appointment by Suharto; nothing shows the funder placing them or steering decisions.

cases.n: Ford-funded Berkeley graduate Widjojo ran Indonesia's planning agency
cases.rank: Head of National Development Planning Agency (1967-83); Coordinating Minister for Economics, Finance and Industry (1973-83)
cases.d: Widjojo Nitisastro, one of the Ford Foundation-funded University of Indonesia economists trained at Berkeley (the 'Berkeley Mafia'), led that group into the top of Suharto's government. After taking his doctorate at Berkeley under the programme, he led the economists who presented a stabilisation plan to Suharto at the army staff college seminar in August 1966. He then headed BAPPENAS, the national development planning agency, from June 1967 to March 1983 and wrote Indonesia's Five-Year Development Plans, which set the direction of the economy for that period.
cases.cite: Widjojo Nitisastro, The Indonesian Development Experience (ISEAS, 2011)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Foundation-funded training followed by appointment; nothing shows the funder steering his decisions.

cases.n: Ford-funded Berkeley graduate Ali Wardhana was Suharto's finance minister
cases.d: Ali Wardhana, one of the University of Indonesia economists trained at Berkeley on Ford Foundation money and counted among the 'Berkeley Mafia', ran Indonesia's finance ministry for 15 years. He studied at the University of Indonesia, earned his doctorate at Berkeley under the Ford-funded programme, and served as Suharto's Minister of Finance from June 1968 to March 1983, one of the longest-serving ministers in Indonesian history. The finance ministry controls the national budget, taxes and borrowing.
cases.cite: Hal Hill and Thee Kian Wie, Bulletin of Indonesian Economic Studies
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Foundation-funded training followed by appointment; nothing shows the funder steering his decisions.

cases.n: US- and Ford-funded Chicago graduates took Pinochet's economic posts
cases.rank: Ministers of finance, economy, planning; Central Bank presidents
cases.d: Chilean economists trained at the University of Chicago under a US-funded exchange, the 'Chile Project', took the top economic posts in General Augusto Pinochet's military government; they became known as the 'Chicago Boys'. The project began in the mid-1950s as a US government Point Four aid scheme linking Chicago's economics department with Santiago's Catholic University. Between 1955 and 1973, 126 Chilean students trained under it, funded through US aid to 1964 and then by the Ford Foundation. Their 189-page plan 'El ladrillo' ('the brick') became the junta's economic programme in 1975. Graduates then held top posts: Sergio de Castro (Economy 1975-76, Finance 1976-82), Pablo Baraona (Economy 1976-79), Miguel Kast (Planning, Labor, Central Bank), Sergio de la Cuadra (Central Bank, Finance 1982) and Rolf Lüders (Economy and Finance 1982-83).
cases.cite: Milton and Rose Friedman, Two Lucky People (1998); University of Chicago-Catholic University exchange records as summarised in the Wikipedia article 'Chicago Boys'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): US-funded training followed by appointment by Pinochet; nothing shows the funders placing them or steering decisions.

cases.n: Chicago-trained Sergio de Castro ran Pinochet's economy and finance
cases.rank: Minister of Economy (1975-76); Minister of Finance (1976-82)
cases.d: Sergio de Castro, a graduate of the US-funded Chile Project linking the University of Chicago with Chile's Catholic University, carried that group's programme into Pinochet's government. He was a co-author of 'El ladrillo', the 'Chicago Boys' economic plan that the military junta adopted. He was Minister of Economy from April 1975 to December 1976 and Minister of Finance from December 1976 to April 1982, when the 1982 debt crisis ended his term.
cases.cite: Chilean government records; Wikipedia biography citing Chilean sources
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): US-funded training followed by appointment; nothing shows the funders steering his decisions.

cases.n: Chicago-trained Miguel Kast held Pinochet's planning and central bank posts
cases.rank: Minister of Planning (1978-80); Labor Minister (1980-82); Central Bank governor (1982-83)
cases.d: Miguel Kast, one of the Chilean economists trained at the University of Chicago and known as the 'Chicago Boys', held a run of senior posts in Pinochet's government. He studied at the Catholic University of Chile and took a master's at Chicago. Under Pinochet he headed the planning office ODEPLAN, then the labour ministry, and in 1982 became governor of the Central Bank of Chile, which sets interest rates and controls the money supply.
cases.cite: Chilean government records; Wikipedia biography citing Chilean sources
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): US-funded training followed by appointment; nothing shows the funders steering his decisions.

cases.n: China's vice-minister of public security sat as Interpol president
cases.rank: Vice-Minister of Public Security (2004-18) while Interpol president (2016-18)
cases.d: China placed one of its senior police officials at the head of Interpol, the international police cooperation body: Meng Hongwei was elected Interpol's first Chinese president on 10 November 2016 while still serving as China's Vice-Minister of Public Security. He disappeared after flying to China on 25 September 2018; on 7 October the Communist Party's discipline commission said he was under investigation for bribery, and Interpol received his resignation. In January 2020 a Tianjin court sentenced him to 13 and a half years for taking more than 14.5 million yuan (about $2.1 million) in bribes. His wife Grace Meng, granted asylum in France, says the case is political.
cases.cite: Tianjin No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, judgment of 21 January 2020; Reuters, 21 Jan 2020
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open election of a member state's official to head Interpol; no decision shown serving China.

cases.n: UAE interior official elected Interpol president after UAE donations
cases.rank: Inspector General, UAE Ministry of Interior; Interpol president (2021-25)
cases.d: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) put one of its own interior ministry officials at the head of Interpol, the international police cooperation body, after giving it large donations. Major General Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi, inspector general of the UAE Interior Ministry, was elected Interpol president in Istanbul on 25 November 2021 with about 69% of the votes in the third round. Before the vote, 19 NGOs opposed him, 35 French parliamentarians wrote to President Macron, and a report by former UK Director of Public Prosecutions David Calvert-Smith called him unsuited and questioned UAE donations to Interpol. Britons Matthew Hedges and Ali Issa Ahmad accuse him of responsibility for their torture in UAE custody; in March 2022 French anti-terrorism prosecutors opened a preliminary inquiry. The UAE denies the accusations.
cases.cite: French National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office, preliminary inquiry (March 2022); The Guardian, 24 March 2022
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open election after open donations; no decision inside Interpol shown serving the UAE.

cases.n: UAE donations to Interpol's foundation matched all other members
cases.rank: Interpol funding through the Interpol Foundation for a Safer World
cases.d: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) gave Interpol, the international police cooperation body, donations reported at about $54 million through the Interpol Foundation for a Safer World, set up in 2013. That sum is estimated to equal the statutory contributions, the fixed annual dues, of the other 194 member countries combined. Critics say the money helped the UAE win the right to host Interpol's 2018 General Assembly and helped elect its interior ministry official Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi as Interpol president in 2021. A report by former UK Director of Public Prosecutions David Calvert-Smith raised the same concern in April 2021; Interpol rejected it.
cases.cite: David Calvert-Smith, report on UAE and Interpol (April 2021); The Guardian, 7 April 2021
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open donations to an Interpol foundation; no people placed inside or decisions shown.

cases.n: Durão Barroso — WEF 'Global Leader for Tomorrow' 1993, later PM
cases.rank: Prime Minister of Portugal (2002-04); European Commission president (2004-14)
cases.d: The World Economic Forum (WEF), the Geneva foundation that runs the annual Davos meeting of business and political leaders, picked José Manuel Durão Barroso for its leadership network in 1993, while he was Portugal's foreign minister. He went on to be Prime Minister of Portugal (2002-04) and European Commission president (2004-14). The WEF picks rising figures for this network: Global Leaders for Tomorrow from 1992, renamed the Forum of Young Global Leaders in 2003-04, and lists Barroso among its 1993 Global Leaders for Tomorrow. Membership is a WEF selection, not a finding of influence; no forum has found that the network directed government decisions.
cases.cite: World Economic Forum, 'The World Economic Forum: A Partner in Shaping History 1971-2020' (WEF, 2019/2020), list of 1993 Global Leaders for Tomorrow
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Selection for a forum's leadership network; record says no decisions directed.

cases.n: IEA says 14 of Boris Johnson's cabinet were its 'alumni'
cases.d: The Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA), a London free-market think tank and UK partner of the Atlas Network, claimed that 14 members of Boris Johnson's first cabinet had come through its programmes. The Atlas Network is a US-based organisation that funds, trains and links free-market think tanks around the world, which it calls partners. When Johnson formed his cabinet in July 2019, the IEA told supporters that 14 of those around the cabinet table, including Chancellor Sajid Javid, Foreign Secretary Dominic Raab and Home Secretary Priti Patel, were 'alumni of IEA initiatives'. Javid had said in 2015 that the IEA 'deeply influenced' his views. Matthew Elliott, chief executive of the Vote Leave campaign, had founded the TaxPayers' Alliance, another Atlas partner. The claim is the IEA's own; the Guardian reported it.
cases.cite: The Guardian, 'How the right's radical thinktanks reshaped the Conservative party', 29 Nov 2019
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A think tank's own claim about cabinet alumni; no decisions shown serving it.

cases.n: Atlas-partner IPA's policy director became Human Rights Commissioner
cases.rank: Australian Human Rights Commissioner (2014-16); Assistant Minister for Industry, Energy and Emissions Reduction (2021-22)
cases.d: Tim Wilson moved from the Institute of Public Affairs (IPA), an Australian free-market think tank that is an Atlas Network partner, into a government post and then parliament. The Atlas Network is a US-based organisation that funds, trains and links free-market think tanks around the world, which it calls partners. Wilson was IPA policy director from 2007 to 2013. The Abbott government appointed him Australia's Human Rights Commissioner in 2014; he entered parliament in 2016 and was an assistant minister in 2021-22.
cases.cite: Australian Parliament biography; Atlas Network partner directory
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Think-tank staffer took a government post; no decision shown serving the think tank.

cases.n: Atlas-partner think-tank head became Piñera's chief minister
cases.d: Cristián Larroulet moved from running Libertad y Desarrollo, a Santiago think tank that is an Atlas Network partner, to the centre of Chile's government. The Atlas Network is a US-based organisation that funds, trains and links free-market think tanks around the world, which it calls partners. Libertad y Desarrollo runs a Free Enterprise Training Centre with Atlas. Larroulet, its executive director, had earlier been chief of staff at the Treasury under Hernán Büchi. President Sebastián Piñera made him Minister Secretary-General of the Presidency, the minister who coordinates the government's legislative agenda, from 2010 to 2014, and later head of presidential advisers.
cases.cite: Chilean government records; Atlas Network partner listings
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Think-tank head took a government post; no decision shown serving the network.

cases.n: Atlas think tank Fundación Pensar merged into Macri's party
cases.rank: PRO party of President Mauricio Macri (2015-19)
cases.d: Fundación Pensar, an Argentine think tank in the Atlas Network, merged with PRO, the party formed by Mauricio Macri, who became President of Argentina in December 2015. The Atlas Network is a US-based organisation that funds, trains and links free-market think tanks around the world, which it calls partners. Atlas leader Alejandro Chafuen told The Intercept in 2017 that Atlas-affiliated people were ministers in the new Argentine government; the article does not name them.
cases.cite: The Intercept, 'Sphere of Influence', 9 Aug 2017
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A think tank merging into a party, with unnamed ministers; too vague.

cases.n: Director of NED-funded Atlas think tank signed Venezuela's coup decree
cases.rank: Short-lived coup government of Pedro Carmona (April 2002)
cases.d: The director of Cedice Libertad, the Atlas Network's main think tank in Caracas, which received US government-backed grants, signed the decree of the short-lived government that seized power in Venezuela's April 2002 coup. The Atlas Network is a US-based organisation that funds, trains and links free-market think tanks around the world, which it calls partners. From 1998 Cedice received regular grants from the Center for International Private Enterprise, a core institute of the US-funded National Endowment for Democracy (NED); one grant letter lists NED funds for Cedice to advocate 'a change in government'. The 'Carmona Decree', named after coup leader Pedro Carmona, dissolved the National Assembly and Supreme Court during the coup against Hugo Chávez.
cases.cite: The Intercept, 'Sphere of Influence', 9 Aug 2017, citing NED grant records
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A funded think tank's director signed a coup decree; the coup was an outside seizure, not people placed inside running an institution.

cases.n: Lord Esher, named in Rhodes's secret 'Junta', reshaped the War Office
cases.d: Reginald Brett, Lord Esher, whom Carroll Quigley names as one of three leaders of Cecil Rhodes's secret society, reorganised Britain's army command and advised the king. Historian Carroll Quigley argued in The Anglo-American Establishment (1981) that Cecil Rhodes founded a secret society to extend British rule, whose circle, the Milner Group, placed members in government. Quigley, citing Esher's journals, says Brett was told of Rhodes's plan on 3 February 1890 and named with W. T. Stead and Alfred Milner to the society's 'Junta of Three' in February 1891. Esher chaired the War Office (Reconstitution) Committee with Admiral John Fisher and Colonel George Clarke; its 1904 report created the Army Council and a permanent secretariat for the Committee of Imperial Defence. He declined the War Office and the Viceroyalty of India and advised Edward VII almost daily from 1903.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Reginald Brett, 2nd Viscount Esher'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 3, 38–39
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Membership only; the War Office reform is not tied to the society's aims.

cases.n: Rhodes company director and trustee Earl Grey became Canada's Governor General
cases.d: Albert Grey, 4th Earl Grey, a director of Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company and one of the first trustees of the Rhodes Trust, became Governor General of Canada, the Crown's representative there, from 10 December 1904 to 13 October 1911. He had been Administrator of Rhodesia after Jameson resigned in 1896. Historian Carroll Quigley lists Grey in the 'Circle of Initiates' that Rhodes and the journalist W. T. Stead drew up for Rhodes's secret society in 1891; that membership rests on Quigley.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Albert Grey, 4th Earl Grey'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 12, 39
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Membership only; no decision shown for the society.

cases.n: Milner and his circle in Lloyd George's War Cabinet
cases.rank: Member of the War Cabinet; Secretary of State for War; Colonial Secretary
cases.d: Alfred Milner, whom Carroll Quigley names as the leader of a group descended from Cecil Rhodes's secret society, sat in Britain's five-man War Cabinet and brought an associate into his ministry. Lloyd George asked Milner to join the War Cabinet on 8 December 1916; he sat in it until November 1918, was Secretary of State for War from April 1918 to January 1919 and Colonial Secretary from January 1919 to February 1921. Leo Amery, whom Quigley counts in the group, served under him as personal secretary at the Colonial Office (1919–21). Quigley says Milner held regular 'Ginger Group' meetings with close associates in 1913–1919 to coordinate them as a pressure group; that account is his.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Alfred Milner, 1st Viscount Milner' and 'Leo Amery'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope (1966), p. 951
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Milner held office and met associates, but no decision shown serving the group.

cases.n: Milner Group member chairs the Irish Boundary Commission
cases.d: Historian Carroll Quigley says the Milner Group, a private network of British imperialists formed around Lord Milner's young South African staff (the 'Kindergarten'), placed its member Richard Feetham, a South African judge, in charge of the Irish Boundary Commission of 1924–25. The commission was to fix the border between the Irish Free State and Northern Ireland. Its report was unacceptable to both governments and was buried. Another member, Lionel Curtis, had been involved in the making of the 1921 Anglo-Irish Treaty. Quigley writes that most of Feetham's posts 'came to him as a member of the Milner Group' and that the group's part in the Irish settlement was 'considerably more' than its journal, The Round Table, admitted; those are his claims.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Richard Feetham' and 'Lionel Curtis'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 4 and ch. 9
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Post only; the commission's report was buried and no decision is shown for the group.

cases.n: Lord Halifax: Foreign Secretary Quigley counts in the Round Table
cases.rank: Foreign Secretary; Viceroy of India; Ambassador to the United States
cases.d: Historian Carroll Quigley claims Edward Wood, Lord Halifax, was a member of the inner core of the Round Table, a private network of British imperialists, while he held top state posts. Halifax, a Fellow of All Souls College, Oxford, from 1903, was Viceroy of India (1926–31), met Hitler in November 1937, was Foreign Secretary from 21 February 1938 to 22 December 1940 and defended the Munich Agreement, which handed part of Czechoslovakia to Germany, in the Lords on 3 October 1938. He was then ambassador in Washington until 1946. Quigley writes that Halifax was close to the group from 1903 'but did not really become a member until after 1920' and should 'probably be placed in the inner core'. The membership claim is Quigley's.
cases.cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 5–6; Wikipedia 'E. F. L. Wood, 1st Earl of Halifax'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Membership only; no decision tied to the group.

cases.n: John Buchan: Milner's Kindergarten member as Canada's Governor General
cases.d: John Buchan, the novelist, served on Lord Milner's staff in South Africa until 1903 and is listed as a member of Milner's Kindergarten, the group of young officials who went on to form a private network of British imperialists. He entered Parliament in 1927 and was Governor General of Canada, the Crown's representative there, from 1935 until his death in 1940. Historian Carroll Quigley counts him in the wider Milner Group, which he argues placed its members in high imperial posts; the record does not show any decision Buchan took on the group's behalf.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Milner's Kindergarten'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Record itself says no decision taken for the group.

cases.n: Lord Lothian: Rhodes Trust chief sent as ambassador to Washington
cases.rank: British Ambassador to the United States
cases.d: Philip Kerr, 11th Marquess of Lothian, led the Milner Group, a private network of British imperialists, from 1925 to 1940 while also holding British state posts, according to historian Carroll Quigley. Kerr was General Secretary of the Rhodes Trust, which runs the Rhodes Scholarships, from 1925 until 1939, Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster (August–November 1931) and Under-Secretary for India (1931–32). He met Hitler in January 1935 and May 1937 and argued for revising the Versailles treaty in Germany's favour until March 1939. He was then British ambassador in Washington from 1 September 1939 until he died there on 12 December 1940. The leadership claim is Quigley's, made in The Anglo-American Establishment.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Philip Kerr, 11th Marquess of Lothian'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, p. 4
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Group leader holding posts; no decision in office tied to the group.

cases.n: Round Table's Robert Brand runs Britain's wartime missions in Washington
cases.rank: Head, British Food Mission; UK Treasury representative in Washington
cases.d: The Round Table, a private network of British imperialists, had one of its leaders running Britain's food and Treasury missions in Washington during the Second World War, according to historian Carroll Quigley. Quigley names Robert Brand, a banker, as the network's leader after Lionel Curtis (to 1963) and calls him an 'international financier' of its inner circle. Brand joined the merchant bank Lazard Brothers in 1909 and became a managing director. In 1915 he helped set up the Imperial Munitions Board in Canada. He headed the British Food Mission to the United States (1941–44), was the Treasury's representative in Washington (1944–46) and was made a peer in 1946. The leadership claim is Quigley's; the record shows a member in state posts, not a decision taken for the group.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Robert Brand, 1st Baron Brand'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, pp. 950–951
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Record itself says no decision taken for the group.

cases.n: CFR member John Foster Dulles sets out 'massive retaliation' at the CFR
cases.d: John Foster Dulles, described by the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a private foreign-policy club, as 'a long-serving Council member', was Secretary of State under Eisenhower. On 12 January 1954 he used a televised CFR address to set out the administration's policy of meeting Soviet aggression 'instantly, by means and at places of our choosing', known as massive retaliation. CFR's history calls the speech a break with its off-the-record rule. Earlier CFR members in the same office included Frank Kellogg, who spoke at the Council in 1928 months before the Kellogg–Briand Pact outlawing war, and Henry Stimson.
cases.cite: G. Gavrilis, The Council on Foreign Relations: A Short History (CFR, 2021), pp. 17–19, 41
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A member giving a speech at the club; no decision shown made for it.

cases.n: John J. McCloy: War Department, World Bank, Germany, then CFR chair
cases.rank: Assistant Secretary of War; President of the World Bank; US High Commissioner for Germany
cases.d: John J. McCloy moved between top US posts and the leadership of the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a private foreign-policy club. He was Assistant Secretary of War (April 1941–November 1945), President of the World Bank (1947–49) and US High Commissioner for Germany (1949–52), the official running the American occupation zone. He then chaired the CFR board from 1953 to 1970 while also chairing Chase Manhattan Bank (1953–60) and the Ford Foundation (1958–65), and sat on the Warren Commission, which investigated President Kennedy's assassination, in 1963. CFR's own history names him as board chair.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'John J. McCloy'; G. Gavrilis, The Council on Foreign Relations: A Short History (CFR, 2021)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A career moving between posts and club leadership; no decision shown serving the club.

cases.n: CFR members held about half of top US foreign-policy posts, 1945–72
cases.rank: Senior US foreign-policy officials (State, Defense, Treasury, CIA)
cases.d: Members of the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a private foreign-policy club, filled a large share of senior US foreign-policy posts after the Second World War. A study by Laurence Shoup and William Minter (Imperial Brain Trust, 1977) found that more than half of 502 senior US government officials it surveyed between 1945 and 1972 were CFR members. By its count members held about 42% of top foreign-policy posts under Truman, 40% under Eisenhower, 51% under Kennedy and 57% under Johnson. Eisenhower himself was a member. Membership was not secret; the study measures how far one club's members staffed government.
cases.cite: Shoup and Minter, Imperial Brain Trust (Monthly Review Press, 1977), as summarised in Wikipedia 'Council on Foreign Relations'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Counts open club membership among officials; no placing or steering shown.

cases.n: Operation Countryman: Met corruption inquiry and Masonic lodge claims
cases.d: Freemasons' lodges inside London's Metropolitan Police were alleged to be tied to corruption among its detectives during Operation Countryman (1978–82), an inquiry run by officers from outside forces. Assistant Chief Constable Leonard Burt returned to Dorset in May 1980, and evidence was handed to the Metropolitan Police's own internal unit. Chief Constable Arthur Hambleton alleged obstruction by Commissioner David McNee and the Director of Public Prosecutions; eight officers were prosecuted and none convicted. MP Dale Campbell-Savours later alleged that police membership of particular Masonic lodges was tied to a criminal conspiracy, and Stephen Knight's The Brotherhood gave the operation a chapter. Parliament's requests for the findings were refused on public-interest immunity, a rule that lets the state withhold documents.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Operation Countryman'; Knight, The Brotherhood (1984), ch. 9
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Alleged lodge links in a corruption inquiry with no convictions; too vague.

cases.n: Police lodge members' victims charged; Lancashire pays £170,000
cases.rank: Lancashire Constabulary officers; Chief Constable of Lancashire
cases.d: Members of the Victory Lodge, a Masonic lodge made up mostly of serving Lancashire police officers, were involved in an assault in 1988 for which the victims, not the attackers, were charged. A Leicester shop owner and his son were assaulted at a Blackburn hotel during a lodge ladies' night; the hotel manager was a lodge member and the investigating officer was a Mason. The father and son were acquitted by a jury in February 1989. Their civil action against seven lodge members, the hotel group and the Chief Constable settled for about £170,000, most paid by the Chief Constable. The account comes from journalist Martin Short's 1996 evidence to the Home Affairs Committee, reprinted in his foreword to The Brotherhood.
cases.cite: Martin Short, foreword to Stephen Knight, The Brotherhood (Harper Perennial ed., 2007), quoting his 1996 evidence to the Home Affairs Committee
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A crime by police officers who were lodge members; infiltration is incidental.

cases.n: Ku Klux Klan backs member Hugo Black into the US Senate
cases.d: The Ku Klux Klan, a white-supremacist secret society, helped its member Hugo Black win Alabama's 1926 Democratic Senate primary. Black joined the Knights of Pythias and the Masons as a young man and around 1920 was an officer of his Masonic lodge; he joined the Klan in September 1923. The Birmingham chapter, Robert E. Lee Klan No. 1, was led from 1921 by James Esdale, later Grand Dragon (state leader). By the mid-1920s the Alabama Klan claimed to speak for the state's elite, 'including Masons, bankers, and ministers', and by 1926 Esdale oversaw 148 klaverns (local chapters) with a reported 94,301 members. Black visited all 148 during the race, and afterwards Esdale had him thank a Klan meeting alongside Governor-elect Bibb Graves. Black later sat on the US Supreme Court from 1937.
cases.cite: Encyclopedia of Alabama, 'Ku Klux Klan in Alabama from 1915–1930' (K. Hébert) and 'Hugo L. Black' (S. Suitts); Bhamwiki 'James Esdale'; The Nation, 'Hugo Black: A Personal History'
cases.org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (existing key)

arch.t: US Supreme Court Justice Was Documented KKK Member; Alabama KKK-Masonic Network Used as Political Infrastructure to Reach Highest Judicial Office

cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Electoral backing of a member; no decision in office shown serving the Klan.

cases.n: Ku Klux Klan member Bibb Graves wins Alabama's governorship
cases.d: Bibb Graves, a member of the Ku Klux Klan, a white-supremacist secret society, won Alabama's 1926 governor's race with the Klan's secret endorsement and served 1927–31 and 1935–39. He was almost certainly the Exalted Cyclops (local leader) of the Montgomery Klan. His membership became public when he resigned in 1928, and in 1937, during the Senate row over Hugo Black's appointment to the Supreme Court, Graves acknowledged his former membership. He and Black received gold Klan 'passports' and were nicknamed 'the Gold Dust Twins'. In 1937 Graves appointed his wife Dixie Bibb Graves to Black's vacated Senate seat.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Bibb Graves'; Encyclopedia of Alabama, 'Ku Klux Klan in Alabama from 1915–1930'
cases.org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (existing key)

arch.t: US Supreme Court Justice Was Documented KKK Member; Alabama KKK-Masonic Network Used as Political Infrastructure to Reach Highest Judicial Office

cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Electoral backing of a member; no decision in office shown serving the Klan.

cases.n: Iran-aligned Hezbollah holds two ministries in Lebanon's government
cases.d: Hezbollah, a Shia Lebanese party with an armed wing aligned with Iran, places its own nominees in Lebanon's cabinet. In the 24-member government Prime Minister Nawaf Salam formed in February 2025, Hezbollah's picks hold the public health ministry (Rakan Nasreddine) and the labour ministry (Mohammad Haidar); with its ally Amal it controls six portfolios. Hezbollah holds about 14 of 128 seats in parliament and is listed as a terrorist group by at least 28 countries, including the US and UK.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Hezbollah' (section on Lebanese politics)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A party's open share of cabinet posts; no outside party shown getting inside.

cases.n: US sanctions Hezbollah MPs and its liaison to Lebanon's security agencies
cases.rank: members of parliament; liaison to state security agencies
cases.d: The US Treasury said two sitting Lebanese MPs, Hezbollah's Amin Sherri and Muhammad Raad, acted inside parliament on behalf of Hezbollah, the Iran-aligned armed party. On 9 July 2019 it sanctioned them, the first time it had sanctioned sitting Lebanese MPs. It also sanctioned Wafiq Safa, head of Hezbollah's Liaison and Coordination Unit, which deals with Lebanon's security agencies. A State Department official urged the Lebanese government to cut ties with them; Hezbollah called it a 'humiliation'. Raad is now Hezbollah's deputy secretary-general.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC designations, 9 July 2019, reported by Al Jazeera
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A party's own MPs and liaison unit; no outside infiltration shown beyond normal party roles.

cases.n: Ali Karti: Islamic Movement chief and ex-minister sanctioned
cases.rank: former foreign minister; secretary-general of the Sudanese Islamic Movement
cases.d: The Sudanese Islamic Movement, rooted in the Muslim Brotherhood, placed its members in power during Omar al-Bashir's 1989–2019 rule. Ali Karti was Bashir's foreign minister (2010–2015) and became the movement's secretary-general in June 2021. In September 2023 the US sanctioned him for undermining the transition to civilian rule and obstructing a ceasefire between the army and the Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary group; Canada (April 2024) and the EU (June 2024) followed.
cases.cite: US Treasury designation, Sept 2023; EU Council decision, 24 June 2024, as summarised on Wikipedia
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Former minister later led the movement; no decision shown for it while in office.

cases.n: Sudan's Islamist finance minister and IRGC-trained brigade sanctioned
cases.rank: finance minister; Islamist militia fighting beside the army
cases.d: The US Treasury said Islamists tied to Iran hold posts inside Sudan's wartime government. On 12 September 2025 it sanctioned Gebreil Ibrahim, Sudan's finance minister and leader of the Justice and Equality Movement, which it tied to Islamist leader Hassan al-Turabi, saying he built ties with Tehran. It also sanctioned the al-Baraa bin Malik Brigade, an Islamist militia that grew from Bashir's Popular Defense Forces and has supplied up to 20,000 fighters against the Rapid Support Forces; Treasury said the brigade got training and weapons from Iran's Revolutionary Guards. Treasury used the word 'Islamist', not 'Muslim Brotherhood'.
cases.cite: US Treasury press release, 12 Sept 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Too vague on who got inside what for Iran.

cases.n: Muslim Brotherhood party member heads Libya's High Council of State
cases.rank: chairman of the High Council of State
cases.d: The Libyan Muslim Brotherhood placed one of its party's members at the head of a top state body. Libya's Justice and Construction Party was founded in March 2012 as the Brotherhood's political arm; it won 17 party-list seats in the 2012 congress and had five ministers until 2014. Its member Khalid al-Mishri chaired the High Council of State, the upper consultative body of the Tripoli-based government, from 8 April 2018 to 6 August 2023, and represented it at talks in Palermo, Doha, Moscow and Istanbul. The Muslim Brotherhood is a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Khalid al-Mishri' and 'Justice and Construction Party', citing Libya Observer and Reuters
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A party member chairing a state body; open politics, no decision shown for the movement.

cases.n: UAE-backed southern council's chief becomes Yemen's vice-president
cases.rank: vice-president of the Presidential Leadership Council
cases.d: The United Arab Emirates got its client, the Southern Transitional Council (STC), into Yemen's top leadership. The STC was formed in May 2017 with UAE help to seek a separate southern state. In April 2022 it joined Yemen's eight-member Presidential Leadership Council and its leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi became a vice-president. After an STC offensive in December 2025 and a Saudi-backed counter-offensive, al-Zubaidi fled to the UAE in January 2026 and was removed from the council. A delegation in Riyadh announced the STC's dissolution, which its UAE-based spokesman rejected.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Southern Transitional Council', citing Al Jazeera (7 Jan 2026)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open power-sharing place for a foreign-backed group; no decision shown serving the UAE.

cases.n: Grand Orient de France chief meets Gabon's coup leader, a Freemason
cases.rank: president of the transition (now elected president)
cases.d: The Grand Orient de France, France's largest Masonic body (a society of lodges whose members pledge mutual help), reached out to Gabon's new ruler, described as one of its own.
