cases.d: In the 'mensalão' (big monthly payment) scandal of 2005, Lula's Workers' Party was accused of paying coalition deputies in Brazil's Congress monthly sums for their votes, with the cash drawn from Banco Rural. Documents from Brazil's financial intelligence unit (COAF) confirmed large cash withdrawals from Banco Rural branches in Brasília and Belo Horizonte, made through firms of publicist Marcos Valério, for deputies, their relatives or advisers. In 2012 the Supreme Federal Court found that public money and bank loans had been misused. It convicted Banco Rural's president Kátia Rabello of criminal association, fraudulent management, money laundering and currency evasion, sentencing her to 16 years and 8 months, along with Valério and party leaders including José Genoino.
cases.cite: Supreme Federal Court of Brazil, Ação Penal 470 (2012); Portuguese Wikipedia 'Kátia Rabello'; Wikipedia 'Mensalão scandal'
cases.who: Workers' Party via Banco Rural and Marcos Valério
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Vote-buying by the governing party itself; the bank was a cash channel.

cases.n: Ex-JPMorgan and Deutsche bankers run Argentina's economy and central bank
cases.rank: Minister of Economy; President of the Central Bank
cases.d: Two former JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank executives were put in charge of Argentina's economy ministry and its central bank. Luis Caputo, who had been Mauricio Macri's finance minister (2017–18) and briefly central bank president in 2018, became Javier Milei's Minister of Economy on 10 December 2023. On Caputo's recommendation Milei named Santiago Bausili, who worked at JPMorgan from 1996 to 2007 and later ran debt business at Deutsche Bank, as President of the Central Bank of Argentina, which regulates the country's banks and manages its currency.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Luis Caputo', 'Santiago Bausili' (citing Reuters, 3 Dec 2023; Buenos Aires Times)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Former bankers took posts; no decision shown serving their banks.

cases.n: Mossad chief pressed ICC prosecutor; Israel spied on court staff
cases.rank: chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court
cases.d: Israel's intelligence services tried to steer the International Criminal Court in The Hague, the only permanent court that tries individuals for war crimes, by pressing and spying on its senior staff, according to a May 2024 investigation by the Guardian, +972 Magazine and Local Call. It reported that former Mossad director Yossi Cohen privately pressed prosecutor Fatou Bensouda before she opened an investigation into Palestine, telling her 'You should help us and let us take care of you.' It also reported that Israeli intelligence spied on, hacked and pressured senior ICC staff for nearly ten years, including intercepting communications of Bensouda and her successor Karim Khan. Israel's prime minister's office denied the claims.
cases.cite: The Guardian / +972 Magazine / Local Call investigation, 28 May 2024
cases.org_note: org = target body; infiltrator is mossad
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Pressure and spying from outside; no one inside the court shown working for Israel.

cases.n: Ex-US ambassador Richard Olson secretly helped Qatar lobby
cases.rank: former ambassador and State Department special envoy
cases.d: Richard Olson, a former US ambassador to the UAE (2008–2011) and Pakistan (2012–2015), pleaded guilty in 2022 to illegally helping the government of Qatar influence US officials soon after he left the State Department, where former senior officials are barred for a period from lobbying for foreign governments. He also admitted hiding gifts, such as first-class flights, from a Pakistani-American lobbyist tied to a Qatari official, who paid him $20,000 a month. In 2023 he was sentenced to three years' probation and a $93,350 fine.
cases.cite: US District Court, Washington DC, plea 2022 and sentence 2023; Lawfare, 2 May 2022
cases.org_note: foreign_state = Qatar
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): He acted after leaving office, as an undeclared lobbyist from outside.

cases.n: Saudi funding threat got coalition dropped from UN child-harm list
cases.d: Saudi Arabia and its allies used their funding of UN programmes to get the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen taken off a UN blacklist. The UN Secretary-General's annual 'children and armed conflict' report lists parties to wars that kill and maim children. On 9 June 2016 Ban Ki-moon said he had temporarily removed the coalition from the list because of 'undue pressure' from its supporters, who threatened to stop funding many UN programmes. Saudi Arabia's UN ambassador denied making threats.
cases.cite: UN Secretary-General press remarks, 9 June 2016 (AP)
cases.org_note: org = target body; infiltrator is Saudi Arabia (foreign_state)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open funding pressure from outside the UN.

cases.n: Indian Chronicles: pro-India network used UN-accredited NGOs in Geneva
cases.rank: UN Human Rights Council and European Parliament
cases.d: A network linked to India's Srivastava Group used UN-accredited NGOs, some with direct ties to the group, to get speakers into sessions of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, where they promoted Indian interests and criticised Pakistan. NGOs with UN accreditation may speak at Council sessions. EU DisinfoLab, a Brussels research group, reported this in 2019 and in December 2020 ('Indian Chronicles'). The network revived dead NGOs, impersonated dead rights activists and ran hundreds of fake local news sites (750 across 116 countries by 2020, by later counts). It also worked on the European Parliament, mainly to 'discredit Pakistan'. EU DisinfoLab did not show that the Indian government directed it.
cases.cite: EU DisinfoLab, 'Indian Chronicles' (Dec 2020); BBC; swissinfo.ch, 'Report reveals targeted operation to serve Indian interests at the UN', Dec 2020
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): NGO speakers and fake news sites working from outside; no one inside shown.

cases.n: Slovak ministry plane used in Vietnam's abduction of Trinh Xuan Thanh
cases.d: Vietnamese intelligence got help from inside Slovakia's government to move a man it had kidnapped. Trinh Xuan Thanh, a former Vietnamese state-company executive seeking asylum, was seized in Berlin on 23 July 2017; Germany blamed Vietnamese intelligence, expelled an intelligence officer, and a Berlin court in 2018 jailed one accomplice. In 2019 a Slovak journalist found a €17,000 invoice from Slovakia's interior ministry to Vietnam's for a 26 July 2017 flight to Moscow, and ex-president Andrej Kiska wrote that then-interior minister Robert Kaliňák was behind lending the plane. Thanh was later given life in Hanoi.
cases.cite: Kammergericht Berlin verdict July 2018 (upheld 2019); Slovak interior ministry invoice reported 2019
cases.org_note: foreign_state = Vietnam
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An invoiced loan of a ministry plane; no one shown working for Vietnam.

cases.n: Sue Mi Terry charged as South Korean intelligence agent in Washington
cases.rank: former CIA analyst and policy adviser to US officials
cases.d: US prosecutors charged that South Korea's National Intelligence Service (NIS) recruited Sue Mi Terry, a former CIA analyst and Council on Foreign Relations fellow, to work for it inside Washington's policy world from 2013. The Council on Foreign Relations is a leading US foreign-policy think tank. She was indicted in July 2024 as an unregistered foreign agent. Prosecutors said she passed notes from a 2022 private meeting with Secretary of State Antony Blinken and wrote op-eds at the NIS's request, in exchange for designer goods and over $37,000 for her programmes. In October 2026 the Justice Department agreed to drop the charges after one year if she stays out of trouble; she signed a statement acknowledging contacts with and some sponsorship by South Korean officials but no wrongdoing.
cases.cite: US District Court, Southern District of New York, indictment July 2024; deferred prosecution Oct 2026

arch.t: Council on Foreign Relations — Submergence of US Sovereignty (Insider Testimony)

cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): She worked at a think tank, outside any government body, so no institution was entered.

cases.n: Pakistan's ISI paid Ghulam Nabi Fai to lobby the US Congress on Kashmir
cases.rank: members of Congress (campaign donations and lobbying)
cases.d: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), its main spy agency, paid Ghulam Nabi Fai at least $3.5m to lobby US officials on Kashmir, according to US prosecutors. Fai ran the Kashmiri American Council in Washington, which prosecutors called a front for the ISI. He also gave political donations, including to Representatives Dan Burton and Joe Pitts, who said they did not know the source. The FBI arrested him in July 2011. He pleaded guilty in December 2011 and was sentenced in March 2012 to two years.
cases.cite: US District Court, Eastern District of Virginia, plea Dec 2011, sentence Mar 2012
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Lobbying and donations through a front from outside Congress.

cases.n: Iran Experts Initiative: Tehran cultivated scholars at Western think tanks
cases.rank: Pentagon official and US policy circles
cases.d: Iran's Foreign Ministry ran a project, the Iran Experts Initiative, to cultivate Iranian-heritage academics at Western think tanks so they would promote Tehran's positions, according to leaked ministry emails reported by Semafor and Iran International in September 2023. It began in 2014 on a proposal by diplomat Saeed Khatibzadeh. Think tanks are research groups that advise governments. Pentagon official Ariane Tabatabai was linked to it, prompting House Armed Services chairman Mike Rogers to object. The Pentagon reviewed her case and in October 2023 said she had been properly vetted and kept her security clearance.
cases.cite: Semafor and Iran International, Sept 2023 (leaked Iranian ministry emails); Pentagon statement Oct 2023
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Cultivating think-tank scholars from outside; the record does not say what the one linked official did inside.

cases.n: Dutch cocaine fugitive 'Bolle Jos' protected inside Sierra Leone's elite
cases.d: Jos Leijdekkers ('Bolle Jos'), on the Dutch and EU most-wanted lists for cocaine trafficking, has 'high-level protection' in Sierra Leone and two sources said he is married to President Julius Maada Bio's daughter Agnes, Reuters reported on 25 January 2025, citing three sources and video. The footage shows him two rows behind the president at a New Year's Day mass. Sierra Leone said it was investigating and the head of immigration was dismissed; the government denies knowing his whereabouts.
cases.cite: Reuters exclusive, 25 Jan 2025; Dutch Public Prosecution Service statements
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Too vague: reported protection, but no one named inside acting for him.

cases.n: Benjamin Bol Mel: Kiir's state contractor moved into the vice presidency
cases.d: Benjamin Bol Mel, a businessman whose company held South Sudan government contracts, moved into the country's top offices. He is president of ABMC Thai-South Sudan Construction, which received government road contracts worth tens of millions of dollars without competitive bidding, and he served as President Salva Kiir's principal financial adviser and private secretary. The US sanctioned him under the Global Magnitsky corruption order on 21 December 2017. He was named one of South Sudan's vice presidents on 10 February 2025 and deputy secretary general of the ruling SPLM, before a decree removed him from both posts on 12 November 2025.
cases.cite: US Executive Order 13818 designations, 21 Dec 2017; presidential decrees of Feb and Nov 2025; Radio Tamazuj, 'U.S. sanctions Benjamin Bol Mel over corruption', Dec 2017
cases.who: Benjamin Bol Mel and his companies
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A contractor took top posts; no decision in office shown serving his firm.

cases.n: Al-Qaeda-affiliated leaders in the Taliban government, UN monitors say
cases.d: At least three key leaders in Afghanistan's Taliban government are affiliated with al-Qaeda, the UN Security Council's sanctions Monitoring Team assessed in June 2023. The team reports each year on al-Qaeda and the Taliban. Its sixteenth report (December 2025) says al-Qaeda keeps close ties with the Taliban and a presence in several provinces, and that the Pakistani Taliban (TTP), with about 6,000 fighters, has strong support from elements within the Taliban; one member state said TTP chief Noor Wali Mehsud's family receives a monthly payment from the Taliban. The Taliban reject the reports.
cases.cite: UN Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team, reports of June 2023 and Dec 2025 (16th report), as reported by Dawn and the Washington Examiner
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Affiliation of leaders only; no al-Qaeda steering of decisions shown.

cases.n: Slovak PM's chief adviser co-founded firm with 'Ndrangheta-linked man
cases.rank: chief state adviser to the prime minister
cases.d: Mária Trošková, chief state adviser to Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, had co-founded a company in 2011 with Antonino Vadalà, an Italian businessman with suspected links to the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia. Journalist Ján Kuciak, murdered on 21 February 2018, had been finishing an article showing this and on other Italian businessmen in eastern Slovakia with suspected 'Ndrangheta links. It was published on 28 February 2018. Trošková and security council secretary Viliam Jasaň stepped down that day, saying their names were being misused; Fico resigned in March after mass protests.
cases.cite: Aktuality.sk, Kuciak's posthumous article, 28 Feb 2018; Slovak Spectator
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Only a business link between a PM's aide and an 'Ndrangheta-linked man; no action for the mafia shown.

cases.n: Huistas trafficking leader sat in the Central American Parliament
cases.d: US prosecutors say Freddy Salazar Flores, a sitting member of PARLACEN, the Central American Parliament (a regional assembly of Central American states), is a leader of the Huistas, a drug-trafficking organisation on Guatemala's border with Mexico, together with his father-in-law. That would mean the organisation had one of its own leaders holding a seat in a regional parliament. Both men appeared in a Washington court in May 2025 on a 2017 indictment for importing cocaine. Neither has been tried.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice, District of Columbia, indictment 2017, initial appearances May 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Shows a trafficking leader holding a regional parliament seat, but nothing showing he used the seat or the parliament for the group.

cases.n: El Salvador officials secretly bargained with MS-13 and Barrio 18
cases.d: According to the US Treasury, two Salvadoran officials, the director of prisons and the head of the Social Fabric Reconstruction Unit (a government programme for violence-hit neighbourhoods), secretly negotiated with the leaders of the MS-13 and Barrio 18 gangs. The gangs got privileges and money inside the prisons; in return they were to keep homicide numbers down and give the government electoral support. El Faro, a Salvadoran news site, reported the talks from 2020, and Treasury imposed sanctions in December 2021. The government denies it, and no case has been tried.
cases.cite: OFAC designations, December 2021; El Faro reporting from 2020
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A secret deal between government officials and gangs; the gangs did not get people or money inside, the government bargained with them from outside.

cases.n: Jamaica's government shielded the Shower Posse leader from extradition
cases.rank: head of government and security forces
cases.d: Christopher Coke led the Shower Posse, a gang based in Tivoli Gardens, a Kingston neighbourhood in the constituency of Prime Minister Bruce Golding. When the United States asked for Coke's extradition, the Jamaican government resisted for nine months and hired a Washington law firm to lobby against it. The police and army operation to arrest him in 2010 killed at least 69 people. Coke pleaded guilty in New York in 2011. Golding had already resigned over the affair, and a 2016 commission of enquiry found the operation unjustified in how it was carried out.
cases.cite: US v. Christopher Coke, S.D.N.Y., plea August 2011; West Kingston Commission of Enquiry report, 2016; Wikipedia, 'Bruce Golding' (MP for West Kingston)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Shows the government resisted extradition, but nothing in the record says the gang's people or money were inside government.

cases.n: Yaba trafficker list named a sitting MP for Cox's Bazar
cases.d: Bangladesh's own government list of yaba traffickers (yaba is a methamphetamine pill) named Abdur Rahman Bodi, the member of parliament for Cox's Bazar, the district through which almost all yaba enters the country. That placed the trade's alleged patron in parliament. He was convicted in February 2018 of concealing wealth and jailed for three years, but the trafficking allegations were never tried. In 2019 102 dealers, several of them his relatives, surrendered in a staged ceremony.
cases.cite: Dhaka Special Judge's Court, Anti-Corruption Commission case, conviction February 2018
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An MP named on a trafficker list and convicted only of hiding wealth; nothing shows an outside group using him or his office.

cases.n: Venezuelan general armed the FARC
cases.d: The FARC, Colombia's guerrilla army, had a retired Venezuelan army major general, Cliver Alcala Cordones, supplying it with firearms, he admitted in a US court. Alcala was charged in the same 2020 US indictment as President Nicolas Maduro, which alleges that senior Venezuelan officers worked with the FARC to move cocaine; prosecutors use the name Cartel de los Soles for that network. Alcala surrendered to the US Drug Enforcement Administration in Colombia, pleaded guilty to providing material support, including firearms, to the FARC, and was sentenced to 260 months in April 2024. He was the first defendant in that indictment to be sentenced.
cases.cite: US v. Alcala Cordones, S.D.N.Y., plea 2023, sentence April 2024
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A retired general supplying the FARC; record does not show him using any state post on its behalf.

cases.n: Los Pochos trafficking group led by a Guatemalan mayor
cases.d: Erik Suniga Rodriguez led a Guatemalan drug-trafficking organisation, Los Pochos, while serving as a town mayor, according to the US Treasury. In December 2019 Treasury sanctioned him under the Kingpin Act together with the organisation, four associates and five Guatemalan companies. It sanctioned the group again in February 2024, noting a change of leadership and that its members were still involved in local politics.
cases.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, December 2019; redesignation under E.O. 14059, February 2024
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A trafficker who was also a mayor; nothing in the record shows the mayor's office used for the group.

cases.n: Captagon producer held a seat in Syria's parliament
cases.d: Amer Khiti, a sitting member of Syria's parliament, was sanctioned by the UK in March 2023 and the EU in April 2023 over companies used to produce, package and move captagon, an amphetamine-type pill smuggled across the Middle East. The captagon trade thereby had one of its own operators holding a seat in the national legislature.
cases.cite: UK FCDO designation, March 2023; Council of the EU designation, April 2023
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A captagon producer who was an MP; nothing shows the seat or parliament used for the trade.

cases.n: Thai senator charged over a Myanmar-linked drug network
cases.d: Prosecutors charged that a drug network linked to Myanmar reached into Thailand's upper house through Senator Upakit Pachariyangkun. He was indicted in 2023 on narcotics trafficking and money-laundering charges tied to a Myanmar businessman arrested in Bangkok in 2022, whom the United States had sanctioned for supporting Myanmar's military government. The senator's Thai-American son-in-law was among those arrested, and Thailand's Narcotics Control Board seized property worth over 400 million baht from his homes. The drugs came from Shan State, a production area in Myanmar.
cases.cite: Thai Office of the Attorney General indictment, 2023; Narcotics Control Board seizures; OFAC designations of the associated network
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A senator charged with trafficking himself; no use of his office for the network shown.

cases.n: Kenyan MP and ports minister named a drug kingpin
cases.d: Harun Mwau was designated by the US as a drug kingpin in June 2011 while a sitting member of Kenya's parliament. He had earlier headed the national anti-corruption agency, funded a presidential campaign, and been appointed assistant transport minister with responsibility for container arrangements and the Ports Authority, which gave him a say over the port through which drugs would pass. He resigned after being named in parliament and has always denied the allegations. A police investigation cleared him, in what researchers described as controversial circumstances.
cases.cite: OFAC Kingpin Act designation, June 2011; Kenyan parliamentary naming and subsequent police inquiry
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Kingpin designation of an MP and minister; record says his post gave him a say over the port but shows no decision made for traffickers.

cases.n: Ruling party figures and heroin traffickers in Mozambique
cases.d: Heroin traffickers in Mozambique worked for three decades in what researchers call 'a tight integration' with figures in the ruling party. The 2018 research for the Global Initiative and ENACT, by Haysom, Gastrow and Shaw, pointed to near-zero heroin seizures in Mozambique as evidence that state protection kept the trade moving. It named a principal figure who was designated as a trafficker abroad while remaining a prominent businessman at home. Members of his family were arrested in Portugal and Eswatini, and one was shot dead in Maputo in 2012. None was charged in Mozambique.
cases.cite: Global Initiative and ENACT research by Haysom, Gastrow and Shaw, 2018; LSE International Development working paper 18-190
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Research inference of ruling-party integration from low seizures; no named official or inside action shown.

cases.n: Escobar of the Sahara network included Moroccan MPs
cases.d: The Escobar of the Sahara network, a cannabis and cocaine trafficking organisation named after a jailed Malian trafficker, had Moroccan politicians among its members. In June 2026 a Casablanca court sentenced 29 people after a two-year trial, among them a construction figure and former head of a regional council, who got 12 years, and two former members of parliament from the governing party, who got 10 each. The case began when the Malian said his Moroccan political associates had seized his assets after his 2019 arrest. Charges covered drug and gold trafficking, corruption and laundering. One defendant was acquitted and appeals are open.
cases.cite: Casablanca Court of Appeal, verdicts 26 June 2026
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Former MPs convicted as network members; nothing shows their seats or offices used for it.

cases.n: Kings Romans network controls part of a Lao economic zone
cases.d: The Kings Romans network, headed by Zhao Wei, gained control of part of Laos through a state concession. In 2007 Laos granted the Chinese company Kings Romans a concession over the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone, on the Lao side of the area where Laos, Thailand and Myanmar meet. In January 2018 the US Treasury sanctioned Zhao Wei and his wife over heroin and methamphetamine trafficking and laundering. The US State Department reported in 2024 that the zone is controlled and administered in part by transnational criminal organisations, and that no complicit official has been investigated or prosecuted. Laos arrested more than 20,000 people for drug offences between 2015 and 2019.
cases.cite: OFAC Transnational Criminal Organizations designation, January 2018; US State Department Trafficking in Persons Report 2024
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An open state concession to a company later found to be run by a crime network; no officials shown placed or paid inside.

cases.n: Scam-compound owners protected by Cambodian politics, one a senator
cases.d: The owners of Cambodian fraud compounds, sites where trafficked workers are forced to run online scams, have had political protection, and one of them sat in Cambodia's Senate. US Treasury designations (sanctions that freeze assets and bar dealings) in December 2019, September 2024 and October 2025, and matching UK designations, named Cambodian tycoons and companies and repeatedly gave political protection as the reason the compounds operate openly. One designated figure was a serving senator. The designations are executive findings; Cambodian courts have prosecuted none of them.
cases.cite: US Treasury OFAC designations, December 2019, September 2024 and October 2025; UK sanctions designations
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Political protection cited in general terms; record does not show who inside government acted for the compounds or how.

cases.n: EU review finds cocaine networks have got inside EU ports
cases.d: Cocaine smuggling networks have significantly penetrated EU ports, including the likely corruption of some port staff, a 2025 joint review by the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA) and the World Customs Organization (WCO), which coordinates customs services worldwide, concluded. Its evidence was the size of the seizures: more than 1,826 tonnes of drugs were seized in or bound for EU ports between January 2019 and June 2024, 1,244 tonnes of it at the ports themselves and 82 percent of it cocaine, mostly at Antwerp and Rotterdam. The average consignment was too large to move without help from inside, and the review placed the weak point in staff access rather than in screening technology. Belgian customs reported a record 116 tonnes seized at Antwerp in 2023.
cases.cite: European Union Drugs Agency and World Customs Organization joint report, 2025; Belgian customs figures, January 2024
cases.rank: Container terminals across the EU (shipping, freight & ports)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An inference from seizure volumes of 'likely' staff corruption across EU ports; no specific insiders shown.

cases.n: Scam-compound boss advised two Cambodian prime ministers
cases.d: Chen Zhi, founder of Cambodia's Prince Group, served as an adviser to two Cambodian prime ministers while, according to a US indictment in Brooklyn, his group ran scam compounds where trafficked workers held under debt bondage carried out investment fraud. The United States and United Kingdom designated (sanctioned) the Prince Group in October 2025 with 146 individuals and entities, adding nine people and 26 entities on 23 June 2026. A sitting Cambodian senator, Kok An, and his network were designated over the same scam-compound economy in April 2026. Chen Zhi was stripped of his Cambodian citizenship and sent to China in January 2026. Treasury cited at least $10 billion lost by Americans to Southeast Asian scam operations in 2024.
cases.cite: OFAC designations under E.O. 13581 as amended, 23 June 2026 (Treasury release sb0538) and 14 October 2025; designation of Senator Kok An and network, 23 April 2026; US v. Chen Zhi, E.D.N.Y. indictment unsealed October 2025
cases.rank: Senator's companies and a scam-compound network (casinos & junkets)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A scam boss who advised prime ministers; nothing shows the advisory role used to steer decisions for his group.

cases.n: Philippine mayor linked to scam hub found to be a foreign national
cases.d: Offshore gambling and scam operators in the Philippines had a town mayor on their side who was later found to be a foreign national. Philippine offshore gaming operators (POGOs) were companies licensed to run online gambling for customers abroad, and the sector employed tens of thousands. Alice Guo, mayor of Bamban in Tarlac province, was linked to a licensed operation in her town that was found to host fraud compounds and laundering, and she was later found unable to lawfully hold office. Senate hearings in 2024 exposed the abuses. The Philippine Ombudsman dismissed her in August 2024, and a Manila court later ruled she had never been qualified to serve. The president ordered the sector shut by the end of 2024, which displaced the operations rather than ending them.
cases.cite: Philippine Presidential directive, July 2024; PAGCOR licence revocations; Philippine Senate committee hearings, 2024; Philippine Ombudsman dismissal order, August 2024 (Philstar, Inquirer, GMA News); Manila Regional Trial Court ruling on Guo's disqualification, June 2025 (Manila Bulletin)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A mayor linked to a gaming operation; record shows no decision she made for it, and her foreign nationality is not tied to any outside party.

cases.n: Moscow funded the Communist Party USA, rising to $3m a year by 1987
cases.d: The Soviet state secretly paid for the Communist Party USA, an American political party that ran candidates for office, from 1959 to 1989. Payments began at $75,000 in 1959 and rose to $3 million in 1987; a receipt signed by party leader Gus Hall is held in the KGB archives. The FBI followed the money through two senior party officials, Jack and Morris Childs, who were its informants from 1952 (Operation SOLO) and carried funds from Moscow. The Soviet party cut off funding in 1989 after Hall attacked Gorbachev's reforms, and the American party had to cut its daily newspaper to a weekly.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Communist Party USA' (citing KGB archive receipt signed by Gus Hall; Tromblay on Operation SOLO)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Soviet funding of a political party, which is not a government body, international body or company.

cases.n: Romania's top court annuls presidential vote after Russian-backed campaign
cases.d: Romanian intelligence documents, declassified by President Klaus Iohannis on 4 December 2024, said that the first-round winner of the presidential election, Călin Georgescu (22.94%), rose through a campaign funded and coordinated by a 'state actor', which Romanian authorities identified as Russia. One TikTok account, reportedly registered to Bogdan Peșchir, paid about €381,000 to accounts promoting Georgescu, and more than 25,000 accounts were involved. On 6 December 2024 the Constitutional Court annulled the election. In March 2025 the electoral bureau barred Georgescu from the rerun, and in September 2025 he and 21 others were charged with plotting a coup.
cases.cite: Romanian Supreme Council of National Defence (CSAT) documents, 4 Dec 2024; BBC News, 4 Dec 2024; Guardian, 6 Dec 2024; Reuters, 9 Mar 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Online campaign funded from outside; no one placed inside an institution.

cases.n: Russian 'illegals' cultivated a Clinton campaign co-chair and US policy circles
cases.d: Russia's foreign intelligence service, the SVR, placed long-term 'illegals' (agents living under false identities without diplomatic cover) in the United States with orders to build ties to academics, industrialists and policymakers and report on US policy. One, Cynthia Murphy (real name Lidiya Guriyeva), cultivated Alan Patricof, a venture capitalist who had co-chaired Hillary Clinton's 2008 presidential campaign; her handlers told her to 'build up relations little by little'. The FBI arrested ten agents on 27 June 2010. None was charged with obtaining classified material. On 9 July 2010 all ten pleaded guilty to acting as unregistered agents and were swapped in Vienna for four prisoners held by Russia, including Sergei Skripal.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice, 28 Jun 2010; FBI, 'Operation Ghost Stories', 31 Oct 2011; NYT, 28 Jun 2010
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Agents never got inside a government body; no classified material obtained.

cases.n: Chinese military intelligence chief allegedly gave $300,000 for US Democrats
cases.d: Donor Johnny Chung testified to a House committee in May 1999 that General Ji Shengde, then head of China's military intelligence, told him 'I will give you 300,000 U.S. dollars' for the Democrats, and that $35,000 of his donations came via the general through Liu Chaoying, an aerospace executive. In 1997 the Washington Post reported that a Justice Department investigation found evidence that Chinese agents had tried to steer foreign money to the Democratic National Committee before the 1996 election, using the Chinese embassy to coordinate. China denied it. Several fundraisers, including Chung, John Huang and Charlie Trie, pleaded guilty or were convicted of campaign-finance crimes, and the party returned donations.
cases.cite: Washington Post, 13 Feb 1997; NYT, 12 May 1999; Senate Governmental Affairs Committee final report, 10 Mar 1998
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Donations to a party with no official shown receiving money in return for favour.

cases.n: Ex-CIA officer Jerry Chun Shing Lee took MSS cash as CIA's China agents vanished
cases.d: Jerry Chun Shing Lee, a CIA officer with top-secret clearance from 1994 to 2007, was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) in Shenzhen in April 2010, when two MSS officers gave him $100,000 in cash and promised to 'take care of him for life'. He deposited hundreds of thousands of dollars in cash in Hong Kong bank accounts from 2010 to 2013. In the same period the CIA lost 18 to 20 of its informants in China, who were killed or imprisoned. Arrested by the FBI in January 2018, he was charged with conspiracy to commit espionage, pleaded guilty in May 2019 and was sentenced in November 2019 to 19 years.
cases.cite: South China Morning Post, 16 May 2018; US Department of Justice, Nov 2019
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Recruited after leaving the CIA; not inside any institution at the time.

cases.n: Ex-CIA officer Kevin Mallory sold defence secrets to Chinese intelligence
cases.d: Kevin Mallory, a former US Army soldier, State Department security agent, CIA officer and contractor who had held top-secret clearance, was approached in 2017 by an officer of China's Ministry of State Security posing as a headhunter. He then gave his Chinese contacts US defence secrets, including top-secret documents. A jury convicted him on 8 June 2018 of conspiracy to transmit national defence information to a foreign government, and in May 2019 he was sentenced to 20 years. He had left government service and was working as a consultant when the approach came.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice, 17 May 2019; Wikipedia 'List of Chinese spy cases in the United States'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Recruited after leaving government service; not inside any institution.

cases.n: Ex-CIA officer Alexander Ma gave Chinese handlers secrets, then joined FBI
cases.rank: Former CIA officer; FBI contract linguist
cases.d: Alexander Yuk Ching Ma, a CIA officer from 1982 to 1989, gave classified material to Chinese intelligence handlers in return for cash and gifts, and later took a job as a contract linguist for the FBI, which hired him while it monitored him. He was arrested in 2020 and pleaded guilty on 24 May 2024, under a deal expected to bring about ten years in prison. The case showed a former CIA officer passing secrets to China decades after leaving the agency.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice, 24 May 2024; Wikipedia 'List of Chinese spy cases in the United States'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Passed secrets after leaving the CIA; FBI hired him while monitoring him.

cases.n: Chinese state port builder accused of funding Rajapaksa's 2015 campaign
cases.d: China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), a Chinese state-owned contractor that built Sri Lanka's Hambantota port with Chinese state loans, is accused of funding President Mahinda Rajapaksa's January 2015 re-election campaign. A leaked US embassy cable said Sri Lanka had to accept CHEC as builder to obtain the loan. Sri Lankan newspapers reported in 2015 and 2016 that police investigators were examining the payments, and in 2018 State Minister Eran Wickramaratne called for an inquiry after further reports. CHEC denied funding the campaign. In July 2017, unable to service its debts, Sri Lanka leased Hambantota for 99 years to a Chinese state firm.
cases.cite: NYT, 25 Jun 2018; Sunday Observer, 1 Jul 2018; BBC News, 29 Jul 2017
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Campaign money only, with no favour in return described.

cases.n: Loans-for-shares: bankers who funded Yeltsin took Russia's top firms
cases.d: In 1995 a group of Russian commercial bankers got President Boris Yeltsin's government to hand them shares in the country's largest state companies in return for loans, under a scheme proposed by Vladimir Potanin of Oneximbank and endorsed by deputy prime minister Anatoly Chubais. The government was short of money, including for Yeltsin's 1996 re-election campaign. The auctions were rigged and run by politically connected insiders. Potanin acquired Norilsk Nickel at a bargain price, and Mikhail Khodorkovsky's Menatep took a 78 percent stake in the oil company Yukos, worth about $5 billion, for $310 million. The scheme created the businessmen known as oligarchs, some of whom then financed Yeltsin's re-election and took government posts.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Loans for shares'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open, rigged privatisation scheme rather than people placed inside.

cases.n: Banker Potanin became Russia's First Deputy PM after loans-for-shares
cases.d: Vladimir Potanin, president of Oneximbank and the proposer of the 1995 loans-for-shares scheme, which gave politically connected banks shares in Russia's biggest state companies in return for loans, served as Russia's First Deputy Prime Minister from 14 August 1996 to 17 March 1997, under Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and President Boris Yeltsin. Through the scheme Potanin and Mikhail Prokhorov came to own 54 percent of Norilsk Nickel, the nickel and palladium producer. His appointment came weeks after Yeltsin's re-election, which the bankers had helped fund. After leaving government he returned to business and remained Norilsk Nickel's main owner.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Vladimir Potanin'; Wikipedia, 'Loans for shares'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Banker took a government post; no decision shown for his firm.

cases.n: Tycoon Berezovsky, Yeltsin's campaign funder, entered the Security Council
cases.rank: Deputy Secretary of the Security Council
cases.d: Boris Berezovsky, a businessman who had controlled the main state television channel ORT since December 1994, helped organise the 'Davos Pact' of tycoons who bankrolled President Boris Yeltsin's 1996 re-election campaign. On 30 October 1996 Yeltsin appointed him Deputy Secretary of Russia's Security Council, the body that advises the president on defence and security, a post he held until November 1997. From April 1998 to March 1999 he was Executive Secretary of the Commonwealth of Independent States, the grouping of former Soviet republics. He and Badri Patarkatsishvili also helped Roman Abramovich take control of the oil company Sibneft in the 1995–1997 loans-for-shares auctions.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Boris Berezovsky (businessman)'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Tycoon took a government post; no decision shown serving him.

cases.n: Karachi affair: submarine deal commissions funded Balladur's campaign
cases.d: Commissions paid on France's 1994 sale of Agosta 90B submarines to Pakistan, a contract worth about €826 million, were partly used to finance the 1995 presidential campaign of Prime Minister Édouard Balladur, according to reported French court findings. Commissions of 6.25 percent, about €50 million, were reportedly paid to lobbying firms and officials in both countries; the businessman Ziad Takieddine received millions. Pakistan's Benazir Bhutto government had chosen the French boats over cheaper British ones. In 2002 a bomb in Karachi killed eleven French engineers working on the submarines; Pakistani investigators blamed militant groups, while some European reports linked the attack to the cancellation of the commissions, which Pakistan rejected.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Karachi affair'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): No outside party: commissions from the state's own arms sale funded a campaign.

cases.n: US says Peevski used bribes to control key Bulgarian institutions
cases.rank: State Agency for National Security head (2013); key institutions
cases.d: Delyan Peevski, a Bulgarian MP and media owner, was sanctioned by the US Treasury in June 2021 under the Global Magnitsky Act, a US law that targets corruption, for 'regularly' using influence peddling and bribes to shield himself from scrutiny and to exert control over key Bulgarian institutions and sectors. His family's New Bulgarian Media Group reportedly owned six of the 12 largest newspapers by 2013. On 14 June 2013 parliament elected him head of the State Agency for National Security (DANS), the counter-intelligence agency; thousands protested and he stepped down the next day. The protests contributed to Prime Minister Plamen Oresharski's resignation. The UK sanctioned Peevski in February 2023.
cases.cite: US Treasury designation, June 2021; UK FCDO sanctions, Feb 2023; Wikipedia, 'Delyan Peevski'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): No official on the receiving end of the bribes is identified.

cases.n: Sri Lanka central bank bond sale favoured governor's son-in-law's firm
cases.d: In February 2015 Sri Lanka's central bank, under Governor Arjuna Mahendran, advertised Rs 1 billion of 30-year bonds but accepted about Rs 10 billion, and Perpetual Treasuries, a bond dealer owned by Mahendran's son-in-law Arjun Aloysius, received about Rs 5 billion at 12.5 percent. A presidential commission reported in December 2017 that Mahendran was directly responsible for losses of LKR 11,145 million. In March 2018 a Colombo court issued an arrest warrant alleging he had passed confidential central bank information to Perpetual Treasuries; Aloysius had been arrested in February. Mahendran denied wrongdoing and stayed in Singapore, which declined to extradite him, and in 2022 a special court dismissed the charges.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Arjuna Mahendran'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Governor favouring his own relative's firm; no outside party paid or placed him.

cases.n: Eli Lilly's US president Alex Azar became Health Secretary
cases.rank: Secretary of Health and Human Services
cases.d: Alex Azar, president of Lilly USA, the largest division of the drug maker Eli Lilly, from 2012 to January 2017, became US Secretary of Health and Human Services, the department that includes the Food and Drug Administration and the Medicare programme, which pays for many Americans' medicines. The Senate confirmed him on 24 January 2018 by 55 votes to 43. During his time at Lilly the price of its top-selling insulin roughly tripled, and Lilly was one of three companies accused in a class-action lawsuit over insulin pricing. Senator Ron Wyden, who voted against him, said Azar had 'never, not one time, signed off on a decrease in the price of a drug.'
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Alex Azar'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Drug executive took a post; no decision shown serving Lilly.

cases.n: Raytheon's head of lobbying Mark Esper became US Defense Secretary
cases.d: Mark Esper, hired in July 2010 as vice-president of government relations, the lobbying arm, at the weapons maker Raytheon, moved from that job into the posts that buy Raytheon's products. He was confirmed as Secretary of the Army on 15 November 2017 by 89 votes to 6. After serving as acting Secretary of Defense from June 2019, he was confirmed as the 27th US Secretary of Defense on 23 July 2019 by 90 votes to 8. The Defense Department is the main customer for Raytheon's missiles and other military systems.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Mark Esper'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Lobbyist took a post; no decision shown serving Raytheon.

cases.n: Goldenberg: Pattni's firm drew Kenyan public money for fake gold exports
cases.rank: Finance Minister and Central Bank of Kenya
cases.d: Goldenberg International, a company run by businessman Kamlesh Pattni, was given a monopoly on gold exports in November 1990 and paid compensation from Kenyan public funds worth about 35 percent above its foreign-currency earnings, though its exports may have been minimal or nonexistent. Finance minister George Saitoti authorised an extra 15 percent over the objections of Treasury advisers. David Munyakei, a Central Bank of Kenya clerk, exposed the scheme in 1993 and was fired. The cost was estimated at more than 10 percent of Kenya's annual GDP. The Bosire Commission reported in February 2006, tracing KSh 158.3 billion in Goldenberg-linked transactions and recommending charges against Saitoti, but a court ruled that year that he could not be charged.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Goldenberg scandal'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): No payment to any official or insider is identified.

cases.n: Anglo Leasing: phantom firms got Kenyan security contracts via ministers
cases.org_label: Anglo Leasing Finance and related phantom firms
cases.d: Phantom companies, beginning with the British firm Anglo Leasing Finance, were given heavily overpriced Kenyan government security contracts that were never delivered, with ministers named as involved. In the first case a French firm quoted about €6 million to replace Kenya's passport printing system, but the contract went to Anglo Leasing at about €30 million. In January 2006 John Githongo, the government's former anti-corruption chief, released a report naming ministers Kiraitu Murungi, David Mwiraria and Chris Murungaru and Vice-President Moody Awori, and said President Mwai Kibaki was complicit; all denied wrongdoing. Mwiraria and Murungi resigned in February 2006. No one was punished, and a UK Serious Fraud Office probe was halted.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Anglo-Leasing scandal'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Phantom firms with no outside party behind them identified.

cases.n: Radia tapes: lobbyist for Tata and Reliance and India's cabinet posts
cases.org_label: Niira Radia (lobbyist for Tata and Reliance)
cases.d: Niira Radia, a corporate lobbyist whose clients included India's Tata Group and Reliance Industries, was recorded by the income tax department over six months in 2009, while the new cabinet was being formed after the general election. Transcripts published in 2010 suggested she had influence over how ministerial posts were allocated, including the telecom ministry held by A. Raja. The recordings became a foundation of the 2G spectrum case, in which the government was accused of selling mobile radio spectrum cheaply to ineligible companies; the national auditor put the potential loss at ₹1,760 billion. In February 2012 the Supreme Court cancelled 122 licences. Raja resigned and was later acquitted, and Radia left lobbying in 2011.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Niira Radia'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Too vague: tapes only suggest a lobbyist's influence over cabinet posts.

cases.n: Thirteen officials held over El Chapo's 2015 Altiplano tunnel escape
cases.rank: Federal prison system and Altiplano prison command
cases.d: Officials of Mexico's federal prison system were charged over Joaquín 'El Chapo' Guzmán's second escape. On 11 July 2015 the Sinaloa Cartel leader left the Altiplano maximum-security prison through a tunnel dug into his cell. By September judges had ordered 13 public officials held for trial: a former national coordinator of federal prisons, a former director general, the Altiplano prison's director and commander, and nine monitors from the control room that watched his cell. It was his second escape from a maximum-security prison in 14 years.
cases.cite: Fox News/AP, 'Number of Mexican prison officials held in connection to Chapo Guzmán escape rises to 13' (25 Sep 2015); Wikipedia, Joaquín Guzmán
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Record does not say the charged officials worked for the cartel.

cases.n: US testimony says Zetas gave $12m to Veracruz governor's campaign
cases.d: Testimony in US trials of Los Zetas members said the cartel financed a governor's election in Veracruz. A 2017 review by University of Texas law students of statements from more than 20 Zetas tried in Austin, San Antonio and Del Río reported that in 2004 the Zeta commander Efraín Torres gave $12 million, through the businessman Francisco Colorado Cessa, to support Fidel Herrera's campaign for governor. The same testimony described Zetas using Colorado's oil-services company ADT Petroservicios, a Pemex contractor, to launder money. Herrera, governor from 2004 to 2010, denied cartel links; the testimony was never tested against him in court, and he died in 2025.
cases.cite: El Financiero (7 Nov 2017); Wikipedia, Fidel Herrera Beltrán
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Campaign money only, with no favour in return described.

cases.n: Félix Gallardo, ex-federal agent, used Sinaloa governor's connections
cases.rank: Governor of Sinaloa's household and state officials
cases.d: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, who built the Guadalajara Cartel, began inside the state. He had been a Mexican Federal Judicial Police agent and worked as a family bodyguard for Sinaloa governor Leopoldo Sánchez Celis, becoming godfather to the governor's son. The governor's connections helped him build his trafficking organisation, and he brokered corruption of state officials. US officials said he later stayed as a guest at the house of Sinaloa governor Antonio Toledo Corro, who denied it. Félix Gallardo was arrested on 8 April 1989 and has been imprisoned since, moving to house arrest in 2022.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo (citing Los Angeles Times and others)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Too vague on which officials were corrupted and how.

cases.n: Ex-justice minister Santofimio convicted as co-author of Galán murder
cases.rank: Former Minister of Justice and senator
cases.d: A former Colombian justice minister and senator was convicted of helping the Medellín Cartel kill a presidential candidate. Alberto Santofimio Botero had been justice minister in 1974–75, a senator and twice a presidential candidate. In October 2007 he was sentenced to 24 years as a co-author of the August 1989 assassination of Luis Carlos Galán, on testimony from the Escobar hitman Jhon Jairo 'Popeye' Velásquez. A court overturned the verdict in 2008, but on 31 August 2011 the Supreme Court reinstated the 24-year sentence. He was paroled in March 2020. In 2018 he was placed under investigation over the 1984 killing of Justice Minister Rodrigo Lara Bonilla.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, Alberto Santofimio
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): He held no post at the time; an accomplice to murder, not an insider.

cases.n: President Petro's son says traffickers' money entered the 2022 campaign
cases.org_label: Samuel Santander Lopesierra and Gabriel Hilsaca
cases.d: Money from a convicted drug trafficker reached the campaign of Colombia's president, according to the president's own son. Nicolás Petro, a former regional legislator on the Caribbean coast, was arrested on 29 July 2023 and charged. Prosecutors said about $270,000 had been delivered to him by Samuel Santander Lopesierra, known as the 'Marlboro Man', who was convicted of drug trafficking in the US, and by Gabriel Hilsaca, and that part went to Gustavo Petro's 2022 campaign. Nicolás Petro told prosecutors the campaign received money of dubious origin, then pleaded not guilty. The president said he would not interfere.
cases.cite: WLRN/AP (4 Aug 2023); El Tiempo; Vanguardia (3 Aug 2023)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Campaign money only, with no favour in return described.

cases.n: Ñeñepolítica: wiretaps of a trafficker discuss buying votes for Duque
cases.d: Wiretaps of a drug trafficker suggested he moved money to buy votes for Iván Duque in Colombia's 2018 presidential election. José Guillermo 'Ñeñe' Hernández, said by Colombian and US authorities to be a partner of the trafficker Marcos Figueroa, was recorded during a Barranquilla murder investigation. In audio published in March 2020 he spoke of vote-buying money for the second round and of enlisting businessmen. He was a main guest at Duque's inauguration and was killed in Brazil in May 2019. The prosecutor's office and Congress's accusations committee closed their inquiries, and no court found that Duque or Álvaro Uribe took part.
cases.cite: Colombia Reports (4 Mar 2020); El Tiempo (Fiscalía archive decision); El Universal Cartagena (15 Dec 2021)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Campaign vote-buying talk, with no favour in return described.

cases.n: Cachiros video shows traffickers offering cash to Castro's brother-in-law
cases.rank: Secretary of Congress; Libre party campaign
cases.d: The Cachiros, a Honduran trafficking clan, negotiated with a senior figure in the ruling family's party. In video secretly recorded in 2013 and published by InSight Crime and Univision on 3 September 2024, Cachiros members including Devis Leonel Rivera Maradiaga offered Carlos Zelaya, brother-in-law of President Xiomara Castro, $650,000 for her 2013 campaign and discussed past bribes to former president Manuel Zelaya. Carlos Zelaya, then secretary of Congress, said he took no money and acted without Castro's knowledge. He and Defence Minister José Manuel Zelaya, Castro's nephew, resigned on 31 August 2024, days before the video appeared. Castro called the affair a coup plot.
cases.cite: El Faro (4 Sep 2024); InSight Crime; AP via ABC News (Sept 2024)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Offer of campaign money, with no favour in return described.

cases.n: Presidential candidate Mario Estrada sought Sinaloa Cartel campaign cash
cases.rank: Presidential candidate (offered state posts and ports)
cases.d: A Guatemalan presidential candidate tried to sell the state to the Sinaloa Cartel. Mario Estrada, who ran for president in 2018 and 2019 and at times polled in the top five, asked people he believed were cartel representatives for millions of dollars in drug money for his campaign. In return he promised, if elected, 'unfettered access' to Guatemala's airports and ports, high government posts for cartel members and a share of profits, and asked them to hire hitmen to kill rivals. The contacts were US informants. He pleaded guilty to cocaine importation conspiracy and on 11 February 2020 a New York court sentenced him to 15 years.
cases.cite: US Attorney's Office, Southern District of New York, press release (11 Feb 2020)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Never took office, and the 'cartel' contacts were US informants.

cases.n: Alleged 'Octopus' gang leader Aleksei Petrov advised Bulgaria's DANS
cases.d: Bulgarian police said a man they accused of leading an extortion gang had been working inside the national security agency. Aleksei Petrov became an informant for DANS, the State Agency for National Security, in 2001 and an official adviser in 2008. On 10 February 2010 he was detained and accused of heading a criminal group called 'Octopus' engaged in racketeering and extortion. The charges were later narrowed to two cases from 1998 and 2000, the investigation was closed for lack of evidence in 2014, and he was acquitted in July 2021. He ran for president in 2011. Petrov was shot dead in Sofia on 16 August 2023.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Aleksei Petrov (businessman)'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An alleged gang leader advised the security agency, but nothing shows the post was used for the gang.

cases.n: US-sanctioned Gafur Rakhimov elected head of world amateur boxing
cases.d: A man the US Treasury listed as a member of a transnational crime network became head of the International Boxing Association (AIBA), which then ran Olympic boxing. In February 2012 the Treasury sanctioned the Uzbek businessman Gafur Rakhimov among people it accused of belonging to the 'Brothers' Circle', a Eurasian criminal group. Rakhimov, who denies wrongdoing and has never been charged, was elected AIBA president in November 2018 despite criticism from the International Olympic Committee. In June 2019 the IOC suspended AIBA's recognition and ran boxing at the Tokyo Games itself. Rakhimov resigned on 15 July 2019. Boxing's Olympic place stayed in doubt for years afterwards.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'International Boxing Association (amateur)' and 'Gafur Rakhimov' (citing US Treasury, Feb 2012; IOC, June 2019)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A sanctioned man was elected boxing chief; no decision shown serving a crime network.

cases.n: Inagawa-kai boss Ishii got billions in credit from Sagawa and brokers
cases.rank: Sagawa Kyubin, Nomura and Nikko Securities
cases.d: Susumu Ishii, head of the Inagawa-kai, one of Japan's largest yakuza groups, from 1985 to 1990, got large sums out of major Japanese companies. He received credit and loans totalling about $2.5 billion from the delivery firm Sagawa Kyubin, whose payments to politicians caused a corruption scandal from 1992 that helped bring down the ruling Liberal Democratic Party. Using $200 million in loans from Nomura and Nikko Securities, Japan's leading brokers, he bought 27 million shares in Tokyu Corporation and made a profit of almost $2 billion. When his links to the brokers became public, Nikko's president and Nomura's chairman and president resigned. Ishii died in 1991.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Susumu Ishii' and 'Sagawa Express' (citing The Independent, 1993; New York Times, 1994)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Companies lent money to a yakuza boss; no one placed inside them is shown.

cases.n: Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank lent ¥30bn to corporate racketeers
cases.d: Sokaiya, corporate racketeers often tied to the yakuza who extort companies by threatening to disrupt shareholder meetings, got money out of Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, then one of Japan's largest banks. The bank's loans to sokaiya, granted during the late-1980s bubble, amounted to ¥30 billion. Tokyo prosecutors raided the bank in 1997, and its former president and chairman, Kuniji Miyazaki, hanged himself at home that year. In a separate case three top executives of Nomura Securities pleaded guilty to payments to a sokaiya who held enough Nomura shares to propose his own choice for the board. Japanese law bans benefits given for statements or votes at shareholder meetings.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank' and 'Sōkaiya'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Racketeers extorted money from outside; no one placed inside the bank.

cases.n: Gang leader Lo Fu-chu co-chaired Taiwan's legislative judiciary committee
cases.d: A self-described gang leader sat in Taiwan's parliament and helped run the committee that oversees the justice system. Lo Fu-chu called himself a leader of the Celestial Alliance, formed in the mid-1980s by mob bosses jailed together. He was an independent member of the Legislative Yuan from 1996 to 2002, leading an 11-member bloc. He joined its judicial committee in 1998 and became one of its three co-chairs in 2000, which drew wide protest; Justice Minister Liao Cheng-hao reportedly refused to attend while Lo sat on it. This was the period of 'black gold' politics, when a 1994–95 campaign led to 320 local councillors being prosecuted. Lo was convicted of stock manipulation in 2013.

cases.n: ICICI veteran Buch chaired India's market regulator amid conflict claims
cases.rank: Chairperson, Securities and Exchange Board of India
cases.d: Madhabi Puri Buch, who worked at ICICI Bank from 1989 and was chief executive of ICICI Securities from 2009 to 2011, became the first private-sector head of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), the stock-market regulator, on 1 March 2022, after five years as a board member. In August 2024 Hindenburg Research alleged that she and her husband had held stakes in offshore funds that it said Vinod Adani used in Adani Group shares, which SEBI was investigating. The Congress party alleged she kept receiving ICICI benefits while at SEBI. She and ICICI denied the claims. Her term ended in February 2025, and in May 2025 the Lokpal ombudsman dismissed complaints for lack of evidence.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Madhabi Puri Buch'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Conflict claims dismissed; no decision shown serving ICICI.

cases.n: Ombudsman: ECB chief's seat in bankers' Group of Thirty risked undue influence
cases.d: The Group of Thirty, a private club whose 30 members include heads of large private banks alongside central bank governors from about 19 countries, had the President of the European Central Bank, Mario Draghi, as a member. The ECB is the central bank and main bank supervisor of the euro area. In January 2018 the European Ombudsman, Emily O'Reilly, asked Draghi to leave the group, saying his membership could be seen as giving its banking members undue influence. The group's members have also included two presidents of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Group of Thirty'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Membership of a club only; no decision shown.

cases.n: Iraq paid Tongsun Park to lobby the UN Secretary-General on Oil-for-Food
cases.d: Saddam Hussein's government paid the South Korean businessman Tongsun Park, already known from the 1970s 'Koreagate' bribery of US congressmen, to use his access to the United Nations leadership. In 1992 Samir Vincent, an Iraqi-born American working unofficially for Baghdad, recruited Park to help set up a programme easing sanctions on Iraq. Park acted as a go-between with Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, a friend, and the Oil-for-Food Programme began in late 1996, partly after his lobbying. He received about $2 million. In July 2006 a US federal jury convicted him of conspiracy, the first conviction from the Oil-for-Food investigation, and in February 2007 he was sentenced to five years in prison.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Tongsun Park', citing US court records 2006–07; NPR, Jan 2007
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Paid lobbying of the Secretary-General from outside, not someone inside the UN.

cases.n: UN inquiry: nine UNRWA staff in Gaza may have joined the 7 October attack
cases.d: Members of armed Palestinian groups were found among the staff of UNRWA, the UN agency that runs schools and aid for Palestinian refugees and is headquartered in Amman and Gaza. In January 2024 Israel alleged that 12 UNRWA employees took part in the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023; UNRWA fired them and major donors suspended funding. The UN's internal investigators, OIOS, concluded in 2024 that nine staff may have been involved, and they were dismissed; evidence was insufficient for nine others. A separate review led by Catherine Colonna found Israel had not shown evidence for its wider claim that many staff belonged to armed groups. In October 2024 Israel's parliament banned UNRWA from operating in Israel.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'UNRWA and Israel', citing UN OIOS findings Aug 2024 and Colonna review 22 Apr 2024
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Staff took part in an attack; nothing shown done inside UNRWA for the groups.

cases.n: Industry-tied experts on EU food-safety agency panels, auditors found
cases.who: Food and chemical industry, incl. ILSI
cases.rank: Expert panels and board of the European Food Safety Authority
cases.d: Experts tied to the food and chemical industries sat on the panels of the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), the EU agency in Parma that gives the scientific advice on which EU food, pesticide and additive rules are based. In 2012 the European Court of Auditors criticised EFSA for 'frequent conflicts of interests', some undeclared, and several of them involved the International Life Sciences Institute (ILSI), a research group founded and funded by food companies including Coca-Cola. The campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory counted 58% of EFSA experts with conflicts of interest in 2013 and 46% in 2017. EFSA tightened its independence rules after the findings.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'European Food Safety Authority', citing European Court of Auditors special report 2012 and Corporate Europe Observatory 2013, 2017
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Conflicts of interest found, but no EFSA decision shown serving industry.

cases.n: Hezbollah seized west Beirut and won a cabinet veto in 2008
cases.d: Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Shia party and armed group, won a veto inside Lebanon's government by force in 2008. In early May 2008 the cabinet declared Hezbollah's private fibre-optic telephone network illegal and removed the security chief of Beirut airport, Brigadier General Wafic Shkeir, seen as close to Hezbollah. Its leader Hassan Nasrallah called this a 'declaration of war'; from 8 May its fighters and allies took over much of west Beirut, and about 70 to 110 people were killed. The government withdrew both decisions on 10 May. The Doha Agreement of 21 May gave Hezbollah and its allies a 'blocking third' of cabinet seats, enough to veto decisions, which shaped Lebanese governments for years after.
cases.cite: Wikipedia '2008 Lebanon conflict' and 'Hezbollah', citing UN, Human Rights Watch and Doha Agreement text
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open armed seizure and a public power-sharing deal, not infiltration.

cases.n: Houthi movement took over Yemen's state and runs it through its own council
cases.rank: Head of state functions (Supreme Political Council) and cabinet
cases.d: The Houthi movement, a Zaydi Shia armed group from northern Yemen, took control of Yemen's capital and its state institutions. Its fighters captured Sanaa's government buildings on 21 September 2014; in December they evicted oil company officials, blocked the port director in Hodeidah and fired four provincial governors. After President Hadi resigned on 22 January 2015, the Houthis declared parliament dissolved and on 6 February 2015 issued a 'constitutional declaration' putting their Revolutionary Committee in charge. On 28 July 2016 they and allies set up the Supreme Political Council, which performs head-of-state functions and appoints the cabinet in Sanaa. The UN called it a clear violation of Yemen's constitution. It still governs most of Yemen's population.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Houthi takeover in Yemen' and 'Supreme Political Council', citing UN statements and Reuters
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An open armed takeover of the state.

cases.n: Janjaweed-born RSF made a state force; its chief Hemedti reached the top
cases.rank: Deputy head of Sudan's Sovereignty Council; state paramilitary
cases.d: The Rapid Support Forces, built in August 2013 from the Janjaweed militias that Sudan's government had used in Darfur, were placed inside the state under the intelligence service and army, and their leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, rose to the top of government. In 2017 he used the RSF to take Darfur gold mines, and his firm al-Junaid became Sudan's biggest gold trader. After the 2019 coup against Omar al-Bashir he became deputy head of the ruling council and joined the Sovereignty Council on 21 August 2019. RSF forces killed about 100 protesters in Khartoum on 3 June 2019. In April 2023 the RSF went to war with the army. On 7 January 2025 the US found it had committed genocide.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Rapid Support Forces' and 'Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo', citing US State Department, Jan 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): The state built the RSF itself; no outside party got in.

cases.n: Kahanist Ben-Gvir, convicted of backing a terror group, became police minister
cases.d: A leader of the Kahanist movement, which follows the banned anti-Arab Kach party, was given ministerial control of Israel's police. Itamar Ben-Gvir was Kach's youth coordinator and was convicted in 2007 of incitement to racism and of supporting a terrorist organisation, Kach. His party Otzma Yehudit is seen as Kach's ideological successor. Under the coalition deal of late 2022 he became head of a new National Security Ministry over the police, including the Border Police in the West Bank. The cabinet reappointed him in March 2025 over the Attorney General's objections. On 10 June 2025 the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Norway froze his assets and banned travel, accusing him of inciting settler violence.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Itamar Ben-Gvir', citing Times of Israel and UK government statement, 10 Jun 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open coalition appointment; no police decision shown serving the movement.

cases.n: Azov commander Vadym Troyan became Kyiv police chief, then deputy minister
cases.rank: Kyiv region police chief; acting head of National Police; deputy interior minister
cases.d: Members of the Azov movement, a nationalist militia founded in 2014 by Andriy Biletsky, who had led the far-right Patriot of Ukraine and Social-National Assembly, moved into top police posts. Azov was first a volunteer unit funded through the Interior Ministry and on 11 November 2014 was made part of the National Guard. On 31 October 2014 its deputy commander Vadym Troyan was appointed police chief of Kyiv region. He went on to be first deputy and acting head of the National Police and, from February 2017 to September 2019, a deputy minister of internal affairs. Biletsky himself was elected to parliament in 2014. The appointments drew criticism because of the movement's far-right origins.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Azov Brigade' and 'Vadym Troyan', citing Ukrainian government decrees and press
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Militia members appointed to police posts; no decisions shown.

cases.n: Svoboda, heir to a Social-National party, held deputy PM and two ministries
cases.rank: Deputy Prime Minister; agriculture and environment ministers; three governors
cases.d: Svoboda, an ultranationalist party descended from the Social-National Party of Ukraine, which in the 1990s was accused of neo-Nazism for recruiting skinheads and using neo-Nazi symbols, placed its members in Ukraine's government after the 2014 revolution. In the Yatsenyuk government formed on 27 February 2014, Oleksandr Sych became Deputy Prime Minister, Ihor Shvaika Minister of Agrarian Policy and Andriy Mokhnyk Minister of Environment. In early March party members were made governors of the Poltava, Ternopil and Rivne regions. Svoboda left the coalition on 24 July 2014, its ministers resigned on 12 November 2014, and President Poroshenko dismissed the three governors on 18 November.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Svoboda (political party)', citing Ukrainian government records 2014
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open coalition seats; no decisions shown.

cases.n: Irish ministers Haughey and Blaney sacked over alleged arms plan for IRA
cases.rank: Minister for Finance; Minister for Agriculture; army intelligence officer
cases.d: The Arms Crisis of 1970 was an alleged plan by two serving Irish cabinet ministers and an army intelligence officer to bring in weapons for republicans in Northern Ireland, linked to the IRA and the Northern Citizen Defence Committees. Taoiseach Jack Lynch dismissed Finance Minister Charles Haughey and Agriculture Minister Neil Blaney on 6 May 1970 after they refused to resign; Kevin Boland resigned in protest, saying Lynch and Defence Minister Jim Gibbons had known. Captain James Kelly of army intelligence was involved. Charges against Blaney were dropped, and in October 1970 Haughey, Kelly and two others were found not guilty of conspiracy. Haughey later became Taoiseach. The case is listed as contested because the trial ended in acquittal.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Arms Crisis', citing Irish trial record 1970
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Ministers' own alleged plan; no outside party shown placing or recruiting them.

cases.n: Oath Keepers list held 370 serving police and 100 military members
cases.rank: Police and military personnel; elected officials
cases.d: The Oath Keepers, an anti-government militia that recruits from police and the military, had members working in law enforcement and the armed forces. In September 2021 hackers took its membership files and Distributed Denial of Secrets released data on about 38,000 apparent members, including applications from serving police officers, some filed after the 6 January 2021 attack on the US Capitol. In September 2022 the Anti-Defamation League found that over 370 names appeared to be current law enforcement employees and over 100 current military personnel, and dozens of elected officials were also linked. Founder Stewart Rhodes was convicted of seditious conspiracy on 29 November 2022 and sentenced to 18 years; his sentence was commuted in January 2025.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Oath Keepers', citing ADL report Sept 2022 and US DOJ
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Membership list of police and soldiers only; no decisions inside police or military shown serving the group.

cases.n: Germany dissolved a special forces company over far-right extremists in it
cases.rank: Kommando Spezialkräfte (KSK), Germany's army special forces
cases.d: Far-right extremists built up inside the KSK, the German army's elite special forces unit based in Calw. Federal police reportedly uncovered in 2018 a plot involving KSK soldiers to kill prominent politicians and attack immigrants on a 'Day X', and prosecutors investigated neo-Nazi gestures at a KSK farewell party. In June 2020 Defence Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer announced that the 2nd Commando Company would be dissolved and not replaced, after what the ministry described as a notable build-up of right-wing extremists in the unit, and she spoke of a 'toxic leadership culture'.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Kommando Spezialkräfte', citing German Defence Ministry, June 2020
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Extremists among the unit's own soldiers; no defined outside party shown placing them.

cases.n: Breakaway Tiger commander Karuna made Sri Lanka's integration minister
cases.d: The leader of an armed group that fought alongside Sri Lanka's forces was brought into parliament and the cabinet. Vinayagamoorthy Muralitharan, known as Karuna Amman, had been the Tamil Tigers' top commander in the east before breaking away in July 2004 and forming the TMVP, which fought the Tigers with the Sri Lankan army. UNICEF and Human Rights Watch accused the group of recruiting child soldiers, and rights groups linked it to disappearances; he denied this. He became an MP in October 2008, Minister of National Integration in March 2009 and a vice-president of the ruling SLFP in April 2009. In March 2025 the UK sanctioned him over alleged wartime abuses.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Karuna Amman', citing UNICEF, Human Rights Watch and UK FCDO, Mar 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open appointment of an ex-rebel leader to cabinet; no decision shown serving his group.

cases.n: French generals led a putsch in Algeria; army officers then ran the OAS
cases.rank: Generals and colonels of the French army
cases.d: Supporters of keeping Algeria French had their people at the top of the French army and used them against the government. On 21–26 April 1961 four generals, Maurice Challe, Edmond Jouhaud, André Zeller and Raoul Salan, seized Algiers with units including the Foreign Legion's 1st Parachute Regiment, to stop President de Gaulle ending the Algerian War. The putsch failed; Challe and Zeller got 15 years, and Salan and Jouhaud were sentenced to death in absentia. Salan and colonels such as Yves Godard and Antoine Argoud then led the OAS, a clandestine armed group that killed Algiers police chief Roger Gavoury in May 1961 and tried to kill de Gaulle at Petit-Clamart in August 1962.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Algiers putsch of 1961' and 'Organisation armée secrète', citing French military tribunal records
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A mutiny by the army's own generals; no outside party placed them.

cases.n: Serving army officer Purohit co-founded Hindu nationalist Abhinav Bharat
cases.rank: Lieutenant Colonel, Indian Army military intelligence
cases.d: Abhinav Bharat, a Hindu nationalist group, counted a serving Indian Army intelligence officer, Lieutenant Colonel Prasad Shrikant Purohit, among its founders, and Maharashtra's anti-terrorism squad said serving and retired army officers had taken the group over. The squad linked Purohit and Sadhvi Pragya Singh Thakur to the bombings of 29 September 2008 in Malegaon and Modasa, which killed six people.
