Purohit said he had joined the group to gather intelligence as part of his job, and an army court of inquiry heard 59 witnesses say so. Thakur was later elected a BJP MP. In 2025 a special court of the National Investigation Agency acquitted all seven accused, finding conspiracy not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Abhinav Bharat', '2008 Malegaon blasts' and 'Prasad Shrikant Purohit', citing Maharashtra ATS and NIA court
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Army officers joining an outside group, not the group getting inside or steering the army.

cases.n: Blue Shirts: Chiang's secret officers' society inside the Kuomintang
cases.rank: Army, ruling party and intelligence bureau
cases.d: The Blue Shirts Society was a secret ultranationalist faction set up in 1932 by Chiang Kai-shek inside his Nationalist party, the Kuomintang, mainly from young army officers who had trained at the Whampoa Military Academy. Membership was strictly secret and Chiang never publicly acknowledged it. Its members spread through the military and the party, competing with a civilian faction, the CC Clique, and some joined the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics, the regime's espionage and assassination service. Membership peaked at about 10,000 in 1935. In 1938 the new Three Principles of the People Youth Corps was placed largely under Blue Shirt influence.
cases.cite: Blue Shirts Society (Wikipedia, citing Jeffrey Crean)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A faction the party's own leader created inside his party; no outside party.

cases.n: Can Lao: Nhu's secret party placed cells across South Vietnam's state
cases.rank: Army, police, civil service and assembly
cases.d: The Cần Lao Party was set up on 2 September 1954 by Ngô Đình Nhu and his brother Ngô Đình Diệm, who became South Vietnam's president; Nhu was its general secretary. It worked covertly through cells whose members often knew only a few others. Members were placed in the army, civil service, police, national assembly, schools and media, and membership grew from about 10,000 in 1955 to 1,386,757 active members in 1962. Historian Bernard Fall called it 'a state within a state'. After the November 1963 coup in which Diệm and Nhu were killed, the party was banned and dissolved.
cases.cite: Cần Lao (Wikipedia, citing Bernard Fall)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): The ruling family's own secret party; no outside party.

cases.n: Secret IRB recruited Irish Volunteer leaders and launched the 1916 Rising
cases.d: The Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB), a secret oath-bound society founded in 1858 to win an independent Irish republic, backed the founding of the Irish Volunteers militia in November 1913 and then recruited the Volunteers' senior members into the IRB, so that a body with no stated republican aim could be used for one. A secret IRB Military Committee of Tom Clarke, Seán Mac Diarmada, Joseph Plunkett, Thomas MacDonagh and Patrick Pearse planned a rising, and in January 1916 the IRB Supreme Council fixed Easter Sunday as its date. The Easter Rising followed. Michael Collins later served as president of the IRB Supreme Council from 1920 to 1922, and its council voted 11–4 to accept the 1921 Anglo-Irish Treaty.
cases.cite: Irish Republican Brotherhood (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): The body infiltrated was a private militia, not a government, international body or company.

cases.n: Black Dragon Society counted ministers and generals; army used its network
cases.rank: Cabinet ministers; senior army officers; intelligence
cases.d: The Black Dragon Society (Kokuryūkai) was an ultranationalist society founded in 1901 by Uchida Ryōhei as the successor to Tōyama Mitsuru's Gen'yōsha, with the stated aim of keeping Russia north of the Amur River. Its members included Japanese cabinet ministers, senior army officers and intelligence operatives. The Imperial Japanese Army used the society's network for espionage, sabotage and assassination during the Russo-Japanese War, the annexation of Korea and the Siberian Intervention, and it organised Manchurian guerrillas against Russian forces. The American occupation authorities ordered it disbanded in 1946.
cases.cite: Black Dragon Society (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Members included officials, but the record shows the army using the society, not the society steering the state.

cases.n: Rosicrucian Wöllner made Prussia's minister of justice and religion
cases.rank: Minister of Justice; head of the Office for Worship
cases.d: Johann Christoph von Wöllner was a supreme director of circles of the Order of the Golden and Rosy Cross, a secret Rosicrucian society, and a friend of fellow member Johann Rudolph von Bischoffswerder; King Frederick William II of Prussia was himself a member under the order name Ormesus. In 1788 the king made Wöllner Minister of Justice and head of the Office for Worship. Under the decree of 9 July 1788 he helped set up a commission to oversee religious activity across Prussia, with powers to confiscate money and property. Frederick the Great had earlier called him 'a treacherous and intriguing priest'.
cases.cite: Johann Christoph von Wöllner (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An official belonged to a secret society; nothing shows it steered his decisions.

cases.n: Carbonária's 40,000 members drove Portugal's 1910 republican revolution
cases.d: The Portuguese Carbonária was a secret, anti-clerical revolutionary society, refounded in 1896 by Artur Augusto Duarte da Luz de Almeida and organised in a hierarchy of cells with military training. It took part in plots against the monarchy; King Carlos I and his heir Luís Filipe were assassinated on 1 February 1908 in a conspiracy involving the Carbonária. By 1910 the society had about 40,000 members, and it played a key role in the revolution of 5 October 1910 that ended the monarchy and created the Portuguese Republic.
cases.cite: Carbonária (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A revolutionary uprising from outside; no members placed inside institutions shown.

cases.n: Sun Yat-sen's secret Tongmenghui became the core of China's ruling party
cases.d: The Tongmenghui was a secret society and underground resistance movement founded in Tokyo on 20 August 1905 by Sun Yat-sen, Song Jiaoren and others, by merging Sun's Xingzhonghui, the Guangfuhui and other revolutionary groups. Its members organised against the Qing dynasty, and after the 1911 Xinhai Revolution Sun became Provisional President of the new Republic of China in January 1912. In August 1912 the Tongmenghui formed the nucleus of the Kuomintang, the Nationalist party that later ruled China and then Taiwan.
cases.cite: Tongmenghui (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A revolutionary movement that later formed a party; no infiltration of an institution shown.

cases.n: Santamaria's Catholic 'Movement' took hold of Labor unions; party split
cases.rank: Australian Labor Party and trade unions
cases.d: The Catholic Social Studies Movement, founded in Victoria in 1941 by B. A. Santamaria with the backing of Archbishop Daniel Mannix, gained a large influence over the 'Industrial Groups', anti-communist factions organised by Catholic members inside the Australian Labor Party and its trade unions from the late 1940s. After the 1954 federal election Labor leader H. V. Evatt turned on the 'Groupers', saying they held disproportionate influence in the party. This led to the 1955 Labor split: many Groupers resigned or were expelled, several unions left, and they formed what became the Democratic Labor Party. The split and the DLP's preferences to the Liberals are described as a major reason Labor stayed out of federal power for almost 30 years.
cases.cite: Industrial Groups (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): The bodies taken over were a party's factions and unions, not a government, international body or company.

cases.n: Haqqania seminary graduates fill the Taliban government's ministries
cases.rank: Interior, foreign, higher education and other ministries
cases.d: Darul Uloom Haqqania, a Deobandi seminary at Akora Khattak in Pakistan nicknamed the 'University of Jihad', has supplied much of the leadership of Afghanistan's Taliban. After the Taliban took power in August 2021 its graduates held senior posts including acting Interior Minister Sirajuddin Haqqani, acting Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi, Higher Education Minister Abdul Baqi Haqqani and Hajj Minister Noor Mohammad Saqib; the school said the justice and water ministers and various governors, commanders and judges were also alumni. Its chancellor Samiul Haq, called the 'Father of the Taliban', wrote in 2015 that about 90 percent of the religiously educated people in the Taliban government were graduates or sons of graduates. The seminary reserves 400 places for Afghan students.
cases.cite: Darul Uloom Haqqania (Wikipedia, citing Rassler and Brown; Samiul Haq 2015)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Seminary alumni holding posts; nothing shows the school steering them.

cases.n: RSS-founded think tank VIF supplied Modi's security adviser and PMO chiefs
cases.rank: National Security Adviser; Prime Minister's Office
cases.d: The Vivekananda International Foundation (VIF), a Delhi think tank set up in December 2009 by Vivekananda Kendra, an organisation of the RSS-led Hindu nationalist family (Sangh Parivar), supplied several of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's top officials in 2014. Its founding director, former Intelligence Bureau chief Ajit Doval, became National Security Adviser; Nripendra Misra became Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister, and P. K. Mishra Additional Principal Secretary. Other VIF figures went to the NITI Aayog planning body, the Lieutenant Governor's post in Delhi, the state broadcaster Prasar Bharati and the national journalism institute. The VIF says it has no formal links to the RSS or BJP. Doval remains National Security Adviser.
cases.cite: Vivekananda International Foundation (Wikipedia, citing Tehelka Aug 2014, The Caravan Nov 2017, Business Standard Jun 2014)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Think-tank people took posts; no decision shown serving the think tank.

cases.n: RSS 'dual membership' of ministers Vajpayee and Advani broke India's government
cases.d: After the Janata Party won India's 1977 election, former leaders of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, the RSS's political wing, took major posts: Atal Bihari Vajpayee became External Affairs Minister and L. K. Advani Information and Broadcasting Minister. Other Janata leaders pressed them to give up their membership of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation, while in government. Vajpayee, Advani and other former Jana Sangh members chose to stay in the RSS. The dispute fed the collapse of Prime Minister Morarji Desai's government, which resigned on 19 July 1979, and the RSS-linked members then founded the Bharatiya Janata Party in 1980.
cases.cite: Janata Party (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Ministers kept RSS membership; no decision shown that the RSS steered.

cases.n: RSS full-timer of 17 years Khattar made Haryana's chief minister
cases.rank: Chief Minister of Haryana; Union Minister
cases.d: Manohar Lal Khattar joined the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation that trains and supplies cadres for the BJP, in 1977 and became a full-time organiser (pracharak) about three years later, working in that role for 17 years before the RSS moved him to the BJP in 1994. Elected to the Haryana assembly for the first time in 2014, he was sworn in as the state's Chief Minister on 26 October 2014, the BJP's first in Haryana, and held the post until 2024. On 10 June 2024 he became Union Minister of Power and of Housing and Urban Affairs in Modi's government.
cases.cite: Manohar Lal Khattar (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An RSS organiser's career path to chief minister; no decision shown serving the RSS.

cases.n: Pentagon watchdog: six senior officers endorsed Christian Embassy in uniform
cases.rank: Generals and colonels at the Pentagon
cases.d: Christian Embassy, an evangelical group affiliated with Campus Crusade for Christ (now Cru) and founded in 1975 to minister to members of Congress, officials and diplomats, filmed a promotional video in 2004 in which seven military officers, in uniform at the Pentagon, endorsed it. After the video went online in November 2006 the Military Religious Freedom Foundation asked the Defence Department's Inspector General to investigate. The Inspector General's July 2007 report found that six senior officers, four generals and two colonels, had improperly endorsed and taken part in a non-federal group while in uniform, some implying they spoke for senior military leaders; a chaplain was found to have given the group a 'selective benefit', and one general had called it a 'quasi-federal entity'.
cases.cite: Christian Embassy (Wikipedia, citing DoD Inspector General report, July 2007)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Officers endorsed a group in uniform; no decisions steered by it shown.

cases.n: Claremont's John Eastman wrote Trump's plan to block the 2020 count
cases.rank: President's legal strategy; Vice President's certification role
cases.d: John Eastman, founder and director of the Claremont Institute's Center for Constitutional Jurisprudence and a former chair of a Federalist Society practice group, wrote memos at the request of someone in the Trump administration arguing that Vice President Mike Pence could hold up certification of the 2020 election, calling the vice president 'the ultimate arbiter'. Pence rejected the argument when they met on 5 January 2021. In March 2022 federal judge David O. Carter found it 'more likely than not' that Eastman and Trump plotted to obstruct the certification. Eastman was indicted in Georgia in August 2023, but those charges were dropped in November 2025, when Trump also pardoned him. The California Supreme Court ordered him disbarred on 15 April 2026.
cases.cite: John C. Eastman (Wikipedia, citing Eastman v. Thompson ruling March 2022 and California State Bar Court)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An outside lawyer's advice to a president; no think tank placing people or steering an institution.

cases.n: Adam Smith Institute papers became the poll tax and rail privatisation
cases.d: The Adam Smith Institute, a London free-market think tank founded in 1977 by Madsen Pirie and Eamonn Butler, wrote policy that British governments turned into law. It published Douglas Mason's proposal to replace local rates with a flat per-head charge, and its papers of 1981–1985 set out the basis of the poll tax, introduced as the Community Charge in Scotland in 1989 and in England and Wales in 1990, then abolished after protests. Its 1987 paper The Right Lines proposed competing private train franchises on a separately owned network, which John Major's government enacted. Its 1981–83 Omega Project produced 19 papers, one per government department. The Thatcher government relied on it, the Centre for Policy Studies and the IEA for policy.
cases.cite: Adam Smith Institute (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Published think-tank proposals adopted by government; open influence from outside.

cases.n: Fabian Society got 229 members into Parliament in 1945 and shaped policy
cases.d: The Fabian Society, a socialist society founded in London in 1884 to move Britain gradually towards socialism by working through institutions, had 229 of its members elected to the House of Commons at the 1945 general election, which brought Clement Attlee's Labour government to power; Attlee and Hugh Dalton were among Fabians in Labour's leadership. Sidney Webb, a leading Fabian, had earlier written the constitution of the Labour Representation Committee, which borrowed heavily from the society's founding documents. Its Fabian Colonial Bureau, set up in October 1940 with Rita Hinden as secretary, strongly influenced the colonial policy of the Attlee government from 1945 to 1951.
cases.cite: Fabian Society (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Members elected openly and public advocacy; no placing or steering beyond that shown.

cases.n: Gremialista leader Guzmán drafted Pinochet's 1980 constitution
cases.rank: Constitutional commission; adviser to the junta
cases.d: Jaime Guzmán founded the Movimiento Gremial, a Catholic conservative student movement, at the Catholic University of Chile's law school in March 1967. After the 1973 coup he became a trusted adviser to General Augusto Pinochet without holding an official post, and was legal adviser to the Ortúzar Commission, formed on 26 September 1973 to draft a new constitution. He is called the principal architect of the 1980 Constitution, approved in a plebiscite under the dictatorship, which governed Chile for four decades. He founded the Independent Democratic Union (UDI) party in 1983 and was assassinated in 1991. Chileans voted to replace the constitution in 2020 but rejected two drafts.
cases.cite: Jaime Guzmán (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): One adviser's role in drafting a constitution; no group shown placing members.

cases.n: IPES think-tank chief Golbery founded Brazil's SNI spy service after 1964
cases.who: IPES / Golbery do Couto e Silva
cases.rank: Head of the National Information Service; presidential chief of staff
cases.d: The Institute for Research and Social Studies (IPES) was a conservative think tank founded in Rio de Janeiro in 1962 by business leaders Augusto Trajano de Azevedo Antunes and Antônio Gallotti. It ran anti-government propaganda and worked to co-opt organisations opposing President João Goulart, and a 1963 parliamentary inquiry investigated it. General Golbery do Couto e Silva headed the institute. After the military coup of 31 March 1964 Golbery became the first head of the new National Information Service (SNI), the regime's intelligence agency, from June 1964 to 1967, and later chief of staff of the presidency from 1974 to 1981. In 1966 the regime declared IPES an 'entity of public utility'.
cases.cite: Instituto de Pesquisas e Estudos Sociais; Golbery do Couto e Silva (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Think-tank head later ran the spy service; no decision shown serving the think tank.

cases.n: Harvard advisers steered Russia's privatisation; Harvard paid $26.5m
cases.d: The Harvard Institute for International Development (HIID) received $40.4 million from USAID, without normal competitive bidding, for a 1992–1997 project led by economist Andrei Shleifer and lawyer Jonathan Hay to help rebuild Russia's economy, including advising on the privatisation of state industry. Oversight was later described as lax. In 1997 USAID ended a $14 million grant after Shleifer was accused of helping his wife's investments in Russia while advising its government. The US government sued, and in 2005 Harvard agreed to a $26.5 million settlement. The Russia scandal was one reason a Harvard task force recommended closing HIID in 2000.
cases.cite: Harvard Institute for International Development (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An open advisory contract; the scandal was an adviser's personal investments.

cases.n: Matsushita Institute trained 66 politicians, including two prime ministers
cases.who: Matsushita Institute of Government and Management
cases.d: The Matsushita Institute of Government and Management was founded on 21 June 1979 by Kōnosuke Matsushita, the founder of Panasonic, with his own money, to 'cultivate young leaders to guide Japan into the twenty-first century'. It is known for training young people to win elections. By 2006, 66 of its 213 graduates had won elected office, including 28 members of the House of Representatives. Its graduates include Democratic Party Prime Minister Yoshihiko Noda, Liberal Democratic Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and Seiji Maehara and Itsunori Onodera.
cases.cite: Matsushita Institute of Government and Management (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A school training politicians who won elections; no steering shown.

cases.n: 'Kaduna Mafia' network said to fill Nigeria's top military-era posts
cases.rank: Central bank governor; defence and finance ministries; chief of staff
cases.d: The 'Kaduna Mafia' is a name, popularised by journalist Mvendaga Jibo, for a loose network of northern Nigerian civil servants, businessmen, intellectuals and officers based in Kaduna that took shape after 1966. People named as members held top posts: Shehu Musa Yar'Adua as Chief of Staff, Supreme Headquarters (1976–1979), Adamu Ciroma as Central Bank Governor (1975–1979) and later Finance Minister, Iya Abubakar as Defence Minister, and Mamman Daura as editor of the New Nigerian. The network is said to have had its greatest success under Obasanjo's military regime and to have returned under the Yar'Adua and Buhari governments. Most claims of its control are hedged, and its membership is unknown.
cases.cite: Kaduna Mafia (Wikipedia, citing Fagbola 1987, William Graf 1988, Daily Trust 2016)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A loose, hedged network with unknown membership; too vague.

cases.n: Ex-NU chairman Wahid elected president by NU-dominated party, Indonesia
cases.d: Abdurrahman Wahid led Nahdlatul Ulama (NU), Indonesia's largest Muslim organisation with tens of millions of followers, as chairman from 1984 to 1999. In 1998 he approved the creation of the National Awakening Party (PKB), which was dominated by NU members and made him head of its advisory council. The PKB named him its presidential candidate in February 1999, and on 20 October 1999 the People's Consultative Assembly elected him Indonesia's fourth president by 373 votes to 313 over Megawati Sukarnoputri. He was impeached and removed on 23 July 2001.
cases.cite: Abdurrahman Wahid (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A religious leader elected president openly; no steering shown.

cases.n: ABIM Islamic youth founder Anwar entered cabinet and Islamised schooling
cases.rank: Education and finance ministries; Deputy Prime Minister
cases.d: Anwar Ibrahim co-founded the Malaysian Islamic Youth Movement (ABIM) in 1971 and was its second president. In 1982 he joined Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's party UMNO, on advice that Mahathir was committed to Islamisation, and entered government. He became Minister of Culture, Youth and Sports in 1983, Agriculture in 1984, Education in 1986, Finance in 1991 and Deputy Prime Minister in 1993. As Education Minister he made many curriculum changes, and analysts link the rise of social conservatism and Islamism among Malays to the Islamisation of schooling under him. He became Prime Minister in 2022.
cases.cite: Anwar Ibrahim (Wikipedia)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A movement founder's ministerial career; no steering by the movement shown.

cases.n: Former Israeli energy minister Gonen Segev spied for Iran
cases.rank: Former energy minister and Knesset member
cases.d: Gonen Segev, Israel's minister of energy and infrastructure in 1995–96 and a former member of the Knesset, Israel's parliament, was recruited by Iranian embassy officials in Nigeria in 2012. He met Iranian intelligence handlers, travelled to Iran twice, received encrypted communications equipment and passed them information. Israel's Shin Bet security service and police announced his arrest in June 2018, after he was refused entry to Equatorial Guinea and sent to Israel. On 9 January 2019 he pleaded guilty to espionage under a deal that dropped the more serious charge of aiding an enemy in wartime, and in February 2019 he was sentenced to 11 years in prison.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Gonen Segev' (Shin Bet statement, Jun 2018; Jerusalem District Court plea, Jan 2019)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Recruited years after leaving office, so he held no post inside government when he spied.

cases.n: Apartheid South Africa's secret fund bid for a US paper and senators' seats
cases.rank: US Senate elections and a Washington newspaper
cases.d: South Africa's Department of Information ran a secret propaganda programme, Project Annemarie, from the mid-1970s, paid from a slush fund hidden in the defence budget with the Bureau of State Security (BOSS) as banker; estimates put the cost at about $72 million or more. Using US publisher John P. McGoff as a front, it tried in 1974 to buy The Washington Star, and it contributed to the electoral defeats of US Senators John Tunney and Dick Clark, who opposed American involvement in Angola's war. South Africa's Erasmus Commission concluded in 1978–79 that Prime Minister John Vorster knew everything; Vorster and Information Minister Connie Mulder were forced out.
cases.cite: Erasmus Commission reports, Dec 1978 and Jun 1979; Wikipedia, 'Information Scandal'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Covert propaganda and a bid to buy a newspaper from outside; no one placed inside.

cases.n: Foccart's Élysée Africa cell ran networks inside former French colonies
cases.d: Jacques Foccart, secretary-general for African and Malagasy affairs to Presidents Charles de Gaulle and Georges Pompidou from 1960 to 1974, built personal networks (réseaux) tying French officials to the leaders of newly independent former colonies, such as Gabon's Omar Bongo and Côte d'Ivoire's Félix Houphouët-Boigny. He negotiated cooperation accords covering finance, education and the military, some defence agreements with secret clauses allowing French intervention, and was given charge of the secret services and of overseeing elections. With Houphouët-Boigny he encouraged French military interventions in Gabon in 1964 and Chad in 1969. Under this system, called Françafrique, the president's African cell, business networks and French intelligence made Africa decisions without parliamentary scrutiny.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Jacques Foccart'; Wikipedia, 'Françafrique'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): France's own Africa policy apparatus; too vague who got inside what.

cases.n: US-funded exile Ahmed Chalabi led Iraq's Governing Council
cases.rank: President of the Iraqi Governing Council
cases.d: Ahmed Chalabi's Iraqi National Congress (INC), an exile opposition group, ran on US government money for years: The Guardian estimated CIA funding in the 1990s at about $100 million, and the US Government Accountability Office found the State Department paid the INC nearly $33 million from March 2000 to September 2003. After the 2003 invasion, the US-run Coalition Provisional Authority gave Chalabi a seat on the Iraqi Governing Council, which he chaired in September 2003. On 19 May 2004 the US stopped its payments, and the next day Iraqi police backed by US soldiers raided his offices, amid reports, which he denied, that he had passed US secrets to Iran.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Ahmed Chalabi' (citing The Guardian; GAO)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open appointment by the occupation authority; no decision shown serving his US funders.

cases.n: India's RAW allegedly helped unite Sri Lanka's opposition against Rajapaksa
cases.d: India's foreign intelligence agency, the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), was alleged to have helped bring Sri Lanka's divided opposition together against President Mahinda Rajapaksa before the January 2015 presidential election. Reports in The Sunday Times and other outlets said RAW's Colombo station chief helped coordinate opposition talks, persuaded Ranil Wickremesinghe not to stand so that a single candidate had a better chance, and kept in touch with former president Chandrika Kumaratunga, who helped convince Maithripala Sirisena to run. Sirisena won. The station chief was reportedly expelled before the vote. India's government and Sri Lanka's new foreign minister denied the claims. India was concerned about Chinese submarines docking in Sri Lanka in 2014.
cases.cite: The Sunday Times and others, Jan 2015, as summarised in Wikipedia, '2015 Sri Lankan presidential election'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Worked on opposition politicians from outside, not inside a state body.

cases.n: Japan accused of buying whaling-commission votes with aid
cases.rank: Member-state votes at the International Whaling Commission
cases.d: Japan was accused of using development aid to win votes at the International Whaling Commission (IWC), the body that regulates whaling worldwide, while it pressed to lift the ban on commercial whaling. It gave US$320 million in aid to Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada, Guinea, Morocco, Panama, St Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines, St Kitts and Nevis, and Solomon Islands, and Caribbean members consistently voted with Japan from 2001. Antigua and Barbuda's prime minister Lester Bird acknowledged a 'quid pro quo', and Dominica's former fisheries minister Atherton Martin said Japan used money 'crudely to buy influence'. Japan denies vote-buying and notes that it also aids anti-whaling states.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'International Whaling Commission' (citing Greenpeace, ABC and press statements by Lester Bird and Atherton Martin)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open aid to member governments; no one placed inside the commission.

cases.n: DEA probe of Fuerza Popular's secretary general over laundering
cases.rank: Congressman and secretary general of Fuerza Popular
cases.d: Reports in May 2016 said the US Drug Enforcement Administration was investigating Joaquín Ramírez, a congressman and secretary general of Fuerza Popular, Keiko Fujimori's party, for money laundering. A Peruvian pilot working as a DEA informant said he had given the agency a recording in which Ramírez said he had laundered $15 million for the 2011 Fujimori campaign through his petrol stations. Ojo Público reported that the DEA's main target was alleged trafficker Miguel 'Eteco' Arévalo. The DEA said Keiko Fujimori was not under investigation, and Ramírez called the claims a political attack. He resigned from the party post on 18 May 2016, during the presidential run-off campaign.
cases.cite: Peru Reports, 18 May 2016; América TV, May 2016
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Unclear whose money was laundered or who got inside what; the target was another man.

cases.n: Ex-head of Peru's anti-drug police investigated over traffickers' links
cases.d: A secret police intelligence note sent to Peru's police commander in June 2023 linked General Deny Rodríguez Bardales, who had headed Dirandro, the national police's anti-drug directorate, in 2022, to anti-drug officers held for trafficking. The note said four officers and a sergeant under his command had ties to two sergeants who are jailed and on trial for drug trafficking in Loreto, the Amazon region bordering Colombia. Anti-drug prosecutors in Loreto and a team in Lima opened an investigation listing Rodríguez among those investigated, and he was retired at the end of December 2023. He said the police inspectorate had reviewed his case and found no responsibility.
cases.cite: El Comercio, 2024
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Ties run through subordinates to jailed police sergeants; too vague who got inside what.

cases.n: Narco clan's mayor of Ypejhú ordered killing of journalist Pablo Medina
cases.d: The Acosta family, a clan that ABC Color reporter Pablo Medina had linked to drug trafficking and killings, held the mayoralty of Ypejhú, a town on Paraguay's border with Brazil, through Vilmar 'Neneco' Acosta. Medina and his companion Antonia Almada were shot dead in 2014. Acosta fled to Brazil, where he was caught and later extradited. In December 2017 a Paraguayan court sentenced him to 29 years in prison plus 10 years of security measures as the intellectual author of the murders, finding that Medina's reporting on the clan's drug trafficking had put him on a hit list. The case became a reference point in Paraguay's debate about 'narcopolítica', drug money in local politics.
cases.cite: ABC Color, 19 Dec 2017; La Nación (Paraguay), 20 Dec 2017
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A clan member who was mayor ordered a murder; no use of the office shown.

cases.n: Cocaine trafficker sat in the Dominican Chamber of Deputies
cases.rank: Member of the Chamber of Deputies
cases.d: A man running a cocaine smuggling operation into the United States won a seat in the Dominican Republic's Chamber of Deputies. Miguel Andrés Gutiérrez Díaz was elected for Santiago in 2020 for the ruling Modern Revolutionary Party. While still a sitting deputy he was arrested in Miami on a US indictment for conspiracy to import cocaine. He pleaded guilty to drug trafficking and money laundering, admitting he sent cocaine to Florida in containers and boats between 2014 and 2020, about 5,000 kilograms according to his plea agreement. In April 2024 a federal court in Miami sentenced him to 16 years.
cases.cite: El Día, 4 Apr 2024; Bloomberg/AP, 2021
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): A trafficker held a seat; no use of the office shown.

cases.n: Kenya's security minister named five MPs and tycoons as drug suspects
cases.d: In December 2010 Kenya's internal security minister, George Saitoti, told Parliament that sitting MPs were among people under investigation for drug trafficking. The list, drawn from a joint US–Kenyan inquiry, named MPs Hassan Joho, William Kabogo, Harun Mwau and Gideon Mbuvi, and Mombasa businessman Ali Punjani. A 2010 US embassy report alleged that Joho, later governor of Mombasa county, was involved in trafficking and that his brother was the clearing agent for containers holding a ton of cocaine in 2004. All denied the claims. Saitoti died in a 2012 helicopter crash and no one on the list was convicted; police said in 2015 they had found no evidence against Mwau.
cases.cite: Correctiv, 'Kenya's drug barons', 16 Apr 2015
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Names on a suspect list with no conviction or use of office shown.

cases.n: Reputed rosewood baron made vice-president of Madagascar's Senate
cases.d: Madagascar's rosewood traffickers, who logged protected forests after the 2009 coup and exported the timber mainly to China, have had one of their reputed leaders placed in the national legislature. Sources of the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) named Erick Lambert Besoa as one of the top timber barons behind the logging. In 2021 President Andry Rajoelina nominated him to the Senate, and he became its vice-president. The EIA described him as a suspected trafficker accused of involvement in silencing environmental activists. He has not been charged. The EIA estimates up to 2.26 million rosewood logs are stockpiled in Madagascar, of which the government has declared about a tenth.
cases.cite: African Arguments, Oct 2024; EIA, 'Convention Evasion', 3 Mar 2022
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Reputed trafficker given a Senate seat, but nothing shows the Senate acted for traffickers.

cases.n: Saudi king's $100m 'gift' to Spain's King Juan Carlos
cases.d: Saudi Arabia's King Abdullah transferred $100 million in 2008 to a Swiss bank account of a Panamanian foundation, Lucum, whose sole beneficiary was Spain's then head of state, King Juan Carlos I. Geneva prosecutor Yves Bertossa investigated whether the money was a commission linked to the Spanish-built high-speed railway between Mecca and Medina; Juan Carlos's former partner Corinna Larsen received €65 million of it. In December 2021 the Swiss closed the case, saying a link to the rail contracts could not be sufficiently established, and fined Mirabaud bank for failing to report the money. In March 2022 Spain's prosecutors also closed their inquiry, saying any crimes were covered by the immunity the constitution gives the head of state. Juan Carlos, who abdicated in 2014, had left Spain in 2020.
cases.cite: Ara (2020); Catalan News (13 Dec 2021); Catalan News (2 Mar 2022)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Even as alleged, a commission for helping Spanish firms win a contract, not Saudi people or money steering Spain's state.

cases.n: UAE adviser George Nader funnelled $3.5m to buy access to US candidates
cases.d: George Nader, an adviser to senior officials of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), used a US businessman, Ahmad 'Andy' Khawaja, to pass at least $3.5 million in illegal political contributions into the 2016 US election, the US Justice Department said. Nader's UAE company sent $4.9 million to Khawaja's company under a false software licensing agreement, and Khawaja made the donations in his own name to political committees, first around Hillary Clinton and then, after the election, $1 million to Donald Trump's inaugural committee. Prosecutors said the aim was access to and influence with a presidential candidate, and that Nader reported to a senior UAE official by encrypted message. The indictment was unsealed in December 2019; in July 2023 Nader was sentenced to a further one year and eight months.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice press release (18 July 2023); Al Jazeera (6 Dec 2019)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Covert campaign donations from outside; no one inside government shown acting for the UAE.

cases.n: Azerbaijan's oil company secretly paid for 10 US lawmakers' Baku trip
cases.d: Azerbaijan's state oil company, SOCAR, secretly paid for ten members of the US Congress and 32 congressional staff to attend a 2013 conference in Baku, hiding the source through US non-profits. A confidential report by the House Office of Congressional Ethics, revealed by the Washington Post in May 2015, said SOCAR sent about $750,000 through the groups, which falsely told Congress they were the sponsors; guests received rugs, crystal tea sets and silk scarves worth $2,500 to $10,000. House rules bar foreign governments from paying for such trips. Kemal Oksuz, head of the Houston non-profit Turquoise Council, pleaded guilty on 10 December 2018 to hiding SOCAR's funding from the House Ethics Committee, after being extradited from Armenia.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice press release (10 Dec 2018); Washington Post via Texas Tribune (13 May 2015)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Hidden-source paid trip and gifts; no decision by lawmakers shown.

cases.n: Sudan's Bashir took $90m in cash from Saudi royals outside the budget
cases.d: Saudi royals paid Sudan's president Omar al-Bashir $90 million in cash that he spent outside the state budget, an investigator told his corruption trial in Khartoum in August 2019. Brigadier Ahmed Ali testified that $25 million came from Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and two earlier payments of $35 million and $30 million from the late King Abdullah. Bashir told investigators the money 'was not part of the state budget and I was the one who authorised its spending', and could not say how it was used. Bashir, who had ruled since a 1989 coup, was overthrown in April 2019. On 14 December 2019 the court convicted him of illegal possession of foreign currency and corruption and sent him to a reform centre for two years.
cases.cite: Al Jazeera (19 Aug 2019); Al Jazeera (14 Dec 2019)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Cash to a president outside the budget; no decision shown serving Saudi Arabia.

cases.n: Ex-ISI chief told Pakistan's top court the ISI funded Bangladesh's BNP
cases.d: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), its main spy agency, paid money into the 1991 election campaign of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), which won that vote and formed Bangladesh's government, a former ISI chief told Pakistan's Supreme Court. Asad Durrani, who headed the ISI in 1990–1992, made the admission in March 2012 during a hearing on the agency's mandate before a bench led by Chief Justice Iftikhar Chaudhry, Bangladesh's Daily Star reported. A UAE-based paper alleged the sum was Rs 50 crore to BNP leader Khaleda Zia, but this was not confirmed. The BNP denied receiving ISI money; Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina accused Khaleda Zia of serving Pakistan.
cases.cite: The Daily Star (16 Mar 2012); Deccan Herald (Mar 2012)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Covert money into a party's election campaign from outside; no one inside government shown acting for the ISI.

cases.n: ISI chief in Kabul as the Taliban chose their prime minister
cases.d: Pakistan's spy chief went to Kabul as the Taliban formed their government, and some analysts say he shaped who led it. Lieutenant-General Faiz Hameed, head of the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), was in Kabul around 4 September 2021, three weeks after the Taliban took power. Pakistani analyst Ayesha Siddiqa said the visit helped decide that Mullah Hassan Akhund, not Abdul Ghani Baradar, would head the government; Akhund was named on 7 September. Pakistan and the Taliban denied any interference, and other experts said Taliban dependence on Pakistan had lessened. The Haqqani network, which the US calls an arm of the ISI, took the interior ministry.
cases.cite: RFE/RL (Sept 2021)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open visit; influence over the Taliban cabinet is only analysts' view.

cases.n: Saudi body paid sitting Italian senator and ex-PM Renzi up to $80,000 a year
cases.d: A Saudi institute controlled by the royal family paid Matteo Renzi, Italy's former prime minister and a sitting senator, to sit on its advisory board. The Italian paper Domani reported in January 2021 that membership of the board of the FII Institute, which runs Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's 'Future Investment Initiative' conference, paid up to $80,000 a year. Renzi was in Riyadh at an FII event when Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte resigned, a government crisis Renzi's party had set off, and flew back overnight. At the event he praised the crown prince. The Democratic Party and others asked him to explain his ties to Riyadh after a US intelligence report linked the crown prince to Jamal Khashoggi's murder.
cases.cite: Domani (26 Jan 2021); Fanpage.it (Feb 2021); Middle East Eye (2021)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open paid board seat; no decision shown serving Saudi Arabia.

cases.n: Saudi cables: money to a Lebanese TV channel and party leader's plea
cases.rank: Lebanese party leaders and MTV television
cases.d: Saudi diplomatic cables published by WikiLeaks in June 2015 show Saudi Arabia being asked for, and in some cases paying, money to Lebanese parties, politicians and media in return for support. One cable says the Lebanese TV channel MTV asked for $20 million and received $5 million. Another quotes Samir Geagea, leader of the Lebanese Forces party, saying through an envoy that the party could not pay salaries and 'I'm ready to do what the kingdom demands.' MP Boutros Harb asked for Saudi money to found a party. A further list shows Saudi 'subscription' payments to about two dozen publications across the Arab world. Saudi Arabia told its citizens to ignore the leak.
cases.cite: Global Voices (20 June 2015); Dawn (2015)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Requests and payments to a TV channel and parties; no official inside an institution shown acting for Saudi Arabia.

cases.n: Turkey jailed Constitutional Court deputy chief as Gülen member
cases.rank: Deputy President of the Constitutional Court
cases.d: Turkish prosecutors said the Gülen movement had a member at the top of the Constitutional Court, the court that rules on whether laws and government acts are lawful. Alparslan Altan, the court's deputy president, was detained a day after the July 2016 coup attempt. In March 2019 a court sentenced him to 11 years and 3 months for membership of an armed terrorist organisation, the label Turkey uses for the movement. Altan denied the charge and said there was no concrete evidence. His case was part of a purge in which more than 150,000 people were removed from state jobs; the European Court of Human Rights later found his detention unlawful.
cases.cite: Turkish Minute, 6 Mar 2019 (citing T24); Turkish Minute, 16 Apr 2019 (ECtHR)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Membership conviction of one judge; no ruling or decision shown steered by the movement.

cases.n: Turkey convicted a UN war-crimes judge as a Gülen member
cases.rank: Judge, UN Mechanism for International Criminal Tribunals
cases.d: Turkey said the Gülen movement had a member sitting as a judge on a United Nations court. Aydın Sefa Akay, a Turkish judge at the UN Mechanism for International Criminal Tribunals, which handles remaining appeals from the Yugoslavia and Rwanda war-crimes tribunals, was detained in Turkey in September 2016 during the purge after the coup attempt. In June 2017 a Turkish court sentenced him to seven and a half years for membership of what Ankara calls 'FETÖ', then released him under a travel ban. The UN mechanism said Turkey's actions breached his protected status as a UN judge with diplomatic immunity. The European Court of Human Rights later faulted Turkey over his arrest.
cases.cite: NBC News (AP), Jun 2017; Turkish Minute, 23 Apr 2024
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Membership conviction of one judge; nothing shows the movement used him at the UN court.

cases.n: RSS economic ideologue Gurumurthy put on India's central bank board
cases.rank: Reserve Bank of India central board
cases.d: The government appointed Swaminathan Gurumurthy, co-convenor of the Swadeshi Jagran Manch, an economic body of the Hindu nationalist RSS, to the central board of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in August 2018, alongside Satish Marathe of Sahakar Bharati. At the board's nine-hour meeting on 19 November 2018, held amid a dispute between the government and the bank over its reserves, Gurumurthy was the most vocal member and won approval for restructuring bad small-business loans up to Rs 25 crore. Governor Urjit Patel agreed to a review of Rs 9.6 lakh crore in reserves and resigned on 10 December 2018. Gurumurthy said the resignation surprised him.
cases.cite: Business Today, 8 Aug 2018 and 20 Nov 2018; The Week, 13 Dec 2018
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Group member appointed to the bank board; nothing shows the RSS steered his positions.

cases.n: Gujarat made RSS school leader Batra's books part of state curriculum
cases.d: Dinanath Batra, a full-time leader of Vidya Bharati, the RSS's school network, had his own books placed in Gujarat's state school curriculum. On 30 June 2014 the BJP government of Gujarat issued a circular listing six of his books, translated into Gujarati, as supplementary reading, and the state education minister said they were compulsory. In November 2014 Haryana's new BJP government named him to its committee of educationalists. Batra had earlier filed 70 objections to national NCERT textbooks and, in February 2014, made Penguin India withdraw and pulp Wendy Doniger's book on Hinduism after a lawsuit.
cases.cite: Wikipedia (Dinanath Batra, citing Indian Express and others)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): State openly adopted a group leader's books; no one placed inside shown steering.

cases.n: 62% of India's new military feeder schools went to Sangh and BJP figures
cases.who: RSS, allied bodies and BJP politicians
cases.d: Under a 2022 public-private scheme, India's Defence Ministry handed most new Sainik Schools, boarding schools that prepare cadets for the National Defence Academy, to bodies tied to the RSS and the ruling BJP. The Reporters' Collective found through RTI requests that of at least 40 agreements signed between May 2022 and December 2023, at least 62% went to such groups: 11 schools owned by BJP politicians or their trusts, 8 run by the RSS or allies and 6 tied to Hindutva or other Hindu religious groups. Vidya Bharati, the RSS school network, received seven affiliations. The ministry declined to share its selection process and said it does not check applicants' political leanings.
cases.cite: The Reporters' Collective, 3 Apr 2024
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open school affiliations awarded under a public scheme, not people placed inside a state body.

cases.n: Gorakhnath Math's head monks held Gorakhpur's seat, then ran Uttar Pradesh
cases.d: The Gorakhnath Math, a Hindu monastery in Gorakhpur, has sent its successive heads (mahants) into elected office for decades and its present head runs India's most populous state. Mahant Digvijay Nath, a national general secretary of the Hindu Mahasabha, won the Gorakhpur Lok Sabha seat in 1967; his successor Avaidyanath held it in 1970 and 1989 and for the BJP in 1991 and 1996; and Yogi Adityanath, Avaidyanath's disciple, won it five times from 1998 and founded his own youth group, the Hindu Yuva Vahini. Adityanath became mahant in 2014 and Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh on 19 March 2017, keeping both roles, and won a second term in 2022.
cases.cite: Wikipedia (Gorakhnath Math; Yogi Adityanath); Deccan Herald, 2022
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Monastery heads won elections openly; no decision shown serving the monastery.

cases.n: Tablighi Jamaat member Javed Nasir made head of Pakistan's ISI
cases.d: Lieutenant General Javed Nasir, a member of Tablighi Jamaat, a worldwide Islamic missionary movement, was appointed Director-General of Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), its main spy agency, by Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif on 14 March 1992, over the army chief's objections and with little intelligence experience. During his 13 months in charge the ISI ran a covert programme to arm the Bosnian army against the UN arms embargo, including airlifting anti-tank missiles, and helped set up an Afghan mujahideen government. He was retired early on 13 May 1993, which commentators attributed to pressure from Arab states over his support for radical movements. He later became a Tablighi missionary.
cases.cite: Wikipedia (Javed Nasir, citing Pakistani and international press)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Spy chief belonged to a missionary movement; nothing shows it steered him.

cases.n: Haghani seminary graduates ran Iran's intelligence ministry and judiciary
cases.d: Graduates and followers of the Haghani Circle, a hardline school of thought centred on a Qom seminary founded in 1964 by clerics including Mohammad Beheshti and Mohammad Taghi Mesbah Yazdi, have repeatedly headed Iran's Ministry of Intelligence, whose minister must by law be a qualified Islamic jurist. Ministers Mohammad Reyshahri, Ali Fallahian, Ali Younesi and Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei came from its circle. Mohseni-Ejei, a Haghani graduate, was intelligence minister from 2005 to 2009, prosecutor-general from 2009 to 2014, and became Chief Justice on 1 July 2021. The EU and US sanctioned him in 2011 for the detention and torture of protesters after the 2009 election.
cases.cite: Wikipedia (Haghani Circle, citing Vali Nasr, The Shia Revival, 2006; Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Eje'i)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Ministers shared a seminary background; no steering by the circle shown.

cases.n: Ennahda leader Ghannouchi given life over 'secret apparatus' in Tunisia
cases.d: Tunisian prosecutors accused Ennahda, the Islamist party that led the government after 2011, of running a 'secret apparatus' that infiltrated state institutions, spied, and was involved in the 2013 assassinations of leftist politicians Chokri Belaid and Mohamed Brahmi. Lawyers for the victims' families first presented documents in 2018 and named Mustapha Kheder as its head. In early June 2026 the Tunis Court of First Instance sentenced party leader Rached Ghannouchi to life plus 30 years for forming a terrorist alliance, gave eleven others life terms and thirteen more 10 to 48 years. Ennahda denied the charges as political, and rights groups called the trial part of a crackdown on opponents.
cases.cite: Al Jazeera, 3 Jun 2026; Asharq Al-Awsat, Jul 2020
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Record does not say which institutions the apparatus got inside or how; too vague.

cases.n: Mali's High Islamic Council forced a rewrite of the national family code
cases.d: Mali's High Islamic Council, the country's top Islamic body, had its demands written into the national family code after mass protests against an earlier version. The National Assembly adopted a new code on 3 August 2009 that expanded women's rights; after marches of up to 50,000 people, President Amadou Toumani Touré sent it back on 27 August. The amended text, endorsed by the council, was adopted on 2 December 2011. It recognises religious marriage, states that a wife must obey her husband and that the man is head of the family, sets marriage at 16 for girls with exceptions from 15, and altered the earlier gains in inheritance. FIDH said the council's demands were met.
cases.cite: FIDH, 9 Dec 2011; Wikipedia (Malian Family Code)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open public protest pressure from outside, not people placed inside.

cases.n: Hefazat-e-Islam's demands rewrote Bangladesh's school textbooks
cases.d: Hefazat-e-Islam, a coalition of Qawmi madrasa teachers and clerics whose 2013 13-point charter demanded sharia law and a changed school curriculum, got its demands written into Bangladesh's state textbooks for 2017. Hefazat members said the government made the 29 changes they had asked for; its leader Shah Ahmad Shafi praised the authorities. Removed items included a poem by Humayun Azad, a Baul essay, a children's Ramayana excerpt and an excerpt from the novel Lalu, while essays on the Prophet and the early caliphs were added. The National Curriculum and Textbook Board's chairman denied Hefazat's influence. Critics said religious content was entering secular literature books.
cases.cite: BenarNews, 17 Feb 2017; Wikipedia (2017 Bangladesh textbooks criticism)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open demands met by government, not people placed inside.

cases.n: Monks put on Sri Lanka's eastern land task force; no Tamils or Muslims
cases.rank: Presidential Task Force for Archaeological Heritage, Eastern Province
cases.d: In June 2020 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa placed senior Buddhist monks on a presidential task force to survey archaeological sites in Sri Lanka's Eastern Province and allocate land to them. Ellawala Medhananda Thera, Panamure Thilakawansha Thera and the chief prelate for the Northern and Eastern Provinces sat alongside the defence secretary, Major General Kamal Gunaratne, who chaired it, a police deputy inspector-general and the head of Derana TV. No Tamil or Muslim member was named, although those communities are over 70% of the province's people. The leader of the Tamil National Alliance wrote to the president objecting, and two minority members were later added.
cases.cite: Daily FT, 4 Jun 2020
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Government openly appointed monks to a task force; no decision shown serving them.

cases.n: Buddhist monks' council met Sri Lanka's president monthly to steer policy
cases.d: President Gotabaya Rajapaksa set up a Buddhist Advisory Council of senior monks from Sri Lanka's three monastic chapters in April 2020 to advise on carrying out government policy, and met it on the third Friday of each month at the Presidential Secretariat with ministry secretaries present. Its first meeting was on 24 April 2020. By September the monks had advised on archaeological sites, monastery land deeds, national security, the National Education Policy and placing Buddhist universities under the education ministry. The government reported acting on their proposals, appointing four state ministers to the education ministry and moving to amend the Antiquities Ordinance for temples built on archaeological sites.
cases.cite: Daily FT, 21 Sep 2020
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open advisory council set up by the president, not infiltration.

cases.n: Santi Asoke sect's followers filled Palang Dharma party and Bangkok council
cases.rank: Bangkok governor and city council; parliament
cases.d: Santi Asoke, an ascetic Buddhist sect, placed its followers in Thai elected office through the Palang Dharma party. Chamlong Srimuang, a sect follower and former general, won the Bangkok governorship in 1985 and founded the party in 1988; sect members gathered the signatures needed to register it, and close to half its 1988 candidates were Santi Asoke followers. In 1990 the party won 49 of the 55 seats on Bangkok's city council, and in 1992 it won 41 and then 47 parliamentary seats and joined the coalition government. Chamlong led the May 1992 protests that forced military ruler Suchinda Kraprayoon out. Thaksin Shinawatra later led the party and served as a minister.
cases.cite: Wikipedia (Palang Dharma Party; Chamlong Srimuang); McCargo, Southeast Asia Research, 1993
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Sect followers won elections; no decision shown pursuing the sect's aims.

cases.n: Unification Church money said to fund Nepal Family Party and its minister
cases.d: The South Korean Unification Church is alleged to have funded Nepal's Nepal Family Party (Pariwar Dal), whose founder Ek Nath Dhakal served as cabinet minister for cooperatives and poverty alleviation from May 2012 and later as minister of peace and reconstruction under K. P. Sharma Oli. Leaked emails from 2017 to 2022, obtained by Newstapa and reported in Nepal in early 2026, show Dhakal asking the church's Asia president for at least $500,000 for the 2017 election and $20,000 a month for the party; the letters mention three former prime ministers. The church took 20 communist MPs abroad for 'principle education'. The church called the documents inauthentic, and the party denied foreign funding.
cases.cite: Nepali Times, 2026; Wikipedia (Ek Nath Dhakal); Kantipur, 4 Feb 2026
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Alleged funding of a party; no decision shown pursuing the church's aims.

cases.n: Ríos Montt's Verbo church elders became Guatemala's presidential secretaries
cases.d: When General Efraín Ríos Montt took power in Guatemala in the coup of 23 March 1982, elders of his Pentecostal-style Church of the Word (Verbo), founded by the California mission Gospel Outreach, entered his government. Two Verbo elders, Francisco Bianchi and Álvaro Contreras, became his personal secretaries and key advisers, and he named Jorge Serrano Elías, a leader of the neo-Pentecostal Elim church, to head the new Council of State after dissolving Congress. Ríos Montt prayed with the elders before going to the palace. His 17-month rule saw the worst of the army's massacres of Maya villagers, and in 2013 a Guatemalan court convicted him of genocide; the verdict was later annulled.
cases.cite: Pew Research Center, 5 Oct 2006; Christianity Today, 23 Apr 1982; Time, 21 Jun 1982
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Church elders served in government; nothing shows the church steered decisions.

cases.n: Ex-New Tribes missionary put in charge of Brazil's isolated-tribes unit
cases.rank: Head of isolated and recently contacted peoples, FUNAI
cases.d: In February 2020 Brazil's government named Ricardo Lopes Dias, an evangelical pastor who spent ten years as a missionary with New Tribes Mission (now Ethnos360), a US group with a history of contacting and converting isolated tribes, to head the department of FUNAI, the federal indigenous agency, that protects isolated peoples. The post gave him detailed information on more than 100 registered isolated groups. Federal prosecutors warned of possible genocide if missionaries gained that data, and in May 2020 appellate judge Antonio Souza Prudente annulled the appointment, citing a conflict of interest and risk to the no-contact policy. FUNAI called the ruling persecution of evangelicals.
cases.cite: Mongabay, May 2020; Associated Press, 5 Feb 2020
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Ex-missionary appointed, then annulled; no decision shown serving the mission.

cases.n: Evangelical bloc gave pastor Feliciano Brazil's human-rights committee
cases.rank: Chair, Chamber of Deputies Human Rights and Minorities Committee
cases.d: Brazil's evangelical bloc in Congress used committee seat deals to take control of the Chamber of Deputies' Human Rights and Minorities Committee in 2013. Other parties gave up seats to the Social Christian Party (PSC), leaving the 18-member committee with five PSC members and six from the evangelical bloc, and on 7 March 2013 it elected pastor Marco Feliciano of the Assembly of God as chair despite his remarks against gay and Black people. Protests followed in several cities and a petition for his removal passed 442,000 signatures. In June 2013 the committee approved a bill to lift the Federal Psychology Council's 1999 ban on treating homosexuality as an illness.
cases.cite: Global Voices, 19 Mar 2013; Associated Press via Star Tribune, 19 Jun 2013
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Elected legislators using normal committee deals; no outside party placing people.

cases.n: Opus Dei member Ollero sat on Spain's abortion appeal for seven years
cases.d: Andrés Ollero, reported by Público to be a member of Opus Dei, the Catholic lay organisation, was a Popular Party deputy from 1986 to 2003 and then joined Spain's Constitutional Court, which rules on whether laws comply with the constitution. In 2014 he was made rapporteur on the Popular Party's appeal against the 2010 abortion law, responsible for drafting the ruling, but seven years later had brought no draft to the full court. He also sat on the bench that refused to hear a challenge to his former party colleague Jorge Fernández Díaz's award of a police medal to the Virgin Mary. In July 2021 the group Abogados Cristianos filed a criminal complaint against him over the delay.
cases.cite: Público; InfoVaticana, 17 Jul 2021
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Judge's reported Opus Dei membership only; no steering by the group shown.

cases.n: Video shows Cyprus president's aides discussing cash for access
cases.rank: Presidential chief of staff and circle
cases.d: A secretly filmed video alleges that money from businessmen could buy access to Cyprus's President Nikos Christodoulides through people close to him. The eight-minute recording, posted online on 8 January 2026, shows his chief of staff Charalambos Charalambous, his brother-in-law and a former energy minister apparently discussing ways round the €1 million limit on campaign donations, cash for access to the presidency, and help for businessmen avoiding EU sanctions on Russia. Charalambous resigned, saying his words were taken out of context. The government did not deny the footage was real but called it a maliciously edited 'hybrid' attack, possibly by Russia. A former Supreme Court judge was appointed to investigate both its origin and those recorded.
cases.cite: Irish Times (15 Jan 2026); Cyprus Mail (13 Jan 2026)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Insiders talking of selling access; outside party too vague.

cases.n: Samherji's ex-board chair became Iceland's fisheries minister
cases.d: Kristján Þór Júlíusson, a former chairman of the board of Samherji, one of Iceland's largest fishing companies, served as Iceland's Minister of Fisheries and Agriculture from November 2017 to November 2021, the post that regulates the industry. In November 2019 the 'Fishrot' leaks showed Samherji paying bribes in Namibia for fishing quotas. A whistleblower said that in 2014 Samherji's chief Þorsteinn Már Baldvinsson introduced Kristján, then health minister, to three Namibians later accused of taking those bribes as 'his man' in government. Kristján said he had not been involved with Samherji since leaving its board about 19 years earlier. About 4,000 people protested in Reykjavík calling for him to resign; he refused.
cases.cite: Iceland Monitor / Morgunblaðið (13 Nov 2019); High North News (26 Nov 2019); Wikipedia, 'Kristján Þór Júlíusson'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Former board chair became minister; no decision shown serving the company.

cases.n: Businessmen hid $200,000 in donations to New Zealand's National Party
cases.org_label: Yikun Zhang and the Zheng brothers
cases.d: Three businessmen, Yikun Zhang and the brothers Colin and Joe Zheng, channelled $100,000 in 2017 and $100,050 in 2018 to New Zealand's National Party, splitting each sum into smaller gifts under other people's names so the true donors would not be publicly declared. The Serious Fraud Office prosecuted them, and in 2022 the High Court found them guilty of obtaining by deception, while clearing them over donations to the Labour Party; they were sentenced to community detention in November 2022. The Court of Appeal later overturned the National Party convictions, finding the men had deceived the Electoral Commission and the party but had not been shown to benefit personally, as the law requires.
cases.cite: New Zealand Herald; RNZ (5 Oct 2022; 30 Nov 2022)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Hidden donations; donors not shown seeking or getting any decision.

cases.n: BND report accused Liechtenstein officials of aiding launderers
cases.d: A report by Germany's foreign intelligence service, the BND, said organised crime had reached inside Liechtenstein's institutions. Published by Der Spiegel on 8 November 1999, it accused unnamed Liechtenstein banks, politicians and judges of cooperating with the Russian mafia and drug cartels to launder money. Prime Minister Mario Frick called it dubious and unfair. In 2000 a member of parliament, Gabriel Marxer, lost his immunity and was arrested; he was acquitted in 2002. An investigator hired by the government, Kurt Spitzer, rejected the allegations but found weaknesses in legal cooperation. The Financial Action Task Force blacklisted Liechtenstein in June 2000, and the country ended anonymous accounts opened by trustees before being removed from the list in June 2001.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, '1999–2001 Liechtenstein financial crisis'; Christian Science Monitor (3 Jul 2000)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Unnamed banks, politicians and judges; too vague to say who got inside what.

cases.n: US firm Richmond's power deal, pushed by PM's office, toppled Tanzania's PM
cases.d: Richmond Development Company, a little-known firm based in Houston, Texas, won a contract to supply 100 megawatts of emergency electricity to TANESCO, Tanzania's state power company, after a drought in early 2006 cut hydropower. Its generators arrived late and did not perform as promised. A five-member parliamentary select committee led by MP Harrison Mwakyembe concluded that the contract had been fraudulently concluded and was unconscionable; the Prime Minister's office was reported to have pushed for the contract to be extended against TANESCO's advice. Prime Minister Edward Lowassa denied wrongdoing but resigned on 7 February 2008, and energy ministers Ibrahim Msabaha and Nazir Karamagi were also forced out.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Edward Lowassa' (Richmond scandal section, citing Tanzanian press)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Bad contract pushed by officials; no outside party shown paying or placing anyone.

cases.n: Pastor on Ghana's state cathedral board had project money paid to his firm
cases.org_label: Rev. Victor Kusi Boateng (Power Chapel Worldwide)
cases.rank: National Cathedral Board of Trustees, run from the Presidency
cases.d: Rev. Victor Kusi Boateng, founder of the Pentecostal church Power Chapel Worldwide, sat as secretary of the board of trustees of Ghana's National Cathedral, President Akufo-Addo's church project, run from the Presidency, which cost the state $97 million: $58 million paid or committed and $39 million owed to the contractor. In January 2023 MP Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa revealed that the project had paid GH¢2.6 million to JNS Talent Centre, a company he linked to Kusi Boateng, and alleged that Kusi Boateng used a second identity. A Deloitte audit released in July 2025 found no loan agreement for the GH¢2.6 million yet project money was used to repay it, and found payments made before contracts were approved. President Mahama dissolved the board on 18 July 2025 and ordered a forensic audit.
cases.cite: Graphic Online, 18 Jul 2025; MyJoyOnline, 16 Jan 2023
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Board member's self-dealing; no outside party.

cases.n: Mexico's financial police probe ex-first lady Sahagún over Legion of Christ
cases.d: Marta Sahagún, presidential spokesperson and then wife of President Vicente Fox (2000–2006), was investigated in 2020 for an 'irregular' link with the Legionaries of Christ, a Catholic religious order founded in Mexico, over public money given to civil society groups during Fox's government. Santiago Nieto, head of the Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF), the finance ministry's anti-money-laundering office, confirmed the inquiry on 7 January 2020 and said it would establish whether there had been an irregularity; no accounts were frozen. In 2002 her brother Alberto Sahagún had told the magazine Proceso that she had been treasurer of the Legionaries in Guanajuato state. Sahagún, who ran the Vamos México foundation, called the claims false. No findings had been published.
cases.cite: Expansión Política, 8 Jan 2020; Zeta Tijuana, 7 Jan 2020
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Unclear what the order got inside or what decision served it; too vague.

cases.n: Ugandan army chief made Ituri a province and named its governor in Congo
cases.d: Uganda's army placed its own appointee at the head of the Ituri region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo during its occupation of north-eastern Congo. General James Kazini, the Ugandan army's chief of staff, decreed Ituri a new 'province' named Kibali-Ituri and appointed Adèle Lotsove as its first governor in June 1999, the International Criminal Court's trial chamber recorded in its 2014 Katanga judgment, which found that Uganda wielded authority there as an occupying power. In December 2005 the International Court of Justice (the UN's court for disputes between states) ruled that Uganda had acted unlawfully, including by looting natural resources and stoking ethnic conflict in Ituri. In February 2022 it ordered Uganda to pay Congo $325 million in five yearly instalments.
cases.cite: ICC Trial Chamber II, Prosecutor v. Katanga, judgment, Mar 2014, para 1200 (ICRC Casebook); JURIST, Feb 2022
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open military occupation, not infiltration.

cases.n: MI5: China's spy ministry uses fake headhunters to reach British MPs
cases.d: China's Ministry of State Security (MSS), its main civilian spy agency, is trying to recruit British MPs, parliamentary staff and officials through fake recruitment agents, according to an 'espionage alert' that MI5, Britain's domestic security service, issued on 18 November 2025. House of Commons Speaker Lindsay Hoyle sent the alert to lawmakers. It named two LinkedIn profiles, 'Amanda Qiu' and 'Shirly Shen', as fronts and said Chinese nationals were doing outreach 'at scale' to collect information and build long-term relationships. Security minister Dan Jarvis said economists, think-tank staff and government officials were also targeted, and announced £170 million to renew civil servants' encrypted technology. China's embassy called the claims fabrication.
cases.cite: AP via PBS NewsHour, 18 November 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Recruitment outreach only; no one shown recruited inside.

cases.n: Ex-mayor of Ecuadorian mining town held as a Los Lobos financier
cases.d: Ecuador's authorities say the gang Los Lobos was financed by a man who had been mayor of the mining town of Camilo Ponce Enríquez. Los Lobos is one of Ecuador's largest gangs and is deeply involved in illegal gold mining. Elías Baldor, mayor from 2019 to 2023, was detained in July 2026 with five other people, including relatives. Interior Minister John Reimberg said Baldor's money let the gang keep local communities terrorised, and police said explosives used in local attacks were traced to a company he owns. The allegations had not been tested in court when he was detained, and he had not commented.
cases.cite: Bloomberg Línea, 'Ecuador detiene a exalcalde señalado como presunto financista de la banda Los Lobos' (28 Jul 2026)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Former mayor funding a gang; no gang placement inside the town hall shown.

cases.n: Meta, OpenAI and Palantir executives made US Army officers
cases.d: Senior executives of technology companies that sell to the US military were sworn in as part-time lieutenant colonels in the US Army Reserve in June 2025, in a new unit called Detachment 201, the 'Executive Innovation Corps'. They were Shyam Sankar, chief technology officer of Palantir; Andrew Bosworth, chief technology officer of Meta; Kevin Weil, chief product officer of OpenAI; and Bob McGrew, an adviser to the AI start-up Thinking Machines Lab. The Army said they would advise on modernisation projects such as its Army Transformation Initiative. Their companies have defence business: Palantir is a close military partner, and Meta and OpenAI work with the contractor Anduril on equipment for soldiers and on counter-drone systems. A second group of executives was commissioned later.
cases.cite: Washington Times, 16 Jun 2025; US Army Reserve; DVIDS
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Executives given reserve commissions as advisers; no decision serving their firms shown.

cases.n: Cerberus founder Steve Feinberg became the Pentagon's number two
cases.d: Steve Feinberg, co-founder and co-chief executive of the private-equity firm Cerberus Capital Management, which manages more than $60 billion and owned the military contractor DynCorp from 2010 to 2020, became US Deputy Secretary of Defense, the official who runs the Pentagon's day-to-day business and budget. The Senate confirmed him by 59 votes to 40 on 14 March 2025 and he was sworn in on 17 March. Critics raised conflicts of interest over Cerberus's defence holdings. His disclosure papers said he had divested from Cerberus but contained a clause showing a continuing financial relationship with the firm. At his confirmation hearing he supported large-scale job cuts in the Defense Department.
cases.cite: Defense News, 14 Mar 2025; Bloomberg, 14 Mar 2025; Washington Times, 11 Mar 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Private-equity chief took a Pentagon post; no decision serving Cerberus shown.

cases.n: SpaceX engineers placed inside the FAA, the agency that licenses SpaceX
cases.d: At least four engineers from Elon Musk's rocket company SpaceX were brought into the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the US agency that licenses and has fined SpaceX's launches, in February 2025, while Musk led the government cost-cutting effort DOGE. Wired, using their LinkedIn profiles, named three of them, including SpaceX senior software director Ted Malaska, and reported that they were onboarded as 'special government employees' before being fully vetted. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said they would help modernise air-traffic control. The FAA had fined SpaceX more than $600,000 for launch violations, and Duffy had promised at his confirmation hearing to review those fines. Senators Tammy Duckworth and Adam Schiff asked the FAA and NASA about conflicts of interest.
cases.cite: Wired, Feb 2025 (via Jalopnik); Axios, 17 Feb 2025; Office of Sen. Duckworth, 28 Feb 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): SpaceX engineers placed at the FAA, but no FAA decision serving SpaceX is shown.

cases.n: Binance did business with the Trump family's crypto firm, then won a pardon
cases.rank: President, via family company World Liberty Financial
cases.d: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, did business with World Liberty Financial, a crypto company launched by Donald Trump and his sons, while seeking relief from US law enforcement. Binance had pleaded guilty in 2023 to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations and agreed to about $4.3 billion in penalties, and its founder Changpeng Zhao served four months in prison in 2024. In May 2025 Binance listed World Liberty's dollar-pegged token USD1, and World Liberty said a $2 billion investment in Binance by an Abu Dhabi fund would be paid in USD1. Days later the SEC dropped its lawsuit against Binance. Trump pardoned Zhao in October 2025. Zhao's lawyer denied any pay-to-play arrangement.
cases.cite: PBS NewsHour/AP, 23 Oct 2025; Forbes, 23 Oct 2025; DL News, Oct 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): An open business deal with the president's family firm; no Binance people or paid officials inside shown.

cases.n: Lutnick's old bank Cantor, now run by his sons, in a Commerce-funded deal
cases.d: Howard Lutnick, for decades chairman and chief executive of the investment bank Cantor Fitzgerald, became US Commerce Secretary in 2025, and his sons took over Cantor's top posts. In January 2026 the Commerce Department agreed to provide $1.6 billion to the company USA Rare Earth on condition that it raised $500 million privately; USA Rare Earth picked Cantor Fitzgerald to help raise a funding round of more than $1 billion, CNBC reported from financial filings. Senators Elizabeth Warren, Chris Van Hollen and Ron Wyden wrote of 'serious concerns' about the deal.
