Wired also reported, from internal documents, that Cantor explored trades on refunds of Trump's tariffs after the Supreme Court rolled them back; Cantor said it executed no such transactions.
cases.cite: CNBC, 2026; Wired, 2026; Sinclair/ABC News, 2026
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Former bank chief's department funded a firm that chose his old bank; no decision by him steering it is shown.

cases.n: Druckenmiller partner Kevin Warsh made Fed chair with $100m undisclosed
cases.d: Kevin Warsh, a partner in the personal investment office of billionaire investor Stanley Druckenmiller, was confirmed by the Senate on 13 May 2026, by 54 votes to 45, as chair of the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, which sets interest rates and supervises the largest banks. In his ethics filings he said he could not disclose the underlying assets of more than sixty financial entities, together over $100 million, because of 'pre-existing confidentiality obligations' to entities that Druckenmiller owns and manages through his firm, Duquesne. Senator Elizabeth Warren asked Druckenmiller on 4 May 2026 to release Warsh from those agreements. Warsh had earlier served on the Fed's board from 2006 to 2011.
cases.cite: CBS News, 13 May 2026; US Senate Banking Committee minority, 5 May 2026
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Investor's partner became Fed chair; no decision serving Duquesne shown.

cases.n: Billionaire Harlan Crow paid for Justice Thomas's luxury travel for decades
cases.d: Harlan Crow, a Dallas real-estate billionaire and Republican donor who funds conservative legal groups, paid for luxury travel for Clarence Thomas, a justice of the US Supreme Court, for more than two decades without it appearing on Thomas's financial disclosures, ProPublica reported in April 2023. The gifts included a nine-day trip to Indonesia in 2019 on Crow's superyacht and private jet, which would have cost over $500,000 to charter, yearly stays at Crow's Adirondacks resort, and other jet flights. Justices must report most gifts worth over $415. Crow has backed the Federalist Society and tort-reform groups, and gave $500,000 to a Tea Party group founded by Thomas's wife. Crow said he never sought to influence the justice.
cases.cite: ProPublica / Texas Tribune, 6 Apr 2023; Black Enterprise, Aug 2023
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Undisclosed gifts to a justice; no ruling serving Crow shown.

cases.n: Hedge-fund billionaire flew Justice Alito; his fund later appealed to him
cases.d: Paul Singer, a hedge-fund billionaire and Republican donor, flew Samuel Alito, a justice of the US Supreme Court, to a luxury fishing lodge in Alaska in 2008 on his private jet, ProPublica reported in June 2023. The lodge's owner, another Republican donor, paid for Alito's stay. Alito did not list the flight on his financial disclosure, which ethics experts said the law required. Singer's hedge fund later appealed to the Supreme Court ten times, and Alito did not step aside from those cases. Before ProPublica's story appeared, Alito answered in the Wall Street Journal, saying he knew Singer only casually and that Singer's name did not appear in the court papers.
cases.cite: ProPublica, 20 Jun 2023; NPR, 22 Jun 2023; Boston Globe, 21 Jun 2023
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Undisclosed gift to a justice; no ruling serving Singer's fund shown.

cases.n: Ex-Amazon UK boss put in charge of Britain's competition watchdog
cases.d: Doug Gurr, formerly country manager of Amazon UK and president of Amazon China, was appointed interim chair of the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), the UK regulator that investigates monopolies and can block mergers, on 21 January 2025. The government accepted the resignation of the previous chair, Marcus Bokkerink, saying it wanted regulators to remove barriers to business and prioritise growth, and announced a new 'strategic steer' for the CMA. At the time the CMA was investigating the UK cloud-computing market, in which Amazon Web Services is the largest supplier; the authority said its board was separate from the team running that inquiry. Gurr was later named permanent chair.
cases.cite: UK government press release, 21 Jan 2025; DatacenterDynamics, Jan 2025; Retail Systems
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Ex-Amazon boss chairs the regulator; no decision serving Amazon shown.

cases.n: Arms-industry lobby chief Guido Crosetto became Italy's defence minister
cases.d: Guido Crosetto, president since 2014 of AIAD, the federation of nearly 200 Italian aerospace, defence and security companies, and since 2020 chair of Orizzonte Sistemi Navali, a warship venture of the state-controlled firms Leonardo and Fincantieri, became Italy's Minister of Defence on 22 October 2022 in Giorgia Meloni's government. The state is often these companies' main customer. He gave up both posts and said he would sell his family businesses, including consultancy firms, within 90 days. The newspaper Domani reported that an AIAD member firm had donated €10,000 to Meloni's party and pointed to links between AIAD's secretary-general and a company in which Crosetto's son held a stake. Crosetto denied any conflict of interest.
cases.cite: Il Post, 23 Oct 2022; Domani, Oct 2022; Open, 27 Oct 2022
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Arms-lobby chief became minister; no decision serving the industry shown.

cases.n: Ex-minister Cédric O lobbied for Mistral AI as France fought AI Act rules
cases.rank: French government position on the EU AI Act
cases.d: Cédric O, France's digital affairs minister until 2022, joined the French AI start-up Mistral AI at its founding in April 2023 as a co-founder and adviser, and became one of the loudest critics of the European Union's draft AI Act, the law setting rules for artificial intelligence. In early November 2023 French officials backed out of a provisional deal in the AI Act negotiations because they objected to proposed restrictions on 'foundation models', the large general-purpose systems that Mistral builds, Bloomberg reported. French senators and the watchdog Corporate Europe Observatory criticised the influence of former officials turned company lobbyists on France's position. Campaigners drove vans through Paris and Brussels criticising O by name.
cases.cite: Bloomberg, 13 Dec 2023; Corporate Europe Observatory, Mar 2024; PYMNTS, 2024
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Former minister lobbying from outside for a start-up; no one placed inside government.

cases.n: Maduro's alleged front man Alex Saab made Venezuela's industry minister
cases.rank: Minister of Industry and National Production
cases.d: Alex Saab, a Colombian-born businessman whom the United States accused of laundering money for Nicolás Maduro's government, was appointed Venezuela's Minister of Industry and National Production on 18 October 2024, replacing Pedro Tellechea. Saab had been arrested in Cape Verde in 2020 and extradited to the US, where he and his partner Álvaro Pulido were charged with running a network that exploited food aid meant for Venezuelans. He was freed in December 2023 in exchange for ten US prisoners held in Venezuela and given a hero's welcome in Caracas. After US forces captured Maduro on 3 January 2026, interim president Delcy Rodríguez removed Saab and merged his ministry with commerce.
cases.cite: Al Jazeera, 18 Oct 2024; Channels TV/AFP, 17 Jan 2026
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Businessman tied to the government itself made minister; no outside party.

cases.n: Secret electoral bonds let firms fund India's ruling party until struck down
cases.rank: Political parties, chiefly the governing BJP
cases.d: Companies used electoral bonds, a scheme India's government introduced in 2018 that let donors give unlimited sums to political parties without their names being made public, to fund parties led by the governing BJP. On 15 February 2024 India's Supreme Court declared the scheme unconstitutional and the data were then published. Donors had bought bonds worth over ₹12,155 crore between 2019 and 2024, and the BJP received more than ₹6,060 crore, nearly half. The largest buyer was the lottery company Future Gaming and Hotel Services, with over ₹1,368 crore, followed by Megha Engineering and Infrastructure with over ₹966 crore. Reporters found that several leading buyers had been raided or were under investigation by federal agencies.
cases.cite: BOOM, 15 Mar 2024; Dawn/AFP, 15 Feb 2024; The Wire, 14 Mar 2024
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open (if anonymous) legal party donations; no officials paid or decisions shown.

cases.n: Beximco tycoon Salman F Rahman held a ministerial post while banks lent
cases.rank: Prime minister's adviser on private industry and investment
cases.d: Salman F Rahman, a leading figure in the Beximco industrial group and one of Bangladesh's richest businessmen, held a ministerial-rank post as Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's adviser on private industry and investment from January 2019, while companies linked to him borrowed heavily from banks. By August 2024 those companies owed about ৳36,865 crore to four state-owned and three private banks, and the Centre for Policy Dialogue described several banks as ruined by embezzlement it attributed to him. After Hasina fell, he was arrested on 13 August 2024 while allegedly trying to flee by boat. The Anti-Corruption Commission has brought money-laundering, loan-default and embezzlement cases, including over IFIC Bank loans of more than ৳1,100 crore.
cases.cite: Dhaka Tribune, 2024; Financial Express, 14 Aug 2024; Wikipedia 'Salman F Rahman'
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Tycoon held an adviser post while his firms borrowed; record does not show he used the post to get the loans.

cases.n: Oil and gas staff given seats in national delegations at COP29
cases.d: At least 1,773 fossil-fuel lobbyists were given access to COP29, the UN climate summit held in Baku in November 2024 where governments negotiate cuts in greenhouse-gas emissions, according to an analysis of the UN's participant lists by the Kick Big Polluters Out coalition. That was more than the combined delegates of the ten most climate-vulnerable countries. Most came through trade associations; the International Emissions Trading Association brought 43 people, including staff of TotalEnergies and Glencore. Others were placed inside official national delegations, which take part in the negotiations: Italy brought employees of Eni and Enel, Japan representatives of Sumitomo, and Canada staff of the oil companies Suncor and Tourmaline.
cases.cite: Kick Big Polluters Out via Euronews, 15 Nov 2024; Global Witness, 15 Nov 2024
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Company staff on national delegations, but no negotiating decision shown serving them.

cases.n: Deep-sea mining executives sat in state delegations at the Seabed Authority
cases.org_label: Deep-sea mining companies (The Metals Company and others)
cases.d: Deep-sea mining companies placed their executives in government delegations at the International Seabed Authority (ISA), the body created under the UN Law of the Sea, based in Kingston, Jamaica, that is writing the rules on whether and how minerals may be mined from the international ocean floor. At the ISA's July 2023 meeting, Climate Home News found at least 33 executives and employees of mining companies on state delegation lists. Gerard Barron, chief executive of The Metals Company, attended as a representative of Nauru, which sponsors one of his company's licences. The UK brought two staff of UK Seabed Resources, the Netherlands two of Royal IHC, and Japan seven from each of its two state-backed mining ventures.
cases.cite: Climate Home News, 8 Aug 2023 (via Business & Human Rights Resource Centre)
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Mining staff on state delegations, but no ISA rule or decision shown serving them.

cases.n: Health minister Mkhize's associates won a R150m department contract
cases.org_label: Digital Vibes (Tahera Mather and Naadhira Mitha)
cases.rank: Minister of Health and his department
cases.d: Tahera Mather and Naadhira Mitha, close associates of South Africa's health minister Zweli Mkhize, used a company called Digital Vibes as a front to win a R150 million communications contract from the national Department of Health for Covid-19 and National Health Insurance campaigns, the Special Investigating Unit (SIU), a state anti-corruption body, found in a report released on 29 September 2021. The SIU found that Mkhize's messages to the department's director-general supported claims he was involved from the outset, that his son Dedani received at least R3.8 million from the contract, and that at least R72 million was wasted. It recommended prosecuting a senior official, Anban Pillay. Mkhize had already left office.
cases.cite: Daily Maverick, 29 Sep 2021; The Citizen, 29 Sep 2021
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Minister's own associates and family profiting; no outside party.

cases.n: ExxonMobil's demands largely written into the EU's cut to due-diligence law
cases.d: ExxonMobil lobbied to strip the EU's Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), a 2024 law requiring large companies to check their supply chains for human-rights and environmental harm and to adopt climate plans, and most of its requests appeared in the law's rewrite. Exxon documents obtained by the Dutch research group SOMO sought withdrawal or, failing that, four changes: delete the climate-plan duty, delete EU-wide civil liability, limit checks to direct suppliers, and limit non-EU firms' duties. The Commission's February 2025 'Omnibus I' proposal and the Council's June 2025 position contained the first three. The final text, adopted on 16 December 2025 and 24 February 2026, removed the climate-plan duty and EU-wide civil liability.
cases.cite: SOMO, 2025; Clifford Chance, Feb 2026
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open lobbying of EU bodies from outside.

cases.n: Donors' projects written into New Zealand's fast-track approvals law
cases.d: Companies and shareholders behind 12 of the 149 projects that ministers chose to write into New Zealand's Fast-track Approvals Bill, a law letting listed developments bypass normal consent processes, had given more than NZ$500,000 to the governing National, ACT and NZ First parties and their candidates in 2022 and 2023, RNZ found in October 2024. They included the Sunfield development's director Christopher Meehan and Speargrass Holdings, about $206,000 to National and ACT; Rod Drury of Coronet Village, $100,000 to ACT in 2022; and a former Kings Quarry director, $55,000 to NZ First. Minister Shane Jones said the Cabinet process had been followed. In May 2025 RNZ reported ministers were still deciding on projects linked to donations.
cases.cite: RNZ, 10 Oct 2024; RNZ, 12 May 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open party donations; record does not show the projects were chosen for them.

cases.n: Oilfield-services lobby head put in charge of US drilling and mining leases
cases.rank: Assistant Secretary of the Interior, Land and Minerals
cases.d: Leslie Beyer, chief executive from 2014 to 2023 of the Energy Workforce & Technology Council, the trade association for US oilfield-services and equipment companies, was confirmed by the Senate in September 2025 as the Interior Department's Assistant Secretary for Land and Minerals Management. The post oversees the Bureau of Land Management, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, the offshore safety regulator BSEE and the surface-mining office, covering about 245 million acres of federal land, 700 million acres of mineral rights and the 1.7 billion-acre outer continental shelf, where oil, gas and coal leases are sold and drilling is regulated. Oilfield companies such as Patterson-UTI publicly welcomed her confirmation.
cases.cite: World Oil, 18 Sep 2025; Patterson-UTI release, Sep 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Lobby head took a post; no decision serving the industry shown.

cases.n: Anduril executive Michael Obadal became the Army's number-two civilian
cases.d: Michael Obadal, a senior director at the weapons maker Anduril Industries, became Under Secretary of the Army, the service's second-highest civilian post, after the Senate confirmed him by 51 votes to 47 in September 2025; he was sworn in on 22 September. Anduril sells drones and other systems to the Army. In his nomination filings Obadal valued his Anduril shares at $250,000 to $500,000 and said he would keep them, with the right to cash them in if the company, then valued at over $28 billion, were sold. Senator Elizabeth Warren called it a 'textbook conflict of interest'. A month before taking office he revised his ethics agreement to say he would hold no Anduril stock.
cases.cite: The Intercept, 1 and 8 May 2025; Inside Defense, Sep 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Anduril executive took a post; no decision serving Anduril shown.

cases.n: Crypto firm Bitfury's top lawyer became chief US bank regulator
cases.d: Jonathan Gould, former chief legal officer of the crypto-mining and blockchain company Bitfury and later a partner at the law firm Jones Day, was confirmed by the Senate in July 2025 as Comptroller of the Currency. The Comptroller heads the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), which charters and supervises national banks, the largest part of the US banking system. Under the GENIUS Act, the 2025 stablecoin law, the OCC also oversees federally licensed issuers of stablecoins, crypto tokens pegged to the dollar, a market then worth about $250 billion.
cases.cite: Radom, 11 Jul 2025; Payment Expert, 14 Jul 2025; PYMNTS, Jul 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Crypto firm's ex-lawyer became regulator; no decision serving Bitfury or crypto shown.

cases.n: Hegseth's church network CREC brought its pastors into the Pentagon
cases.rank: Secretary of Defense; Pentagon worship services
cases.d: Pete Hegseth, the US Secretary of Defense, belongs to the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches (CREC), a network of about 130 Calvinist churches co-founded in 1998 by the pastor Doug Wilson, who calls himself a Christian nationalist and has called women's right to vote 'a bad idea'. From May 2025 Hegseth hosted monthly Christian services inside the Pentagon, streamed on the military's own media channel; the first was led by his CREC pastor Brooks Potteiger and one in February 2026 by Wilson himself. Wilson said CREC's new Washington church served members who had moved to work in the Trump administration, and that the network had never had so many connections in national government. Service members and contractors complained to Military.com about invitations sent under the secretary's title.
cases.cite: Associated Press, 12 Aug 2025; Military.com, 18 Feb 2026
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Defence secretary's church held services at the Pentagon; no policy steered by it shown.

cases.n: Bolsonaro put a 'terribly evangelical' pastor on Brazil's Supreme Court
cases.d: President Jair Bolsonaro had promised evangelical churches, a core part of his support, a 'terribly evangelical' justice on the Supreme Federal Court (STF), Brazil's highest court. He chose André Mendonça, a Presbyterian pastor who had been his Solicitor-General and Justice Minister. The Senate approved him on 1 December 2021 by 47 votes to 32, six above the minimum, after an eight-hour hearing in which Mendonça had to explain how his faith would bear on his rulings. Born in 1972, he can sit until the compulsory retirement age of 75, giving the evangelical movement a seat on the court for about 26 years.
cases.cite: Agência Senado, 1 Dec 2021; Poder360, Dec 2021
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Appointment of an evangelical justice; no rulings or movement steering shown.

cases.n: HTS's Idlib 'Salvation Government' took over Syria's ministries
cases.d: Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), the Islamist armed group that grew out of al-Qaeda's Syrian branch and ran the north-western province of Idlib, moved its own civil administration into the national government after its offensive toppled Bashar al-Assad on 8 December 2024. On about 10 December the rebels' General Command named Mohammed al-Bashir, head since January 2024 of the Idlib-based 'Salvation Government', as head of Syria's caretaker government until 1 March 2025. Al-Bashir said on television that the Salvation Government's ministers would take over the ministries of the new Syrian state. HTS leader Ahmed al-Sharaa was later named interim president.
cases.cite: Enab Baladi, 10 Dec 2024; The National, 9 Dec 2024
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Armed group openly conquered the state; not infiltration.

cases.n: Syria made foreign jihadist commanders generals in its new army
cases.who: Foreign jihadist fighters (Turkistan Islamic Party and others)
cases.d: Foreign fighters from jihadist groups that had fought alongside Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) were given senior ranks in Syria's new army. On 29 December 2024 the Defence Ministry announced 49 appointments; at least six went to foreigners. Abdulaziz Dawood Khudaberdi, a Chinese Uyghur who commands the Turkistan Islamic Party in Syria, a group China calls terrorist, was made a brigadier-general, as were a Turkish and a Jordanian citizen. Colonels included two more Uyghurs and the Albanian Abdul Jashari, head of a group the US designated in 2016. An HTS source called the posts 'a small token of recognition' for jihadists' sacrifices. Western governments warned the new rulers against the appointments in January 2025.
cases.cite: Reuters via The New Arab, 31 Dec 2024; Enab Baladi, Jan 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): New rulers rewarded allied foreign fighters with ranks; no outside party steering decisions shown.

cases.n: HTS intelligence chief Anas Khattab made Syria's interior minister
cases.d: When Syria's interim president Ahmed al-Sharaa, the leader of the Islamist group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), named a 23-member transitional government on 29 March 2025, he kept the security and foreign posts with his own circle. Anas Khattab, a prominent HTS figure who had headed the new state's general intelligence service, became interior minister, in charge of the police. Murhaf Abu Qasra stayed as defence minister and Asaad al-Shaibani as foreign minister, both described as al-Sharaa's close confidants. Other ministries went to technocrats and a few figures from minorities. The appointments left the armed movement that took Damascus in December 2024 in control of the state's coercive and diplomatic arms.
cases.cite: Al-Monitor, 29 Mar 2025; The National, 29 Mar 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Victorious movement filling its own government; not infiltration.

cases.n: Militia commanders sit on Yemen's eight-man ruling council
cases.org_label: Giants Brigades and National Resistance Forces
cases.who: Giants Brigades and National Resistance Forces
cases.d: On 7 April 2022 President Abd Rabbuh Mansour Hadi handed power to an eight-member Presidential Leadership Council, pushed by Saudi Arabia, that included the commanders of the armed groups fighting the Houthis. Abdulrahman Abu Zaraa al-Muharrami, head of the Salafist, UAE-backed Giants Brigades, and Tareq Saleh, commander of the National Resistance Forces, among the largest ground forces, became members; two seats went to the Islamist Islah party's camp. Saudi Arabia pledged $3bn with the UAE. When the council removed the separatist leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi and Faraj al-Bahsani in January 2026, al-Muharrami kept his seat among the six remaining members.
cases.cite: The New Arab, Apr 2022; The National, 7 Apr 2022 and 15 Jan 2026
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open power-sharing council; no decisions shown serving the militias.

cases.n: Hüda Par, tied to Turkish Hizbullah, entered parliament on Erdoğan's lists
cases.d: Hüda Par, a Kurdish Islamist party whose history is tied to Turkish Hizbullah, an armed group responsible for kidnappings and killings in the 1990s and the 2001 murder of Diyarbakır's police chief, won four seats in Turkey's parliament on 14 May 2023 by running its candidates on the lists of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's AKP. After election the four MPs returned to their own party. Its leader Zekeriya Yapıcıoğlu has refused to call Hizbullah a terrorist organisation. Hüda Par calls for gender segregation in schools and public spaces and for criminalising adultery. The deal drew protests, including against the finance minister at a football stadium.
cases.cite: Turkish Minute, 22 May 2023; Duvar English, May 2023
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open electoral alliance; no decisions shown.

cases.n: US-funded Kohelet think tank drafted Israel's judicial overhaul
cases.d: The Kohelet Policy Forum, a Jerusalem think tank founded in January 2012 by Moshe Koppel, wrote the policy papers behind central parts of the judicial overhaul that Benjamin Netanyahu's government pursued in the Knesset in 2023, including government control over the choice of judges and limits on the Supreme Court's power to strike down laws. A Haaretz investigation in March 2021 had found that its main donors were the American billionaires Arthur Dantchik and Jeff Yass; Dantchik's money may have made up 93% of its budget. After months of mass protests, Dantchik said in August 2023 that he had stopped donating to Israeli think tanks, including Kohelet. Kohelet earlier promoted the 2018 Nation-State Law.
cases.cite: Haaretz, 11 Mar 2021; JTA via Jewish News, 5 Aug 2023; Calcalist, Aug 2023
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Think tank's public policy papers; open advocacy from outside.

cases.n: Manhattan Institute's Rufo put on the board that took over New College
cases.rank: Board of trustees, New College of Florida (public university)
cases.d: Florida's governor Ron DeSantis appointed six new trustees to the 13-member board of New College of Florida, a public liberal-arts college, on 6 January 2023; one was Christopher Rufo, a Manhattan Institute senior fellow known for campaigns against critical race theory and diversity programmes, who said the aim was to remake the college. On 31 January the new majority fired the president, Patricia Okker, who called it a 'hostile takeover', and installed Richard Corcoran, a former Republican state House speaker and DeSantis ally, as interim president. DeSantis meanwhile called on all state colleges and universities to dismantle their diversity, equity and inclusion programmes, and the board put the college's own diversity office on the agenda for its next meeting.
cases.cite: Axios Tampa Bay, 1 Feb 2023; Florida Governor's Office, 6 Jan 2023
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Governor's own appointee to a college board; no outside party placing him.

cases.n: India lifted its 58-year ban on civil servants joining RSS activities
cases.d: The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the Hindu nationalist volunteer body from which India's ruling BJP draws its leaders, was opened to the central civil service by an order of 9 July 2024. Since 1966 the Central Civil Services Conduct Rules had barred government servants from taking part in the activities of the RSS and Jamaat-e-Islami. The Personnel Ministry's office memorandum, made public by the opposition Congress party on 21 July, removed the RSS from that bar after 58 years. Congress said bureaucrats could now turn up in RSS uniform; the BJP called the 1966 order unconstitutional. The change lets officials who administer the state also work for the movement whose members lead the government.
cases.cite: Business Standard, 22 Jul 2024; Deccan Herald, Jul 2024
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Rule change allowing civil servants to join RSS; no placement or steering shown.

cases.n: RSS men put at the head of India's state media school and broadcaster board
cases.rank: IIMC director-general; Prasar Bharati Recruitment Board chair
cases.d: The government of Narendra Modi placed people from the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the Hindu nationalist movement behind the ruling BJP, at the head of state media and cultural bodies. In July 2020 Sanjay Dwivedi, linked to the RSS student wing ABVP, was named director-general of the Indian Institute of Mass Communication, the state journalism school. Jagdish Upasane, former editor of the RSS papers Organiser and Panchjanya, chaired the recruitment board of Prasar Bharati, which hires for public radio and television. Sachchidanand Joshi, national president of the RSS affiliate Bharatiya Shikshan Mandal, ran the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, and a Sanskar Bharati member led the Centre for Cultural Resources and Training.
cases.cite: ThePrint, 10 Jul 2020
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Appointments of RSS-linked people; no decisions shown serving the RSS.

cases.n: MILF rebels have run the Bangsamoro government since 2019
cases.rank: Bangsamoro Transition Authority and chief minister
cases.d: The Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), a Muslim armed movement that fought the Philippine state for decades, has run the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) since it was created under a 2019 peace deal. MILF nominees held 41 of the 80 seats in the appointed Bangsamoro Transition Authority, the region's interim parliament and government, and MILF chairman Murad Ebrahim served as interim chief minister. In March 2025 President Ferdinand Marcos Jr replaced him with Abdulraof Macacua, chief of staff of the MILF's armed wing, and named only 35 MILF nominees. A February 2025 law postponed the region's first parliamentary elections from May to October 2025.
cases.cite: PCIJ, 17 Mar 2025; MindaNews, Mar 2025
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Movement governs the region created for it by a peace deal; open, not infiltration.

cases.n: Foundation against Terrorism fed cases to Guatemala's prosecutors
cases.who: Fundación contra el Terrorismo (Ricardo Méndez Ruiz)
cases.d: The Fundación contra el Terrorismo (FCT), a private group founded in 2013 by Ricardo Méndez Ruiz to defend army officers tried for civil-war crimes, worked hand in hand with Guatemala's Public Prosecutor's Office under Attorney General Consuelo Porras (2018–2026). Méndez Ruiz said that under Porras 'dozens' of FCT complaints were accepted, after most had been rejected from 2014 to 2020; the UN human rights office counted at least 81 proceedings from them, mainly against former anti-corruption officials and the journalist José Rubén Zamora. FCT's lawyer also represented the banker whose testimony led to Zamora's arrest in July 2022, handled by the anti-impunity unit (FECI) under Rafael Curruchiche. Porras's successor removed Curruchiche in May 2026.
cases.cite: Reporters Without Borders, 13 Jul 2026
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Private group filing complaints from outside that a friendly prosecutor accepted.

cases.n: Brethren church members staffed Liberal campaigns; Parliament investigates
cases.d: Members of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, a closed Christian sect most of whose members do not vote, were alleged to have campaigned in their thousands for the Liberal Party in Australia's May 2025 federal election, staffing polling booths and harassing independent MPs. The Liberal Party's own review listed the church as a 'support group'. At a parliamentary committee hearing in October 2026, Gareth Hales, son of the church's global head Bruce Hales, admitted campaigning for the Liberals and encouraging others, and having met then-opposition leader Peter Dutton and an adviser the month before, but denied coordinating members. The independent MP Andrew Gee said members followed and intimidated him between booths. The church denies directing anyone.
cases.cite: AAP via Mudgee Guardian, 16 Oct 2026; Sydney Morning Herald
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Church members campaigning openly in an election.

cases.n: Moms for Liberty-backed slates won control of Florida school boards
cases.rank: County school boards (Miami-Dade, Sarasota, Duval and others)
cases.d: Moms for Liberty, a Florida-founded campaign group that wants parents' rights on curricula, books and gender policy written into school rules, organised slates of candidates for elected county school boards. In Florida's August 2022 school board elections it claimed 43 wins, 14 of them heading to runoffs, alongside 25 of 30 candidates endorsed by Governor Ron DeSantis and 35 backed by the 1776 Project PAC. The groups said they had won conservative majorities on the boards of Miami-Dade, Sarasota, Clay, Duval and Brevard counties; in Duval, April Carney beat the board's recent chair. A 2026 Florida Trib analysis found the group's endorsements had become far less successful in its home state.
cases.cite: Axios, 25 Aug 2022; Florida Trib, 20 Jul 2026
cases.drop_reason: Not directly infiltration (Nov 2026 stricter test): Open election campaign for school board seats.

cases.n: Mnuchin's OneWest Bank chief Otting became the top US bank regulator
cases.d: Joseph Otting, chief executive of OneWest Bank from 2010 to 2015, where he worked with its founder Steven Mnuchin, became Comptroller of the Currency, the regulator of US national banks, on 27 November 2017, while Mnuchin was Treasury Secretary. On 20 May 2020 his office finalised a rewrite of rules under the 1977 Community Reinvestment Act, which requires banks to lend in poorer neighbourhoods, broadening what counts as such lending. Community groups said it would cut lending in low-income areas. Congresswoman Maxine Waters suggested the rewrite was shaped by the reinvestment complaints OneWest faced in its merger with CIT. Otting left in May 2020.
cases.cite: Wikipedia, 'Joseph Otting'
cases.inside: A bank chief moved into the regulator of national banks and rewrote lending-duty rules, which a congresswoman linked to complaints his former bank had faced.
cases.drop_reason: Owner judged not directly infiltration (Nov 2026): a bank chief appointed regulator, with no decision shown to serve his former bank

cases.n: Guangzhou security official recruited retired Taiwan spy-agency officers
cases.rank: Military Intelligence Bureau colonels and major general (retired)
cases.d: A Chinese state security official in Guangzhou recruited Chang Chao-jan, a colonel in Taiwan's Military Intelligence Bureau, which runs Taiwan's spies in China, during a 1999 trip. Chang then drew in other retired bureau officers with trips and gifts. Prosecutors said that in Macau in 2012 former Major General Yueh Chih-chung and the official identified more than 20 bureau agents from photographs. The High Court could confirm only that basic personal details such as names were handed over. Terms were 18 months for Chang, 14 for Chou Tien-tzu and 10 for Yueh, upheld by the Supreme Court in December 2025. A fourth man, Wang Ta-wang, was acquitted.
cases.cite: Central News Agency via GlobalSecurity, 3 December 2025; Taipei Times, 21 February 2021
cases.inside: A Chinese security official recruited officers from Taiwan's own spy agency, who then passed on details of colleagues and tried to bring other officers into the ring.
cases.drop_reason: Everyone in the ring is described as retired, so these are former officers recruited after leaving post, and no serving insider is shown.

cases.n: PLA intelligence funded a retired officer's ring of Taiwanese ex-officers
cases.rank: Retired army officers; Rehabilitation Alliance Party
cases.d: China's military intelligence offered Chu Hung-i, a retired Taiwanese army officer doing business in China, funding from 2019 to build a network of former officers, a court found. He recruited six retired officers and founded the Rehabilitation Alliance Party in 2023. China sent NT$2 million over WeChat and NT$670,000 through unregistered channels for its three legislative candidates, who lost and whom prosecutors said were unaware. Chu then had recruits list officers ranked major general or above and record GPS coordinates of sites including the Alishan radar station, sending them over WeChat. In June 2025 the High Court in Taichung gave Chu 10 years and the others three and a half to eight and a half, subject to appeal.
cases.cite: Taipei Times, 26 June 2025; Taipei Times, 8 January 2025
cases.inside: Chinese military intelligence paid a retired officer to recruit former comrades and fund candidates for Taiwan's legislature, and they sent it data on officers and military sites.
cases.drop_reason: Retired officers and campaign money for three candidates who lost and were unaware; nobody got inside a government body, matching the removed Taiwan campaign-funding records.

cases.n: Retired Taiwan security bureau officer accused of passing Palau reports to China
cases.d: Prosecutors say a retired officer of Taiwan's National Security Bureau, the island's main intelligence agency, passed information to China after settling in Palau, one of the few states recognising Taiwan, where he runs a travel business. The man, surnamed Shih, allegedly reported on Palau's support for Taiwan's bid to attend the 2021 World Health Assembly and on delegation details from Palau's 2022 Our Ocean Conference. Prosecutors say he knew retired intelligence officers are barred from working for hostile foreign forces. The indictment was reported on 20 August 2026, with no verdict. The same report said prosecutors had indicted 58 people for espionage since 2025.
cases.cite: TaiwanPlus, 20 August 2026
cases.inside: Prosecutors say a former officer of Taiwan's main intelligence agency reported to China on an ally's support for Taiwan, though retired officers are barred from such work.
cases.drop_reason: A retired officer recruited after settling abroad, reporting on Palau; nothing shows anyone inside Taiwan's agency or Palau's government.

cases.n: Spy-agency major Chen Shu-lung lured a colleague to Shanghai for China
cases.rank: Military Intelligence Bureau major (retired); lieutenant general
cases.d: Chinese intelligence recruited Chen Shu-lung, a retired major from Taiwan's Military Intelligence Bureau, in 2006, the courts found. In 2007 he told China that a former colleague had served as a diplomat in Japan, then lured him to Shanghai, where he was detained for three days and questioned about that work and National Security Bureau staff. The Supreme Court upheld a five-year term. In a second case, then still on trial, prosecutors alleged that Lieutenant General Chen Chu-fan, once deputy commander of the military police, recruited him for China, and that he passed on information about Falun Gong in Taiwan and military planning.
cases.cite: Taipei Times via Liberty Times, undated, about 2014
cases.inside: Chinese intelligence recruited a former intelligence officer who delivered a colleague for interrogation; prosecutors separately alleged a lieutenant general acted as a recruiter for China.
cases.drop_reason: A retired major and a former deputy commander recruited after service; no one inside an institution is shown.

cases.n: Retired Taiwan spy officers accused of selling lists of agents in China
cases.rank: Military Intelligence Bureau major and colonel (retired)
cases.d: Prosecutors allege Chinese intelligence recruited Wang Tsung-wu, a retired major in Taiwan's Military Intelligence Bureau who had gone on intelligence work in China four times, on a 2013 trip there. They say he was asked to build a network in Taiwan and brought in retired colonel Lin Han, his junior at military academy. The two allegedly sold lists of bureau agents operating in China, lists of undercover agents and their activities, and other top-secret material. Each reportedly received about US$100,000 from unknown benefactors, with trips to Macau and Southeast Asia. Investigators raided them, and the report recorded no verdict.
cases.cite: Taipei Times via Liberty Times, about March 2015
cases.inside: Prosecutors say China recruited a retired intelligence officer who brought in a colleague and sold names of Taiwanese agents, which their former agency was meant to protect.
cases.drop_reason: Two retired officers recruited on a 2013 trip after leaving service; no serving insider is shown.

cases.n: PACE barred ex-president Agramunt over Azerbaijan vote inquiry
cases.rank: President of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe
cases.d: An independent inquiry found that Azerbaijan's lobbying had reached the top of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), a body of national MPs that monitors human rights. It reported "strong suspicions" that corruptive activities played a role in Pedro Agramunt's appointment as head of the European People's Party group. In May 2018 PACE barred Agramunt, its former president, from senior posts for 10 years. Jordi Xuclà, Cezar Preda and Azerbaijan's delegation head Samad Seyidov received two-year bans. All denied wrongdoing, and Spain's People's Party said the inquiry had no legal consequences. A separate report said Agramunt played a key role in organising votes favourable to Azerbaijan.
cases.inside: The inquiry strongly suspected Azerbaijan's lobbying network had reached the assembly's own leadership, and a later report says votes were then organised in Baku's favour.
cases.cite: European Stability Initiative summary of the PACE Independent Investigation Body report, April 2018; Armenpress, 16 May 2018; The Guardian via inkl, May 2018; Norwegian Helsinki Committee report
cases.drop_reason: Same PACE inquiry and same finding on Agramunt as the existing case.

cases.n: PACE's Armenia rapporteur Axel Fischer charged over Azerbaijani bribes
cases.rank: PACE rapporteur on Armenia and head of the German delegation
cases.d: German prosecutors allege that Azerbaijan paid Axel Fischer, a former CDU member of the Bundestag, while he sat in the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) from 2010 to 2018. They say he received €21,800 in 2016, and that he voted in Azerbaijan's favour as rapporteur on Armenia in January 2016, on a matter concerning the Karabakh war. Investigators also allege he made speeches favouring Baku and passed on confidential documents early. Prosecutors say former Azerbaijani MP Elkhan Suleymanov recruited him. Fischer denies wrongdoing. His case was separated from Eduard Lintner's trial and was reported paused because of his health.
cases.inside: Prosecutors say Azerbaijan paid the assembly's own Armenia rapporteur, who then voted and spoke for Baku and passed confidential papers early; he denies this and has not been tried.
cases.cite: Hetq, citing German prosecutors, 30 January 2024; Hetq, January 2025; JAMnews on the Munich verdict, 2025; Institute for Reporters' Freedom and Safety, 2025
cases.drop_reason: Same Azerbaijan-money case against Axel Fischer as the existing Bundestag record, only at a later stage.

cases.n: Swiss trial: Karimova's 'Office' sold telecoms access to Uzbekistan
cases.rank: President's daughter, minister and UN envoy in Geneva
cases.d: Swiss prosecutors allege that telecommunications companies paid bribes to Gulnara Karimova, daughter of Uzbekistan's president Islam Karimov, in exchange for access to the Uzbek market. She held ministerial posts and was the country's envoy to the UN in Geneva from 2008 to 2013. They say she led a criminal organisation called "The Office", whose associates used pseudonyms and fictitious contracts, and opened more than 30 Swiss accounts through straw men. Her trial was set to open at the Federal Criminal Court in Bellinzona on 27 April 2026, alongside a former aide, a former asset manager and the bank Lombard Odier, with a verdict expected by the end of May. Uzbekistan jailed her for 13 years in 2020.
cases.inside: Swiss prosecutors say telecoms firms bought entry to Uzbekistan's market by paying the president's daughter, who ran a hidden group using her state position.
cases.cite: Swissinfo, April 2026
cases.drop_reason: Same Karimova telecoms bribery scheme as the existing case, which already records the Swiss trial.

cases.n: Ex-deputy head of Moldova's spy service accused of serving Belarus KGB
cases.rank: Former deputy director, Security and Intelligence Service
cases.d: Romanian investigators allege that Alexandru Bălan, a former deputy director of Moldova's Security and Intelligence Service and earlier its counter-intelligence chief, passed state secrets to officers of Belarus's KGB, including at two meetings in Budapest in 2024 and 2025. He had retired by then, and Moldova's president said he had been cut off from state secrets since 2019. Sources quoted by Digi24 said he first worked with Russian intelligence, which has not been shown. He was arrested at Timișoara airport in Romania on 8 September 2025 on treason charges. Radio Moldova reported that on 28 April 2026 he was swapped for two Moldovan intelligence officers captured in 2025 and held in Russia, so no verdict was reported.
cases.inside: Prosecutors say Belarus's KGB recruited a man who had run counter-intelligence in Moldova's spy service, gaining state secrets through him after he retired.
cases.cite: Romania Insider, September 2025; Radio Moldova, 9 September 2025 and 3 May 2026
cases.drop_reason: The record says he had retired and been cut off from secrets since 2019 before the alleged passing, so he was not inside.

cases.n: Moldovan MP Lozovan jailed for taking party money from criminal group
cases.d: A Chisinau court sentenced Irina Lozovan, a Moldovan MP close to fugitive businessman Ilan Shor, to six years in prison, about two weeks after fellow MP Alexandr Nesterovschi was convicted in March 2025. She was found guilty in her absence of knowingly accepting party funding from an organised criminal group. Her husband, Pavel Gîrleanu, a district councillor in Ocnița, received five years. Her lawyer said the evidence did not prove the offence and that she would appeal. Shor's network is accused of paying for pro-Russian politics in Moldova, and Shor is himself evading a 15-year sentence.
cases.inside: A court found that an MP knowingly took party money from a criminal group; she is described as close to a fugitive whose network funds pro-Russian politics.
cases.cite: IPN, 2025; Moldpres, 31 March 2025
cases.drop_reason: Shows an MP taking party funding from a criminal group, but no decision or action inside parliament or the state serving it.

cases.n: Egis Avia settled over payments behind an Oran airport contract
cases.rank: Algerian public officials over Oran airport
cases.d: The French engineering firm Egis Avia settled a French charge of corrupting a foreign public official over a €4 million contract, signed in 2008, to modernise and equip the Oran airport terminal in Algeria. AFP reported that the firm signed a €390,000 contract with a consulting company registered in the British Virgin Islands, and that this money allegedly paid several Algerian intermediaries, including €12,000 to the son of a former Algerian minister. On 10 December 2019 Egis Avia agreed to pay a €2.6 million fine under a CJIP, a French settlement that involves no trial or guilty plea. A Paris investigating judge was still examining the individuals involved at that time.
cases.cite: AFP via TSA Algérie, 10 Dec 2019; Global Investigations Review, 11 Dec 2019; Transparency France, Jan 2023
cases.inside: French prosecutors treated Egis Avia's payments through an offshore consultancy as corruption of a foreign official to win Algeria's Oran airport terminal contract.
cases.drop_reason: Money reached private intermediaries and a former minister's son; no official inside any Algerian body is shown receiving it or acting on it.

cases.n: Surys settled over kickback scheme at Ukraine's passport printer
cases.rank: Director of the state printing house Polygraph Combine 'Ukraina'
cases.d: Ukrainian investigators say the state printer of passports and ID cards bought security materials from the French firm Surys at inflated prices through an Estonian intermediary controlled by its director, who received improper benefits. They say the materials cost 4 to 6 times the original price, with about €7 million in royalties reaching the Estonian firm from 2018 to 2021. France's financial prosecutor signed a settlement with Surys on 8 July 2025, a Paris court approved it on 3 September, and Ukraine receives €3.37 million. One report says Surys was allegedly forced to transfer the design rights. Ukrainska Pravda reports that Maksym Stepanov, the former health minister who ran the printer until 2016, is a suspect; he is presumed innocent.
cases.cite: NABU, 23 May 2025; Ukrainska Pravda, 6 Sept 2025; United24 Media, 12 Nov 2025
cases.inside: Ukrainian investigators say a state printer's director gained from inflated purchases from a French supplier, which kept selling it security materials and later settled in France.
cases.drop_reason: The director's own firm profited from inflated purchases, so this is an insider's crime; nothing shows the supplier placing or paying anyone to serve it.

cases.n: Alstom consultants passed fees to officials in Latvia, Tunisia, Malaysia
cases.rank: Civil servants and foreign decision makers
cases.d: Consultants paid by the French engineering group Alstom passed a large share of their success fees to foreign decision makers, according to Swiss prosecutors. The Swiss Office of the Attorney General, investigating since October 2007, identified improper payments to civil servants in Latvia, Tunisia and Malaysia. On 22 November 2011 it issued a summary punishment order against Alstom Network Schweiz for failing to take all necessary precautions against bribery, totalling about €31 million, most of it estimated profits. It cleared the group of running a system of bribing foreign officials. Alstom said it was a victim of employees taking kickbacks in two cases and a consortium subcontractor in the third. The sources read do not name the officials or contracts.
cases.cite: The Construction Index, 24 Nov 2011; International Enforcement Law Reporter, 1 Feb 2012
cases.inside: Swiss prosecutors found consultants hired by an engineering group passed success fees to foreign decision makers, including civil servants in Latvia, Tunisia and Malaysia.
cases.drop_reason: No official, contract or decision is named, the penalty was for failing to take precautions, and prosecutors cleared the group of a bribery system.

cases.n: Serbian interior ministry state secretary convicted of trading in influence
cases.d: A Belgrade court found that a state secretary at Serbia's interior ministry used her influence to bend police work in cases touching organised crime. Dijana Hrkalović, in post from 2017 to 2019, was sentenced in January 2025 to 16 months for trading in influence. One charge said she ordered a forensic phone report in a murder case delayed; gang leader Veljko Belivuk was a suspect in that case and was acquitted of it in 2019. Another said she ordered a Novi Sad police chief to put Darko Elez, whom N1 calls a criminal, under false surveillance so other units would not investigate him. She was not charged with cooperating with criminals, denied guilt and could appeal.
cases.inside: A court found the ministry's state secretary steered police work, in cases including one with a gang leader as suspect, though no payment from criminals was charged.
cases.cite: RFE/RL Balkan Service, 22 Jan 2025; N1 Serbia, 11 Oct 2023
cases.org_label: Organised-crime suspects protected through the ministry
cases.drop_reason: No outside party is shown inside: she was not charged with cooperating with criminals, and no payment or instruction from any group appears.

cases.n: Ombudsman: Special Branch shielded UVF killers it ran as informers
cases.rank: RUC Special Branch and CID officers
cases.d: A police watchdog found that RUC Special Branch, the Northern Ireland police's intelligence arm, colluded with members of a Belfast unit of the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), a loyalist paramilitary group. The January 2007 report by Police Ombudsman Nuala O'Loan, known as Operation Ballast, covered ten murders and ten attempted murders in the 1990s. It began after Raymond McCord asked why no one was held for his son's 1997 killing. It found that the inquiry into the 1993 killing of taxi driver Sharon McKenna had the effect of protecting an informer from prosecution. Retired senior officers refused to explain their practices. The Chief Constable apologised, and no prosecutions of officers were expected to be recommended.
cases.inside: The UVF unit's members were also police informers, and detectives' decisions then protected them from prosecution for killings, so police work served the paramilitaries' men.
cases.cite: Irish Times, 22 Jan 2007
cases.drop_reason: Runs the wrong way: police ran informers inside the UVF and shielded their own agents; no UVF people or control inside the police are shown.

cases.n: Ombudsman found police collusion with UVF in the Loughinisland murders
cases.d: The Police Ombudsman for Northern Ireland found in 2016 that collusion between RUC Special Branch, the police intelligence arm, and the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), a loyalist paramilitary group, was a significant feature of a 1994 pub attack. UVF gunmen killed six people and wounded five at the Heights Bar in Loughinisland, County Down, in June 1994. The Ombudsman, responding to the families' complaints, said police informers were involved and one suspect was an informant. He said the original investigation was marked by incompetence, indifference and neglect. Two retired officers later went to the High Court to have the findings quashed, arguing he had exceeded his powers.
cases.inside: The Ombudsman found the UVF gang had police informers in it and that Special Branch's dealings with them were a significant feature of a sectarian massacre.
cases.cite: Statewatch, reproducing Police Ombudsman report, 2016; The Tablet, 2016; News Letter
cases.drop_reason: Runs the wrong way: police informers sat inside the UVF gang; no UVF people or control inside the police are shown.

cases.n: Alstom paid officials in Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Bahamas and Taiwan for contracts
cases.rank: Government officials (offices not given in the source)
cases.d: Alstom, the French power and rail engineering group, paid government officials in several countries to obtain state contracts. A settlement summary lists Indonesia, Taiwan, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and the Bahamas, and says more than $75 million in bribes brought more than $4 billion in contracts, with an estimated net profit of about $300 million, according to the US Justice Department. Alstom paid $772 million to the United States in December 2014, one of the largest penalties under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the US law against bribing foreign officials. The figures cover all the countries together. The sources do not split them by country or name the officials.
cases.inside: A foreign engineering group paid officials in several governments, and those governments' contracts, worth over $4 billion in total, went to the company.
cases.cite: Phillips & Cohen, largest FCPA settlements; FCPA settlement ranking, nordot.app/631164485728306273; FCPA Professor top-ten list via LexBlog, 9 Dec 2019
cases.drop_reason: A multi-country settlement roll-up with no office, official or contract named for Egypt or any listed state; too vague, and the Indonesia case stands as its own candidate (i=140).

cases.n: Siemens paid officials in Venezuela and other states for contracts
cases.rank: Government officials (offices not given in the sources)
cases.d: Siemens, the German engineering group, paid government officials in many countries to win contracts. A settlement ranking lists Venezuela, Israel, Mexico, Vietnam, China, Russia, Argentina and Iraq among them, and a second summary also names Bangladesh. In December 2008 Siemens agreed to pay the United States $800 million in fines and returned profits, $450 million to the Justice Department and $350 million to the Securities and Exchange Commission, over corruption and false business records. The sources do not break the payments or contracts down by country. The Argentine identity-card deal is a separate entry on this map.
cases.inside: A foreign engineering group paid officials in many governments, and those governments' contracts went to the company, according to summaries of the 2008 US settlement.
cases.cite: Phillips & Cohen, largest FCPA settlements; FCPA settlement ranking, nordot.app/631164485728306273
cases.drop_reason: A multi-country settlement roll-up with no office, official or contract named for Venezuela or any listed state; too vague to say who got inside what.

cases.n: US says Fiji hotelier Zhao Fugang paid bribes for China-based actors
cases.rank: Police leadership and senior officials (alleged reach)
cases.d: The US alleges that Zhao Fugang, a China-born hotel owner in Suva, paid bribes to Fijian citizens on behalf of China-based actors. It barred him and his family from entry in October 2026. OCCRP and the Fiji Times reported that a 2020 Fiji police briefing named him as the suspected head of an organised crime network, and police sources said it went to Prime Minister Bainimarama and police chief Qiliho, with no action while they held office. Qiliho set up two companies at Zhao's hotel in 2022. Zhao's lawyer says the law firm's work for Qiliho was separate. Zhao has not been charged and denies wrongdoing. Bainimarama and Qiliho did not respond. No payment to a named official has been shown.
cases.inside: The US alleges a businessman suspected by Fiji's police of running a crime network bribed Fijians for China-based actors; reporters say police leaders then took no action. He denies it.
cases.cite: Al Jazeera, 8 Oct 2026; OCCRP and Fiji Times via In-depth Solomons, 2 Dec 2024; PINA, 28 Nov 2024
cases.drop_reason: A US entry ban on a businessman over bribes to unnamed 'Fijian citizens'; the record says no payment to a named official is shown, so nothing is inside.

cases.n: Senator Erico Galeano got 13 years as an associate of Marset's cocaine ring
cases.d: A cocaine ring run by Sebastián Marset of Uruguay and Miguel Insfrán, alias Tío Rico, counted a serving lawmaker of Paraguay's ruling Colorado Party among its associates, a court found. Erico Galeano was a deputy from 2018 to 2023 and then a senator. Judges found he lent his plane for the ring's logistics, bought a flat while a deputy and sold it for US$1 million in cash to a frontman for Insfrán, and passed large sums through the Deportivo Capiatá club. He got 13 years in March 2026 for money laundering and criminal association. Two appeal courts upheld it; he left the Senate, went to prison in May 2026 and has appealed to the Supreme Court. The reports do not show him using his seat for the ring.
cases.inside: A court found a sitting lawmaker was a cocaine ring's associate who lent it his plane and laundered its money; no vote bent for it is shown.
cases.cite: La Política Online, 4 Mar 2026; OCCRP, 21 May 2026
cases.drop_reason: The record says it does not show him using his seat for the ring; plane loan and laundering are an officeholder's crime outside the institution.

cases.n: Bissau officer accused of a cocaine kidnapping under Indjai's orders, acquitted
cases.org_label: Cocaine traffickers linked by testimony to General Antonio Indjai
cases.d: Suspects in Guinea-Bissau testified that an army officer, Amado Lamine Conte, took part in a cocaine-linked kidnapping on the orders of General Antonio Indjai, a former coup leader wanted by the US. The case, called Operation Red, began in October 2021 when Judicial Police seized 5 kg of cocaine after reports that two men had been kidnapped. GI-TOC, a research group on organised crime, says the victims were reportedly tortured over about 980 kg of stolen cocaine. Police reported several offences, but prosecutors charged only two, which GI-TOC calls selective. It says the prosecutor's choice of a three-magistrate panel breached national law. In April 2022 a Bissau court acquitted Conte and seven others and gave two people suspended sentences. The source reports the claim about Indjai only as testimony.
cases.inside: Testimony alleged a serving army officer acted for a cocaine network under a former coup leader's orders; the court acquitted the officer and the claim was not proven.
cases.cite: Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), 'Cocaine politics in West Africa: Guinea-Bissau's protection networks', 2022
cases.drop_reason: A kidnapping over stolen cocaine with no action inside the army and no group placing the officer; incidental and vague. Its 980 kg background links to the removed seizure record.

cases.n: Guinea-Bissau's justice system suspected of shielding cocaine suspects
cases.org_label: Braima Seidi Bá and cocaine traffickers (acquitted, suspected)
cases.d: GI-TOC, a research group on organised crime, reports signs that cocaine traffickers had protection inside Guinea-Bissau's justice system. In 2019, it says, someone reportedly tried to order Judicial Police officers to release a refrigerated truck before it was searched; it held 789 kg of cocaine. Businessman Braima Seidi Bá was convicted in his absence in 2020, reportedly over 1,869 kg seized in 2019. On 23 June 2022 the Supreme Court overturned the conviction and acquitted him. GI-TOC called the ruling a surprise that 'will no doubt fuel suspicions' the court was acting on political imperatives, and says a new court head had been appointed through a 'highly irregular process', though not that he sat on this appeal. The report shows no payment to any judge or officer.
cases.inside: GI-TOC suspects that cocaine traffickers had protectors inside the police and courts; it reports an attempted truck release and a surprise acquittal, but shows no bribe.
cases.cite: Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), 'Cocaine politics in West Africa: Guinea-Bissau's protection networks', 2022
cases.drop_reason: No party is shown inside: an unnamed person's attempt and a surprising ruling, which the source links to political imperatives, with no payment; too vague.

cases.n: Nigerian army armourers jailed for life over ammunition sold to armed groups
cases.rank: Army armourers and a lance corporal
cases.d: Armed groups and criminals bought stolen ammunition from serving Nigerian soldiers, including men who ran the army's own arms stores, a court-martial in Maiduguri found in September 2025. Sgt Raphael Ameh, an armourer at 7 Division, hid arms in bags of beans and sent them to criminals in Enugu and Ebonyi states, with over 100 bank transactions from July 2022 to June 2024. Sgt Ejiga Musa, a battalion armourer, sold an AK-47 and ammunition. L/Cpl Patrick Ocheje received 20 rounds to sell to terrorist groups. All four accused pleaded guilty; the court called the trade 'aiding the enemy'. Three received life imprisonment and Cpl Omitoye Rufus 15 years. The articles also name police inspectors as partners, without reporting their status.
cases.inside: Buyers from armed groups and criminal gangs paid soldiers holding army armoury posts, who stole ammunition from stores meant for fighting those groups and passed it to them.
cases.cite: TheCable, 23 September 2025; Leadership (Nigeria), 2025; Daily Trust, 2025
cases.drop_reason: Soldiers' own theft and sale of stock to mostly unnamed criminal buyers; no outside party is identified as placing or running anyone inside.

cases.n: Bin Hammam's $40,000 envelopes for Caribbean football officials
cases.d: Mohamed bin Hammam, the Qatari head of Asian football, was standing against Sepp Blatter for the FIFA presidency. FIFA's ethics committee found what it called comprehensive, convincing and overwhelming evidence that at a special meeting of the Caribbean Football Union in Trinidad in May 2011, arranged for him by FIFA vice-president Jack Warner, each member association was offered an envelope holding $40,000, indirectly and under conditions of secrecy. The committee said the payments could probably only be explained by the FIFA presidential election due on 1 June 2011, and that Warner knew of them and condoned them. Both men were suspended and both denied wrongdoing; bin Hammam withdrew, leaving Blatter unopposed, and Warner resigned his FIFA and CONCACAF posts on 20 June 2011.
cases.inside: A candidate's cash was handed to the national associations that vote for FIFA's president, so their votes would be bought rather than freely cast.
cases.cite: FIFA ethics committee preliminary report, reported by Al Jazeera, 22 June 2011
cases.drop_reason: No outside party: bin Hammam was himself the head of Asian football and a candidate in FIFA's own election, so this is vote-buying by an insider within football's own governance, not an outside force reaching into an institution.

cases.n: Contractors' money reached the chairman of the UN budget committee
cases.org_label: foreign companies bidding for UN contracts
cases.rank: Chairman of the UN Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions
cases.d: The Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions advises the UN General Assembly on how the organisation spends its money. Its chairman, Vladimir Kuznetsov, who was also the most senior Russian diplomat at the UN, was convicted by a Manhattan jury on 7 March 2007 of conspiring to launder money. Alexander Yakovlev, a UN procurement officer, had set up an offshore company, Moxyco Ltd, to collect secret payments from foreign companies seeking help to win UN supply contracts; Yakovlev took more than $1 million between 2000 and June 2005. Kuznetsov learned of the scheme in 2000, did not report it, took a share and moved more than $300,000 through his own offshore company, Nikal Ltd, at a bank in Antigua.
cases.inside: Money from firms chasing UN contracts reached the official who chaired the UN's own budget watchdog, the body meant to police that spending.
cases.cite: US Attorney, Southern District of New York, press release, 7 March 2007
cases.drop_reason: Kuznetsov was convicted of laundering a share of another official's bribe proceeds; no decision or action in the budget committee he chaired is shown serving the supplier firms, and the scheme itself is already on the map as the Yakovlev entry.

cases.n: Russian military intelligence officer tried to intern at the ICC
cases.rank: Internship at the International Criminal Court
cases.d: The International Criminal Court in The Hague prosecutes war crimes and had opened an investigation into Russia's conduct in Ukraine. In April 2022 Sergey Vladimirovich Cherkasov, 36, arrived in the Netherlands as Viktor Muller Ferreira, a supposed 33-year-old Brazilian, and sought an internship at the court. The Dutch intelligence service AIVD identified him as an officer of Russian military intelligence, the GRU, living under a long-standing false identity, and said an internship would have given him access to the court's building and systems, letting him gather intelligence, look for or recruit sources and possibly influence proceedings. He was declared a threat to national security, refused entry and put on the first flight back to Brazil.
cases.inside: Russia's military intelligence sent an officer under a false name to work inside the court investigating Russia, to collect and steer what it did.
cases.cite: Dutch AIVD statement, reported by JusticeInfo, 16-17 June 2022
cases.drop_reason: The same GRU officer and ICC internship attempt is already on the map twice ('GRU officer posing as a Brazilian tried to start a job at the ICC' and 'GRU officer with false identity nearly took a job at the ICC'); this would be a third copy. The case itself passes the test as an attempted placement.

cases.n: Seabed Authority secretariat shared data with a deep-sea mining company
cases.rank: Secretariat and Secretary-General of the International Seabed Authority
cases.d: The International Seabed Authority, based in Kingston, is the UN-linked body that decides who may mine the deep ocean floor outside national waters. The New York Times reported in 2022 that, according to documents going back more than a decade, the Authority had shared internal data with an executive of The Metals Company, help that let the firm pick one of the most valuable mining sites in the Pacific. A lawyer for the Secretary-General, Michael Lodge, said no rules were broken. In March 2023 diplomats from Germany, Costa Rica and France accused Lodge of abandoning the neutrality of his office by resisting proposals that could slow approval of the first mining application; Germany said it was seriously concerned, and Lodge called the complaint unsubstantiated.
cases.inside: A mining firm got the regulator's own internal data and, member states said, an administration that pressed for its application rather than judging it.
cases.cite: New York Times reporting, 2022; Associated Press via Islands Business, March 2023
cases.drop_reason: Fails for the same reason as the dropped delegations record, from the other side: the record shows the Authority's secretariat favouring The Metals Company, but no money, post, staff or control of that company inside the Authority. Data sharing and member states' complaints that the Secretary-General was not neutral are a regulator behaving favourably towards an outside applicant, not the applicant placed inside.

cases.n: Latvian MEP investigated over claims she worked with Russia's FSB
cases.d: The European Parliament is the elected chamber of the European Union. In January 2024 The Insider, working with investigative outlets in Latvia, Estonia, Russia and Sweden, reported that the Latvian MEP Tatjana Zdanoka had worked with Russia's Federal Security Service, the FSB, for at least 15 years, citing emails that referred to her work as an MEP and showed her seeking funding from Russian sources for political activity in Latvia and in the Parliament. The Parliament opened an investigation the next day, and several Latvian MEPs wrote that they believed more Russian agents might be sitting in the chamber. Zdanoka denies the allegations. The European Free Alliance had expelled her in April 2022 after she refused to condemn Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
cases.inside: Reporters say a foreign spy service had a working relationship with a sitting member of the EU's parliament, and funded her political work there.
cases.cite: The Insider investigation, January 2024, reported by Jurist, 30 January 2024
cases.drop_reason: Same case as the existing map entry on Tatjana Zdanoka and the FSB.

cases.n: Election supplier's agent allegedly shared Zimbabwe poll contract money
cases.d: The Zimbabwe Electoral Commission, ZEC, buys the materials used to run elections. The South African printing firm Ren-Form supplied ZEC for the 2023 election alongside the Zimbabwean businessman Wicknell Chivayo, whom a Ren-Form sales director called one of our agents over there. A leaked South African Financial Intelligence Centre report, published in April 2025, found Ren-Form received over 1 billion rand from Zimbabwe's finance ministry and passed more than 800 million rand to Chivayo's accounts, and concluded criminal activity could not be ruled out. The NewsHawks found invoices of 23 million rand for a server normally costing about 90,000 rand. Leaked audio captured Chivayo discussing sharing the tender proceeds with officials identified by initials; he says the recordings were faked and apologised to ZEC's chair for the impression created.
cases.inside: Reporting says a supplier's agent was to share poll contract money with people inside the electoral commission that bought the overpriced goods.
cases.cite: Daily Maverick, 8 April 2025, on the South African Financial Intelligence Centre report; The NewsHawks and The Sentry, 2024
cases.drop_reason: No person, payment or decision inside the electoral commission is identified: the only inside link is leaked audio in which the supplier's agent discusses sharing proceeds with officials given by initials, which he says was faked. The documented subject is overpriced procurement and cross-border payments, with the insider angle left too vague to say who got inside what.

cases.n: UN task force: $600m of contracts tainted, multinationals at the centre
cases.org_label: multinational suppliers to the UN and their agents
cases.rank: Procurement and peacekeeping staff at UN headquarters
cases.d: The UN buys billions of dollars of goods and services, much of it for peacekeeping missions. After the oil-for-food inquiry, the UN's internal watchdog OIOS set up a Procurement Task Force in January 2006. Speaking on 10 January 2008, its head said the task force had examined $1.4 billion of contracts and found $600 million of them tainted by corruption and mismanagement, had filed 25 reports and had 300 cases still open. More than half its work involved large multinational companies and their representatives and agents. Eight staff of the Departments of Management and Peacekeeping Operations were put on unpaid leave in 2007, three of whom were later cleared. The task force's findings produced the US conviction of the UN procurement official Sanjaya Bahel.
cases.inside: Suppliers and their agents worked through UN purchasing staff, so hundreds of millions in UN contracts were awarded to serve the companies paying.
cases.cite: UN Office of Internal Oversight Services Procurement Task Force press conference, 10 January 2008
cases.drop_reason: Systemic audit finding: no company, contract or decision inside the UN named; source says corruption OR mismanagement (round 2, 10 Nov 2026)

cases.n: Equalize: private intelligence firm accused of raiding police databases
cases.d: The Milan public prosecutor's office asked for 74 people to be put on trial over the compilation of private dossiers and unauthorised access to law-enforcement databases, in the strand of the Equalize investigation dealing with the firm's clients. The investigation was closed in April 2026 and the request for trial was reported on 21 July 2026. Prosecutors count 832 alleged victims, among them athletes, broadcasters and business figures. Those named include Enrico Pazzali, former owner of a private investigation agency, the IT specialist Nunzio Samuele Calamucci, the banker Matteo Arpe and Stefano Speroni, director of legal affairs at the oil company Eni. A further strand concerns alleged extortion and abusive access. Nothing is proven.
cases.inside: Prosecutors say a private intelligence firm got into the state's own police databases and sold what it found there to paying clients.
cases.cite: Il Sole 24 Ore, 21 July 2026; Milan public prosecutor's office
cases.drop_reason: As written this is unauthorised access to police databases from outside - a hack by a private firm's IT specialist, sold on to clients. The record names clients, victims and the firm's people but shows nobody inside the police or any official paid or recruited, and BRIEF11 excludes hacks unless an insider is shown.

cases.n: IRGC-trained Houthi official runs Yemen interior ministry personnel
cases.rank: Director general of human resources, Houthi-appointed Ministry of Interior
cases.d: Adnan Qasim Ali Qaflah is director general of human resources at the Ministry of Interior run by the Houthi authorities in Sanaa, the armed movement that holds northern Yemen. The United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen, a team of investigators that reports to the Security Council, said in its October 2024 report that until late 2022 he held a senior post at the Houthi office in Tehran and had received intelligence training from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Quds Force, the branch that runs operations abroad. The Panel describes the post as giving control over who is hired into Yemen's police and interior apparatus. Iran denies arming or directing the Houthis.
cases.inside: UN investigators report that a man trained by Iran's Quds Force now decides who is hired into the interior ministry that polices northern Yemen.
cases.cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731, para. 76 (October 2024)
cases.drop_reason: The record shows only that the man was once posted to the Houthi office in Tehran and received Quds Force training, and that his ministry post controls hiring. No Iranian people, money or control inside the ministry and no decision serving Iran; the inside angle would have to be supplied by the reader.

cases.n: Customs broker cleared smuggled weapons at a Yemeni border post
cases.rank: Customs broker at the Shihan border post
cases.d: A Yemeni customs broker at the Shihan border post helped clear smuggled military materiel through customs for the Houthi procurement network, the United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen reported in October 2024. The Panel said the Houthi defence procurement director, Major General Muhammad Ahmad al-Talibi, arranged for the broker to be relocated to Djibouti in 2022, and that the broker was arrested there in February 2024. Customs posts exist to stop banned goods; here the person handling the paperwork was working for the network bringing the goods in. The Panel describes the account as drawn from confidential sources.
cases.inside: The man processing customs paperwork at a border post worked for the smuggling network, so the checkpoint waved through the weapons it was meant to stop.
cases.cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731, case study 6 (October 2024)
cases.drop_reason: A customs broker is a private agent submitting paperwork, not an official inside the customs service, and the network he served was the Houthi authorities' own procurement arm, so no outside party is shown inside an institution. The relocation to Djibouti is already the case study inside the al-Talibi record.

cases.n: Singapore minister Iswaran jailed over gifts from businessmen he dealt with
cases.org_label: Ong Beng Seng and Lum Kok Seng
cases.who: Singapore Grand Prix promoter and a construction group
cases.d: S. Iswaran, Singapore's transport minister, was sentenced on 3 October 2024 to 12 months in prison after pleading guilty to four counts of improperly receiving gifts worth more than 300,000 US dollars and one count of obstructing justice. The gifts came from businessmen with whom he had official dealings, among them the property and hotels tycoon Ong Beng Seng, who holds the rights to the Formula One race in Singapore and was charged after the minister was jailed. Singapore rarely prosecutes ministers, and the case was its first against a serving cabinet member in decades. Iswaran resigned his seat and left the ruling party in January 2024.
