cases.inside: Businessmen whose deals the transport minister oversaw gave him hundreds of thousands of dollars in gifts, and he took them while handling their files.
cases.cite: The Star/ANN, 'Iswaran gets 12-month jail term', 4 October 2024; Malay Mail, 'Singapore to charge Malaysian billionaire OBS', 4 October 2024
cases.drop_reason: The conviction was for improperly receiving gifts and obstructing justice, and the record shows no decision or action by the minister that served the businessmen who gave them. Money reached an office-holder, but the third limb of the test - decisions inside serving the outside party - is absent from the record.

cases.n: Chinese researcher convicted of leaking a Japanese state institute's data
cases.org_label: Beijing chemical company linked to the researcher's family
cases.rank: Researcher, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology
cases.d: Quan Hengdao, a senior researcher at Japan's National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology, a state-funded body that is one of the country's main industrial research institutes, was convicted at Tokyo District Court on 25 February 2025 of breaching Japan's Unfair Competition Prevention Act. He was given a suspended sentence of two years and six months and fined 2 million yen. The court found he had sent the institute's research data on fluorine compounds, used as insulating gas in transformers and other electrical equipment, to a chemical company in Beijing in which his wife is a major shareholder. He had been arrested in June 2023. Reports said he also taught at the Beijing Institute of Technology.
cases.inside: A Chinese company with the researcher's wife as a major shareholder had him inside Japan's state research institute, emailing out its data.
cases.cite: California Insider/AP, 'Chinese researcher convicted in Japan for leaking tech secrets to Chinese firm', 2 March 2025; The Print/PTI, June 2023
cases.drop_reason: Same man and same case as the existing record on the 2023 arrest (Quan Hengdao, fluorine compound data, AIST). This version is the stronger one - it carries the February 2025 conviction and the wife's shareholding - so the existing entry should be updated from this text rather than both being carried.

cases.n: Algeria's former police chief held over alleged ties to French officials
cases.d: Farid Bencheikh, who ran Algeria's national police as Director General of National Security, was ordered into provisional detention by a military court in 2024. He is accused of conspiring against state institutions and, according to media accounts, of collaborating with French officials and foreign activists, and of coordinating media attacks on the presidency and the army. The police directorate he led runs policing across the country. No trial outcome has been published, the authorities have given no detailed account of the alleged contacts, and Bencheikh has not been convicted. Algeria has brought similar charges against several former security chiefs since 2019.
cases.inside: Prosecutors allege the man running Algeria's police worked with officials of another state, which would put a foreign government inside the force that polices Algeria.
cases.cite: North Africa Post, 'Algeria: former head of police in custody for allegedly conspiring with foreign officials', 2 October 2024
cases.drop_reason: Wording is correctly hedged throughout - 'accused', 'according to media accounts', no conviction - but the alleged conduct is conspiring against state institutions and coordinating media attacks on the presidency, with no money, recruitment or act of the police force serving France shown. On its own text this is a military-court prosecution of an ousted security chief, one of several since 2019, not a foreign party inside the force.

cases.n: Houthis took power over who international aid bodies may hire
cases.rank: Approval of staff appointments in international organisations
cases.d: On 17 July 2024 the Houthi authorities in Sanaa required international organisations working in the areas they hold to obtain approval before hiring staff, the United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen reported. In early August 2024 they took control of the Sanaa office of the UN human rights office and seized property, including documents. The Panel also recorded the detention of humanitarian staff. Vetting appointments gives the movement a say in who works inside the aid agencies that feed and treat much of Yemen's population, and in what those agencies can record about it.
cases.inside: By taking the power to approve hiring, an armed movement decides who staffs UN and aid offices, so those bodies are run with its people and under its eye.
cases.cite: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report S/2024/731, para. 156 (October 2024)
cases.drop_reason: A requirement imposed from outside that aid bodies seek approval before hiring, plus a raid on the UN human rights office; no Houthi people inside those organisations and no decision taken inside them serving the movement. The 'inside' line's conclusion that the bodies are 'run with its people' is the writer's inference, not in the record.

cases.n: Omani ministry staff steered subcontracts to a company in its projects
cases.rank: Employees of the Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology
cases.d: Employees of Oman's Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology were convicted of using their posts to secure subcontracting work worth 644,000 Omani rials for a company involved in ministry projects, and of benefiting personally from it. Each was given one year in prison for conflict of interest and a further year for misuse of office, banned from public office and ordered to hand over the money. The case was set out in the 2023 annual report of the State Audit Institution, Oman's public auditor, and reported in October 2024. Neither the employees nor the company were named publicly.
cases.inside: A contractor had people inside the ministry awarding its work, and they steered subcontracts worth 644,000 rials its way and took a share.
cases.cite: Gulf News, 'Oman: Ministry employees jailed for misuse of office and corruption', citing the State Audit Institution 2023 annual report, 14 October 2024
cases.drop_reason: The convictions are for conflict of interest and misuse of office by the ministry's own staff, who benefited personally; no payment, person or control of the unnamed company inside the ministry is shown, and neither the employees nor the firm are identified. This reads as officials abusing their own office over work they had a stake in.

cases.n: Azerbaijan says two FSB officers worked undercover inside Sputnik Baku
cases.rank: Staff of the Sputnik Azerbaijan news office in Baku
cases.d: Azerbaijan's interior ministry said that on 30 June 2025 police raided the Baku office of Sputnik Azerbaijan, part of Russia's state news agency, and detained two officers of Russia's Federal Security Service, the FSB, who it said were working there undercover. Local reports identified them as the office's editor and its director. Sputnik Azerbaijan's accreditation had been suspended in February 2025, though its staff kept working. The detentions came during a sharp deterioration in relations between Baku and Moscow. No formal charges were set out in the announcement, and Russia rejected the accusation.
cases.inside: Azerbaijan says a foreign spy service had two of its officers running a news office in Baku under cover of journalism.
cases.cite: Ukrainska Pravda, 'Two Russian FSB officers working at pro-Russian news agency Sputnik Azerbaijan detained in Baku', 30 June 2025
cases.drop_reason: The office said to hold the two FSB officers is part of Russia's own state news agency, so this is one arm of a state inside another arm of the same state, not an outside party inside someone else's institution. No Azerbaijani government body or company is shown penetrated, no charges were set out and Russia denies it - comparable to the dropped Aginter Press front-news-agency record.

cases.n: Ethiopia holds 91 over revenue networks, including a customs deputy chief
cases.d: Azezew Chane, deputy commissioner of the Ethiopian Customs Commission, is among 91 people held as suspects in organised economic crimes, according to a report dated 6 August 2026. Government Communication Service Minister Enatalem Melese said authorities had identified 109 suspects linked to the networks, and that investigations uncovered networks within the revenues and customs administration that manipulated tax assessments, processed forged payment receipts and deleted electronic records, causing losses of government revenue. The minister said suspects were tied to the networks through accounts held in their own names and in the names of relatives and associates. The arrests were presented as part of a crackdown meant to protect a macroeconomic reform programme from corruption, contraband and organised economic sabotage. No amounts were given and the suspects have not responded publicly.
cases.inside: Smuggling and tax-fraud networks allegedly worked through serving customs officials, so assessments and records inside the agency were altered for them.
cases.cite: The Reporter (Ethiopia), 6 August 2026
cases.drop_reason: The record describes networks found within the revenues and customs administration itself - officials manipulating assessments and deleting records - and names no outside party that placed or paid them. That is officials abusing their own offices, which the test excludes.

cases.n: Russian advisers reported inside Niger's intelligence service
cases.rank: Direction generale de la documentation et de la securite exterieure; presidential guard area
cases.d: A report by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, published in February 2025, says Africa Corps advisers in Niger are stationed mainly in Niamey and help the ruling CNSP, the military council that took power in July 2023, maintain its grip. It says Russian instructors were housed in villas adjacent to the presidential palace, which the report says supports the view that their main role is guarding against internal military dissent, and that a regional contact said Russian advisers work within the premises of the Direction generale de la documentation et de la securite exterieure, Niger's external intelligence service, which the report calls a sign of their integration. The report says there is no confirmed Russian company presence at Niger's gold mining sites.
cases.inside: Russian advisers reportedly sit inside Niger's intelligence service and guard the junta, so a foreign state helps protect the rulers it works with.
cases.cite: Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, February 2025
cases.drop_reason: This is an invited deployment: Africa Corps advisers helping the junta that asked them in, housed near the palace. The only inside element is one unnamed regional contact saying advisers work on the DGDSE's premises, with no decision or action there serving Russia.

cases.n: Russian instructors housed by Burkina Faso's presidency; guard role reported
cases.d: A report by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, published in February 2025, says a Russian intelligence official began intelligence cooperation with Burkina Faso in October 2023, after a visit by Russian deputy defence minister Yunus-Bek Yevkurov, and that Russian instructors were reportedly lodged next to the Presidency, with some troops expected to join the presidential guard. The same report says the African Initiative, presented as a media organisation and run by a local non-governmental organisation, has as its editor-in-chief Artem Kureyev, an officer of Russia's Federal Security Service, with activities allegedly coordinated by Viktor Lukovenko, described as a GRU agent, and with Wagner's former press officer Anna Zamaraeva on its staff. The report presents these placements as reported rather than confirmed.
cases.inside: Russian security personnel are reported to be moving into the unit that protects Burkina Faso's ruler, tying his protection to Moscow.
cases.cite: Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, February 2025
cases.drop_reason: Same as Niger: instructors lodged next to the presidency under an intelligence cooperation opened in October 2023, with troops only 'expected' to join the presidential guard. Nothing placed and no decision shown serving Moscow; the FSB officer edits a media body, not a state institution.

cases.n: Two ICAO staff joined a drone-buying scheme for Libya's Haftar family
cases.rank: employees of the International Civil Aviation Organization
cases.d: The Sentry's April 2026 report says that, according to Canadian authorities, two Libyan employees of the International Civil Aviation Organization, the United Nations aviation body based in Montreal, took part in a 2024 scheme to procure Chinese drones for the family of Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar, whose forces control eastern Libya. It adds that a former organisation employee, James 'Kuang Chi' Wan, was arrested in 2023 over a related attempted sale. Libya has been under a United Nations arms embargo since 2011. The report notes that many of the entities and individuals it names did not respond to its questions, and that much of its evidence comes from anonymous sources and documents.
cases.inside: Staff of a United Nations aviation body worked inside it on buying drones for a Libyan armed faction, Canadian authorities say.
cases.cite: The Sentry, 'Eastern Libya's Top Money Man', April 2026
cases.drop_reason: Two ICAO employees took part in a drone procurement scheme for the Haftar family, but nothing in the record shows ICAO's own powers, functions or decisions used for it. Their employment is incidental to an arms-embargo scheme; the 'inside' line's claim that they 'worked inside it on buying drones' is not supported.

cases.n: Sudan-brokered deal would put rebel leader Gatwech in South Sudan's army
cases.org_label: Simon Gatwech Dual's forces, with Sudanese authorities in Port Sudan
cases.rank: SSPDF Deputy Chief of Defence Forces (agreed, not taken up)
cases.d: The United Nations Panel of Experts on South Sudan, in its final report dated 1 July 2025, says President Salva Kiir's faction, aided by Sudanese authorities in Port Sudan, announced a deal with Simon Gatwech Dual on 4 February 2025. Gatwech, who is under United Nations sanctions, would become a Deputy Chief of Defence Forces of the South Sudan People's Defence Forces and could integrate as many as 21,900 of his fighters into it, as well as appoint figures to political posts. The Panel notes that Gatwech was in the Sudan at the time and must return to Juba within one year, and describes the arrangement as an agreement rather than an appointment already made.
cases.inside: A neighbouring government helped broker a place for a sanctioned rebel commander and 21,900 of his fighters inside South Sudan's army.
cases.cite: UN Panel of Experts on South Sudan, final report S/2025/442, 1 July 2025
cases.drop_reason: A brokered coalition deal, which the test excludes, and the Panel itself says it is an agreement rather than an appointment made - Gatwech was still in Sudan with a year to return. Nobody is inside the army yet and no decision there has served anyone.

cases.n: M23 replaced Congo's mining offices and took the Twangiza gold mine
cases.rank: mining administration, taxation and courts in occupied territory
cases.d: The midterm report of the United Nations Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, dated 30 December 2025, says that after taking Luhihi in mid-February 2025 the AFC/M23 armed movement replaced state services with its own mining office and levied a 30 per cent tax on ore at the pit, with its agents checking ore grades and supervising quantities sent to mills. It took over the Twangiza Mining SA industrial gold mine on 8 May 2025; the company alleged active support from the Rwanda Defence Force, which the movement's coordinator Corneille Nangaa denied, saying the mine was inactive. The Group says the movement set up parallel fiscal structures, established courts and recruited magistrates, stamped passports and issued visas, and effectively usurped core state functions.
cases.inside: A Rwandan-backed movement put its own staff in place of Congo's mining and tax offices, so mine revenue and rules served it instead of the state.
cases.cite: UN Group of Experts on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, midterm report S/2025/858, 30 December 2025
cases.drop_reason: This is conquest: after taking Luhihi the movement replaced state services with its own mining office, courts and tax structures, which the UN Group calls usurping state functions. Nobody is placed inside a Congolese institution that keeps working; the state offices were displaced.

cases.n: MS-13 leaders negotiated benefits with El Salvador's prison chiefs
cases.org_label: MS-13 (Mara Salvatrucha) and its Ranfla Nacional leadership
cases.rank: prison system director and Social Fabric Reconstruction director
cases.d: MS-13 is a street gang whose imprisoned national leadership is called the Ranfla Nacional. A United States indictment, quoted in reporting in February 2023, alleges that from about 2012 its leaders held secret talks arranged by Salvadoran government and prison officials, including the director of Centro Penales, the national prison service, and the director of Tejido Social Reconstruccion. The indictment alleges the gang was given transfers to less secure prisons, better conditions, conjugal visits, cash payments and promised legal changes cutting sentences, and a refusal to extradite leaders, in return for holding down visible killings and delivering political support. Officials often wore masks. The indictment names prison chief Osiris Luna Meza; Carlos Marroquin is also mentioned.
cases.inside: Prosecutors say a gang got the officials running El Salvador's prisons to grant it privileges and block extraditions in exchange for political support.
cases.cite: US indictment quoted by El Salvador Perspectives, February 2023
cases.drop_reason: Duplicate of a case already removed from the map, and it fails on the merits: officials granted a gang prison privileges, cash and blocked extraditions in return for electoral support. The gang received the benefits; nothing shows its money, people or control inside the prison service.

cases.n: Belize audit: minister signed citizenship for a man jailed abroad
cases.org_label: Foreign buyers of Belizean nationality and passports
cases.rank: Minister of State, Immigration and Nationality Department
cases.d: Belize's Auditor General, Dorothy A. Bradley, audited the nationality section of the Immigration and Nationality Department for 2011 to 2013 after the prime minister said Minister Elvin Penner had approved Belizean nationality for Wonhong Kim while Kim was held in Taiwan. The report, dated 31 May 2016, found Kim's certificate signed on 22 April 2013 but booked on 2 September 2013, a residence permit backdated, no fee paid, and no record of him ever entering Belize; his passport was issued on 9 September 2013 without biometrics. Similar gaps were found for Yakup Sut, Jinchen An and others. The auditors wrote that an illegitimate citizenship and passport scheme was operating in violation of the laws.
cases.inside: Foreign buyers obtained Belizean citizenship and passports through a minister and immigration staff who signed, backdated and booked documents outside the law.
cases.cite: Office of the Auditor General of Belize, Nationality Special Report, 31 May 2016
cases.drop_reason: Duplicate of a removed record covering the same minister and the same buyer, Wonhong Kim. The audit also shows no payment to anyone - only that fees were unpaid and documents backdated - so no outside party's money is shown inside the department.

cases.n: Serving Trinidad police officer charged in US cocaine conspiracy
cases.org_label: Cocaine trafficking conspiracy charged in the Eastern District of New York
cases.rank: serving officer, Trinidad and Tobago Police Service
cases.d: Rafael Joseph, described as an active duty officer of the Trinidad and Tobago Police Service, was arrested together with Michael McSween and Clevon Persad on provisional warrants served on 30 December 2025. All three are charged in the United States Eastern District of New York with conspiracy to import cocaine into the United States and with firearms offences. The charges arise from a 2024 Drug Enforcement Administration investigation. The United States Embassy in Port of Spain described the arrest as a blow against public corruption. The reporting does not set out what Joseph is alleged to have done beyond being a serving officer charged in the conspiracy, and the case has not been tried.
cases.inside: Prosecutors say a cocaine-importing conspiracy counted a serving Trinidadian police officer among its members, putting the force inside the trade it polices.
cases.cite: Jamaica Observer, 6 January 2026
cases.drop_reason: The record states outright that it does not set out what the officer is alleged to have done beyond being a serving officer charged in the conspiracy. Too vague to say what got inside what, and the 'inside' line's claim that the force was placed inside the drug trade is not in the record.

cases.n: Uruguay issued a passport to trafficker Sebastian Marset
cases.rank: Foreign Ministry and Interior Ministry officials
cases.d: Uruguay's foreign ministry issued a passport that reached Sebastian Marset, a Uruguayan drug trafficker, after the Uruguayan lawyer Alejandro Balbi processed the application. The document was granted under decree 129 of 2014, which did not bar Uruguayans with criminal records abroad from obtaining a passport. The Ministerio Publico questioned several foreign ministry officials, among them the former vice foreign minister Carolina Ache, and the former interior under-secretary Guillermo Maciel publicly defended the process. Prosecutor Alejandro Machado of the economic crimes unit concluded that no criminal liability could be assigned, and the case was archived on 2 September 2024. Maciel said afterwards that there had been neither an offence nor intent, and that the passport was not the reason for Marset's release.
cases.undone: Case archived on 2 September 2024; the prosecutor found no criminal liability.
cases.inside: A wanted trafficker obtained a Uruguayan passport through the foreign ministry's own handling of his file; prosecutors later found no crime in it.
cases.cite: Montevideo Portal, September 2024
cases.drop_reason: The passport was lawful under decree 129 of 2014, the prosecutor concluded no criminal liability could be assigned and the case was archived. No payment and no official working for the trafficker is shown - the record describes the ministry's own handling of a file.

cases.n: Tongan foreign minister convicted over passports for two Chinese nationals
cases.org_label: Two Chinese nationals who obtained Tongan passports
cases.rank: Minister of Foreign Affairs, later Prime Minister
cases.d: A Tongan politician who later became prime minister was found guilty in 2020 of perjury and of making false statements to obtain a passport for two Chinese nationals, conduct that took place while he was foreign minister. Bribery and money laundering charges brought in the same matter were dropped. Tonga has sold passports before, and the sale of citizenship has repeatedly drawn scrutiny in the Pacific. The case is recorded in a Transparency International anti-corruption helpdesk review of corruption in Pacific island countries, which does not name the minister, the two nationals or the amounts involved.
cases.undone: Bribery and money laundering charges in the same case were dropped; he was convicted of perjury and false statements.
cases.inside: Two foreign nationals got Tongan passports through the minister in charge of them, who then lied in official statements about how it was done.
cases.cite: Transparency International / U4 Anti-Corruption Helpdesk, Overview of corruption and anti-corruption in Pacific island countries
cases.drop_reason: The bribery and money laundering charges were dropped; what remains is a minister lying in official statements to obtain passports for two foreign nationals. That is an office-holder misusing his own powers so outsiders benefited, with nothing showing they paid or placed anyone.

cases.n: Tuvalu's prime minister took money from Japanese and Taiwanese interests
cases.d: A former prime minister of Tuvalu was sentenced to four years in prison for corruption and abuse of office after receiving more than 15,000 United States dollars from Japanese and Taiwanese interests in 2016. Tuvalu is a state of about 11,000 people whose government depends heavily on fishing licence revenue and on aid from partners including Japan and Taiwan, so payments from those quarters reach directly into a very small executive. The case is recorded in a Transparency International anti-corruption helpdesk review of corruption in Pacific island countries, which does not name the former prime minister, the specific companies or bodies that paid, or what they received in return.
cases.inside: Outside Japanese and Taiwanese interests put money directly into the hands of the head of Tuvalu's government, who was convicted of abusing the office.
cases.cite: Transparency International / U4 Anti-Corruption Helpdesk, Overview of corruption and anti-corruption in Pacific island countries
cases.drop_reason: Money from Japanese and Taiwanese interests reached the prime minister and he was convicted of corruption, but the record says it does not state what the payers received. No decision or action inside the government is shown serving them.

cases.n: Albemarle's agents bribed state oil refineries in three countries
cases.d: Albemarle Corporation, a specialty chemicals company based in Charlotte, North Carolina, settled charges under the anti-bribery, recordkeeping and internal accounting controls provisions of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act on 29 September 2023. The Securities and Exchange Commission found that from at least 2009 through 2017 Albemarle used agents, despite significant warning signs, who paid bribes to win sales of refinery catalysts to state-owned oil refineries in Vietnam, India and Indonesia, and to private refineries in India. Albemarle paid more than $103.6 million to the SEC in disgorgement and interest, and the Justice Department entered a non-prosecution agreement with a $99 million fine and about $98 million in forfeiture, most of it met by the SEC payment.
cases.inside: The company's agents paid officials inside state-owned refineries, whose purchasing decisions then went to the company selling the catalysts.
cases.cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission press release 2023-209, 29 September 2023
cases.drop_reason: It passes the test - the company's agents paid officials inside state refineries whose purchasing then went to it - but the same case is already on the map as "Albemarle's agents bribed state refinery officials in Vietnam, India, Indonesia".

cases.n: Lender paid Mexican officials $4m to lend to government employees
cases.rank: Mexican government officials and union officials
cases.d: World Acceptance Corporation, a consumer loan company based in South Carolina, settled charges under the anti-bribery, books and records and internal accounting controls provisions of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act on 6 August 2020. The US Securities and Exchange Commission found that from at least December 2010 through June 2017 its former Mexican subsidiary, WAC de Mexico, paid more than $4 million in bribes to Mexican government officials and union officials to secure the ability to make loans to government employees and to make sure those loans were repaid on time. Money was deposited into accounts linked to the officials and an intermediary handed out large bags of cash. The company paid $17.826 million in disgorgement, $1.9 million in interest and a $2 million penalty.

cases.n: Church front group had LDP candidates sign a five-point policy pledge
cases.rank: House of Representatives members and candidates
cases.d: Before Japan's general election of October 2021 the World Peace Alliance, which Shimbun Akahata describes as a front body of the Unification Church and which is chaired by Masayoshi Kajikuri of the church's International Federation for Victory over Communism, asked Liberal Democratic Party candidates to sign a form it called a confirmation of recommendation, in effect a policy agreement, before it would back them. Its five points were constitutional revision and stronger security, a family education support law, caution on LGBT issues and same-sex marriage, a Japan-Korea tunnel, and blocking communist forces. Akahata named one signer, the LDP member Hiroaki Saito, whose office said he signed it and that about five people took turns in his office making campaign calls. The church's reform director confirmed the form existed.
cases.cite: Shimbun Akahata, 21 and 23 October 2022
cases.inside: A church front body got lawmakers to sign its policy demands and put its helpers in their offices, in exchange for the votes it could deliver.
cases.drop_reason: A front body required candidates to sign its five policy points before backing them, and church helpers made campaign calls in one office. Both are pre-election bargaining and campaign volunteering from outside, and no decision taken in office is shown. The map has already dropped the same patterns (the '290 LDP lawmakers' backing record and two campaign-helper records).

cases.n: Japan's education minister had signed the church's policy pledge
cases.rank: Minister of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology
cases.d: Masahito Moriyama was Japan's education minister, the office that supervises religious corporations. In October 2023 his ministry asked the Tokyo District Court to dissolve the Unification Church, after interviewing more than 170 people said to have been harmed and finding 32 civil judgments awarding 2.2 billion yen to 169 people. In February 2024 the Asahi Shimbun reported that before the October 2021 lower house election Moriyama had himself signed an agreement with an association affiliated to the church, carrying policy proposals on education, constitutional revision and LGBTQ issues, and that he attended a meeting the group organised in his Kobe constituency and took its formal endorsement. Opposition members pressed him on it in a lower house committee.
cases.cite: The Japan Times, 7 February 2024 (reporting Asahi Shimbun); NBC News/AP, 13 October 2023
cases.inside: The minister who decides religious bodies' legal status had signed the church's own policy agreement and taken its election backing, reports say.
cases.drop_reason: The minister had signed the church's policy agreement and taken its endorsement, but what his ministry then did was ask the court to dissolve the church. No decision inside served the outside party - the record shows the opposite.

cases.n: Former church members worked in ex-minister Yamagiwa's constituency office
cases.rank: House of Representatives member; former economic revitalisation minister
cases.d: Daishiro Yamagiwa resigned as Japan's economic revitalisation minister in 2022 over his dealings with the Unification Church. The prefectural assembly member Kuniko Ogawa had made the claim publicly, and A filed a defamation complaint against her in January 2025. Yamagiwa's office says it has severed all ties with the church and that Ogawa's claim is false.
cases.cite: Tansa, The True Mother Files, February 2026
cases.inside: A church member reportedly ran the branch finances and campaign of a lawmaker the church's own reports counted on, though his office denies any tie remains.

cases.n: Serbia's culture minister charged over heritage loss for Kushner project
cases.rank: Minister of Culture; two state heritage institutes
cases.d: The former Yugoslav army General Staff complex in central Belgrade, damaged in the NATO bombing of 1999, was to be demolished and the site leased for a hotel and housing development backed by Jared Kushner's investment firm. Prosecutors charge that four officials manipulated official documents to strip the complex of its heritage protection and clear the way for the project: the culture minister Nikola Selakovic, his ministry's secretary Slavica Jelaca, Goran Vasic, acting director of the Republic Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments, and Aleksandar Ivanovic, acting head of Belgrade's city heritage institute. Vasic had been arrested in early 2025 on suspicion of falsifying the expert assessments used to justify revoking the protected status. The trial opened on 4 February 2026. All four deny wrongdoing.
cases.cite: bne IntelliNews, 4 February 2026; European Western Balkans, 10 December 2025
cases.inside: Prosecutors say officials inside the culture ministry and two heritage institutes faked the papers protecting a state site so a foreign investor's project could proceed.
cases.drop_reason: The Serbia case its own author flagged: officials inside the culture ministry and two heritage institutes are charged with faking the papers that protected a state site, and a foreign-backed project benefited. Nothing shows Affinity Partners placing, paying or controlling anyone - officials misusing their own powers while an outside party gains.

cases.n: Alexion paid Turkish officials to approve prescriptions of its drug
cases.d: The US Securities and Exchange Commission announced on 2 July 2020 that Alexion Pharmaceuticals, a US drug company, would pay more than $21 million over breaches of the books and records and internal accounting controls provisions of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. The SEC found that from 2010 to 2015 the company's Turkish subsidiary, Alexion Turkey, paid Turkish government officials to influence them to approve patient prescriptions of its drug Soliris and to give it other favourable regulatory treatment, and kept false records of those payments. The same order covers Alexion's Brazil and Colombia subsidiaries, which failed to keep accurate records of payments to patient advocacy organisations. Alexion paid $14,210,194 in disgorgement, $3,766,337 in interest and a $3.5 million penalty, without admitting or denying the findings.
cases.inside: The drug company's Turkish arm paid government officials for five years to get patient prescriptions of its drug Soliris approved and its regulatory treatment eased.
cases.cite: US Securities and Exchange Commission press release 2020-149, 2 July 2020
cases.drop_reason: Source names no city and no ministry, agency or official inside: the marker city was the record’s own inference. Recoverable if the underlying SEC/DOJ order names a body (round 3, 10 Nov 2026)

cases.n: Alexion paid Russian health officials over its drug's state budget
cases.d: In the same settlement, announced on 2 July 2020, the US Securities and Exchange Commission found that Alexion Pharmaceuticals' Russian subsidiary made improper payments from 2011 to 2015 to Russian government health care officials. The aim was to affect the regulatory treatment of its drug Soliris, to affect the budget the state allocated to the drug, and to increase the number of approved prescriptions for it. The subsidiary kept false books and records of the payments, and the SEC said Alexion's internal accounting controls were not sufficient to detect or prevent them. Alexion paid more than $21 million in total for the Russian and Turkish conduct and agreed to stop breaching the books and records and internal controls provisions of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act.
cases.inside: The drug company paid officials in Russia's health administration, aiming to influence the state budget set aside for its medicine and the number of prescriptions approved.

cases.d: Herbalife Nutrition Ltd. agreed on 28 August 2020 to pay more than $122 million to resolve a US foreign bribery case, including a criminal penalty of over $55 million under a three-year deferred prosecution agreement on one count of conspiring to violate the books and records provisions of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and about $67 million to the Securities and Exchange Commission. orgs.d: France's English-recognised 'regular' Grand Lodge, founded in Paris in 1913 by a lodge that broke from the Grand Orient and an independent lodge in Bordeaux. In December 2009 Grand Master François Stifani faced a revolt over €17 million spent; in January 2011 a court put the Grand Lodge under an appointed administrator. The United Grand Lodge of England suspended relations on 14 September 2011 and withdrew recognition on 12 September 2012, then restored it in June 2014 after Jean-Pierre Servel replaced Stifani. Membership of francophone African heads of state is widely reported but is not documented in the source used here.

orgs.d: Italy's main Masonic body, founded in 1805 under the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy. Mussolini suppressed Freemasonry in 1925; it was restarted after the Second World War. It originally chartered the P2 lodge and revoked the charter in 1974. The United Grand Lodge of England withdrew recognition in 1993, citing corruption and Mafia accusations, and restored it in March 2023. In September 2015 it reported 22,675 members in 842 lodges.

orgs.d: A Catholic lay order descended from the Knights Hospitaller (papal recognition 1113), seated in Rome since 1834, with about 13,500 knights, dames and chaplains. It is a sovereign subject of international law, a UN General Assembly observer since 1994, and has formal diplomatic relations with 114–115 states. In 2016–17 Grand Master Matthew Festing removed Grand Chancellor Albrecht von Boeselager over condom distribution in a Myanmar aid project; in January 2017 Pope Francis ordered Boeselager reinstated, required Festing to resign and named Archbishop Giovanni Becciu his special delegate.

orgs.d: A Catholic congregation founded by Marcial Maciel in Mexico City on 3 January 1941, part of the Regnum Christi Federation. It runs a network of private schools and universities for Mexico's elite, including the Anáhuac University Network, and its priests serve as chaplains to business leaders in Latin America. The Vatican removed Maciel from ministry in 2006 and in 2010 said his actions were real crimes.

orgs.d: A Catholic traditionalist movement founded in Brazil in 1960 by Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira; national TFPs followed in about 30 countries. Its campaign against land reform is described as contributing to Brazil's 1964 coup. Chile's Frei government banned the Chilean TFP, which welcomed the 1973 coup; South Africa's P. W. Botha wrote to commend it in 1987; Venezuela's Lusinchi government moved to ban it after an investigation found it operating outside the constitution. Successors include the Heralds of the Gospel (2001) and the Instituto Plinio Corrêa de Oliveira; Poland's Ordo Iuris was founded by a TFP-linked association.

orgs.d: A church founded by Apollo Quiboloy in Davao City on 1 September 1985. A US federal grand jury indicted Quiboloy in 2021 for child sex trafficking and misuse of donations, and the US Treasury sanctioned him in 2022. In March 2024 its broadcaster SMNI said former President Rodrigo Duterte had been made administrator of its properties. Police raided the Davao compound from 24 August 2024 and arrested Quiboloy in September 2024.

orgs.d: A self-help company founded near Albany in 1998 by Keith Raniere and Nancy Salzman, with centres in the US, Canada and Mexico; prosecutors called it a front for crime. Its secret women's group DOS branded members and held 'collateral'. Raniere was convicted in June 2019 and sentenced on 27 October 2020 to 120 years; the Second Circuit upheld it in 2022. Emiliano Salinas, son of former Mexican president Carlos Salinas, and Ana Cristina Fox, daughter of Vicente Fox, have been accused of involvement; NXIVM kept dossiers on officials and pushed officials to investigate critics.
orgs.drop_reason: Description shows crimes within a self-help company; the claim that it pushed officials to act is too vague to stand as infiltration without invention.

orgs.hq: Cairo (operations centre); founded at a Kenyan resort
orgs.d: An intelligence alliance chartered on 1 September 1976 by the spy chiefs of France, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Iran, named after the Kenyan resort where it first met; it ran an operations centre in Cairo. Saudi Arabia paid, France supplied technology, and Egypt and Morocco supplied troops and arms. In 1977 French aircraft flew Moroccan and Egyptian troops into Zaire's Shaba province; it armed Somalia in the Ogaden war and gave about $5 million to UNITA in Angola. Saudi intelligence chief Prince Turki al-Faisal described it in a 2002 speech at Georgetown.

orgs.reach_src: Member intelligence services, per Wikipedia 'Safari Club'.
orgs.drop_reason: An alliance of governments' spy chiefs acting abroad together is covert state cooperation, not one party getting inside another's institutions.

orgs.d: A cross-border repression system set up at a meeting called by Chile's DINA in Santiago on 25–28 November 1975; Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia signed, Brazil joined in 1976 and Peru and Ecuador later. Members shared intelligence and kidnapped, tortured and killed exiles across borders; John Dinges documented 654 victims from 1976 to 1980. Operations reached Washington (the 1976 Letelier–Moffitt car bomb) and Europe. In 2016 a Buenos Aires court convicted 15 former officers, the first court ruling to recognise Condor.
orgs.cite: Buenos Aires federal court 'Plan Cóndor' verdict 2016; US National Security Archive, 2025 briefing book
orgs.reach_src: Member states per the National Security Archive and Wikipedia 'Operation Condor'.
orgs.drop_reason: Cross-border kidnapping and killing by cooperating governments is state repression, not infiltration of an institution.

orgs.d: A fake press agency set up in Lisbon in September 1966 under Salazar's regime, run by ex-OAS captain Yves Guérin-Sérac, with Italian neo-fascist Stefano Delle Chiaie among its founders. It allegedly worked against independence movements in Angola, Mozambique and East Timor. Italian judge Guido Salvini found its instructors trained Avanguardia Nazionale members in explosives and linked it to groups behind the 1969 Piazza Fontana bombing. After the 1974 Carnation Revolution its staff fled; a document titled 'Our Political Activity' set out the aim to 'create the conditions favouring the installation of chaos'.
orgs.cite: Investigations of Judge Guido Salvini (Milan); Wikipedia 'Aginter Press'
orgs.drop_reason: Description shows a front press agency training militants; the record shows no one placed inside a government, international body or company.

orgs.d: A merchant bank founded in Sydney in 1973 by lawyer Frank Nugan and former US Green Beret Michael Hand, which opened overseas branches and hired retired senior US military and intelligence officers, with former CIA director William Colby as a lawyer. Nugan was found dead near Lithgow in January 1980; Hand destroyed records and fled Australia in June 1980. The 1985 Stewart Royal Commission found banking-law violations and money laundering but no credible evidence of drug smuggling, arms dealing or CIA involvement; the 1980–83 Joint Task Force on Drug Trafficking disputed that.

orgs.drop_reason: The Royal Commission found banking violations and laundering by the bank's own people but no credible evidence of intelligence involvement; hiring retired officers is not infiltration.

Its membership is drawn often from current and former heads of state; honorary members include Mikhail Gorbachev, Fernando Henrique Cardoso, King Juan Carlos I, Horst Köhler, Princess Beatrix and Manmohan Singh. It has national associations in 35 countries and territories.

It placed US experts in Saudi ministries and agencies on infrastructure and planning projects.

orgs.d: Unofficial offices abroad linked to the public security bureaus of Chinese cities such as Fuzhou, Qingtian, Nantong and Wenzhou. Safeguard Defenders reported in September and December 2022 that they were used to pressure people wanted by China, including dissidents, to return; China says they renew documents and fight fraud. Ireland and the Netherlands ordered stations closed in 2022, the UK said in 2023 they had closed, and US prosecutors charged two men in 2023 over a station in Manhattan (one pleaded guilty in 2024, one was convicted in 2026).

orgs.drop_reason: The record shows unofficial Chinese offices pressuring people abroad, but not anyone inside the host countries' institutions working for them.

orgs.n: United Russia party – foreign party cooperation agreements
orgs.d: United Russia is Vladimir Putin's ruling party. It signs formal cooperation agreements with foreign parties covering delegation exchanges, contacts between legislators and economic cooperation: Austria's FPÖ signed one on 19 December 2016 (expired end 2021) and Italy's Lega on 6 March 2017 (renewing automatically every five years). Bulgaria's Russophiles party signed a memorandum with it for the 2021 elections.
orgs.cite: Agreement texts published by Il Foglio (Lega) and reported by Vindobona (FPÖ)
orgs.drop_reason: The record describes formal, published cooperation agreements between parties, which are open and declared, not hidden placement of people or money.

orgs.n: DITIB – Turkish-Islamic Union for Religious Affairs
orgs.d: Founded in 1984 as the German branch of Turkey's state religious authority, the Diyanet; it runs about 900 mosques in Germany. Its imams are trained in Ankara and paid as Turkish civil servants. German federal prosecutors investigated imams in 2017 for spying on Gülen supporters (case dropped in December 2017), and Germany's interior ministry cut its funding in 2018.
orgs.cite: German Federal Prosecutor's Office 2017; Federal Ministry of the Interior 2018
orgs.drop_reason: The record shows open Turkish state control of a German mosque association and an inquiry into imams spying on individuals that was dropped, not anyone placed inside a government, international body or company.

orgs.drop_reason: The record shows a religious centre aligned with Iran and banned in Germany, with no one placed inside German institutions.

orgs.drop_reason: The record shows a vaccine contract negotiated partly by text and a court ruling on access to the texts, not anyone placed inside the EU's institutions.

orgs.d: Founded in 1930 under the Young Plan to handle German reparations, owned by member central banks, and the oldest international financial institution. It hosts closed meetings of central bank governors (monthly in the 1930s, every two months since 1998) and the Basel Committee whose capital rules countries adopt. In 1939 it transferred Czechoslovakia's gold to the Reichsbank; the 1944 Bretton Woods conference called for its liquidation, reversed in 1948. Carroll Quigley called it 'the apex' of a private world system of financial control.
orgs.cite: Wikipedia 'Bank for International Settlements'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope pp. 324–325
orgs.drop_reason: The BIS is an open body owned by central banks; its gold transfer and closed meetings are its own conduct, and Quigley's 'apex of control' is an opinion, not a record of anyone placed inside institutions.

orgs.n: Bohemian Club gathers presidents and cabinet officers in private
orgs.hq: San Francisco; camp at Bohemian Grove, Sonoma County
orgs.d: The Bohemian Club, a private men's club in San Francisco, brings US presidents, cabinet officers and business leaders together at a closed two-week camp each year at Bohemian Grove in Sonoma County. Members have included several US presidents, usually before election, and many cabinet officers; Richard Nixon was an honorary member. A memo has linked Ronald Reagan's 1983 Social Security cuts to a Bohemian Club meeting in 1981. Journalists founded the club in April 1872, and wealthy and powerful men came to control it.
orgs.drop_reason: A meeting place, not an infiltrator: The Bohemian Club's role in the record is hosting a private summer camp where presidents, cabinet officers and business leaders meet; it does not itself place members, pay officials or control an institution.

orgs.n: Le Cercle chairs included MPs who did not declare the role
orgs.d: Le Cercle, an invitation-only foreign-policy forum, has been chaired by serving British politicians, including the sitting MPs Rory Stewart and Nadhim Zahawi, who did not declare the role to Parliament. Other chairmen included Brian Crozier, Julian Amery, Jonathan Aitken and Norman Lamont. French prime minister Antoine Pinay and intelligence agent Jean Violet founded it in 1952–53, with Konrad Adenauer and Franz Josef Strauss. Apartheid South Africa sent the only official delegation, and the group backed the Renamo and UNITA rebels. Alan Clark wrote in his diaries that it was CIA-funded.

orgs.drop_reason: A meeting place, not an infiltrator: Le Cercle is an invitation-only foreign-policy forum whose role in the record is mainly to host private meetings of politicians and intelligence figures, not to place members or control an institution itself.

orgs.n: Bilderberg dinner promoted the EU Council president's candidacy
orgs.hq: Rotating; first meeting Hotel de Bilderberg, Oosterbeek
orgs.d: The Bilderberg Meetings, a private annual conference of politicians, business leaders and officials, has been used to promote a candidate for a top international post out of public view. In November 2009 a Bilderberg dinner at Val-Duchesse in Brussels promoted Herman Van Rompuy's candidacy for President of the European Council (the post that chairs summits of EU leaders), which he won. The first meeting was held in May 1954 at the Hotel de Bilderberg in Oosterbeek, promoted by Prince Bernhard of the Netherlands. It typically has 120–150 participants; at the 2025 Stockholm meeting, Swedish prime minister Ulf Kristersson attended though not on the published list.
orgs.reach_src: Host countries of documented meetings and nationalities of chairs/attendees named in Wikipedia 'Bilderberg Meeting' and Polskie Radio (2025). The full 23-country 2025 list was not available.
orgs.drop_reason: A meeting place, not an infiltrator: The Bilderberg Meetings are a private annual conference where politicians, officials and business leaders meet; the record shows people promoted or attending there, not the conference itself placing members or controlling an institution.

orgs.d: Skull and Bones, a secret society at Yale University that picks 15 students a year, has had its members rise to the top of the US government, where they sit alongside fellow members bound to the society's secrecy. Members who reached national office include Presidents William Howard Taft and George H. W. Bush, who earlier ran the CIA, President George W. Bush, and Secretary of State John Kerry; in 2004 both major presidential nominees, Bush and Kerry, were members. Henry Stimson ran the War and State departments and Steven Mnuchin the Treasury. It was founded in 1832 and has no documented presence abroad.
orgs.drop_reason: All its cases removed under the Nov 2026 stricter infiltration test

orgs.d: Members of the Thule Society, a German nationalist and occultist lodge formed in Munich in 1918, moved into the leadership of the Nazi movement and later the Nazi state. The society sponsored the German Workers' Party, which became the Nazi Party (NSDAP) by 1920. Historian Nicholas Goodrick-Clarke counts Rudolf Hess and Hans Frank as members, and Alfred Rosenberg, Dietrich Eckart and Gottfried Feder only as guests; he calls longer lists that include Hitler 'spurious'. Hess became Deputy Führer in 1933, and Frank became a Reich minister and, from 1939, Governor-General of occupied Poland. The society dissolved about 1925; what is known of its membership comes from Goodrick-Clarke's study of its records.

orgs.d: Communion and Liberation (CL), a Catholic lay movement founded in Milan in 1954 by Fr. Luigi Giussani, had one of its own running Lombardy, Italy's richest region: Roberto Formigoni, governor for 18 years and an informal CL political spokesman. Prosecutors showed that the Maugeri health foundation in Pavia paid about €61 million in 1997–2011 to businessman Pierangelo Daccò and former regional councillor Antonio Simone, who gave Formigoni holidays, yachts and cash, while the region granted Maugeri about €200 million in favourable health payments. In December 2016 a Milan court sentenced Formigoni to six years for corruption. The movement says it is present in about 90 countries and runs the annual Rimini Meeting.

The society had about 12,000 members by 1977. Ayatollah Khomeini criticised it publicly on 12 July 1983 and Halabi suspended its activities the same day, but it reportedly revived quietly in the 1990s.

Aleksander Stępkowski chaired Ordo Iuris's board, then in November 2015 the new Law and Justice government made him deputy foreign minister for legal and treaty affairs; he left in August 2016. In 2016 Ordo Iuris drafted a near-total abortion ban that the Sejm, Poland's lower house, rejected after nationwide protests. orgs.d: The Trilateral Commission, a private forum of business and political figures from North America, Western Europe and Japan founded in 1973 at David Rockefeller's insistence, supplied much of Jimmy Carter's government. Zbigniew Brzezinski left Columbia University to organise it and served as its director; Carter was a member. When Carter became president in 1977, Brzezinski became his National Security Adviser. In 1980 the Christian Science Monitor counted 21 former members in the administration, including Carter, Vice-President Walter Mondale, Secretary of State Cyrus Vance and Defense Secretary Harold Brown, so members of one private forum held the top foreign-policy and defence posts. Membership was not secret; the overlap was shown by published membership lists.

orgs.n: World Economic Forum (incl. Young Global Leaders)
orgs.d: The World Economic Forum, a Swiss foundation best known for its annual Davos meeting, picks rising politicians for its Young Global Leaders programme, and many of them later led governments. Since 1992 the programme has inducted about 1,400 people; alumni who became heads of government include Justin Trudeau, Emmanuel Macron, Jacinda Ardern, Sanna Marin, Mark Rutte, Alexander De Croo, Sebastian Kurz and Enrique Peña Nieto. Founder Klaus Schwab was reported by CNN in 2022 to have said at a 2017 Harvard talk 'we penetrate the cabinets' and that over half of Trudeau's cabinet were alumni. Political scientists quoted in the same report said there was no credible evidence the Forum controls governments. Schwab stepped down as chair on 21 April 2025; an external investigation found no 'material wrongdoing'.

orgs.d: The Atlas Network, a US foundation founded in 1981 that sets up and funds free-market think tanks abroad, works through those partners to write legislation, meet policymakers and move their staff into government. Its partners' people have taken top posts: David Seymour became New Zealand's deputy prime minister, Fundación Pensar merged into Mauricio Macri's party in Argentina, and Atlas says its partners shaped Javier Milei's reforms. WNYC reported that partners write legislation, and a 2018 academic article said the World Bank's Doing Business work 'follows exactly Atlas' policy recommendations'. ALEC, which drafts model US state laws, is a member.

orgs.d: Member governments have placed their own security officials at the head of Interpol, the body of 196 countries through which police forces ask each other to find and arrest suspects. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) gave about $54 million through the Interpol Foundation, estimated to equal the yearly dues of all other members combined, and in 2021 its interior ministry official Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi was elected president. orgs.d: The Rhodes Trust, set up under the will of the British colonialist Cecil Rhodes in 1902 to promote unity among English-speaking nations, had its own chief placed in Britain's top diplomatic post in the United States. Philip Kerr (Lord Lothian), a member of Alfred Milner's circle of imperialists and founding editor of its Round Table journal, was the trust's General Secretary from 1925 until 1939, when he became ambassador in Washington. He served until his death in December 1940 and worked to win US support for Britain's war effort, including the Lend-Lease aid law passed after his death. The trust's first trustees included Milner, and its Oxford scholarships have produced eight later heads of state or government, among them Bill Clinton, Bob Hawke and Malcolm Turnbull.

orgs.d: The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, a private US charity, steers the work of the World Health Organization (WHO), the UN's health agency, by paying for the programmes it chooses. About 90% of WHO income is voluntary money, nearly all earmarked by donors, so the WHO's member states no longer decide where most of its budget goes. The foundation is WHO's second-largest funder: in 2020 it supplied 45% of WHO funds from non-state bodies. A BMJ Global Health study in October 2025 found its 640 grants worth about $5.5 billion in 2000–2024 went over 80% to infectious diseases and about 60% to polio, with under 1% for non-communicable diseases. The authors said WHO stays open to donor influence unless member states pay more.

orgs.n: International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG)
orgs.d: The International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG) was set up by a 2006 UN–Guatemala agreement to help Guatemalan prosecutors take apart criminal networks inside the state; on this map it is the investigator, not the party reaching in. Congress lifted Pérez Molina's immunity 132–0 and he resigned on 2 September 2015; both were sentenced to 16 years in December 2022. CICIG helped break up over 70 networks before President Jimmy Morales shut it down in 2019.

orgs.d: The Mourides are a Sufi Muslim brotherhood founded in Senegal in 1883 by Amadou Bamba, and their caliph (spiritual leader) trades religious backing for state support and influence. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye visited Caliph Serigne Mountakha Mbacké on 7 August 2025, a visit before the annual Grand Magal pilgrimage that has become customary for heads of state.

He has said a chance meeting with the order's sheikh set him on the Sufi path. The Moroccan state promotes Sufism as an alternative to Salafism. Swiss senator Dick Marty told the Council's Parliamentary Assembly in December 2010 that the group controlled criminal trades including heroin, and found 'credible, convergent indications' of organ trafficking after the 1999 war. The Assembly endorsed the report in January 2011; Thaçi denied it. An EU task force later led to the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, where Thaçi has been on trial for war crimes since 2023. The bank theft he was tried for drained money that the state later had to cover. A Chișinău court convicted him in April 2026 over the 2014 theft of about $1 billion from Moldovan banks.

orgs.d: M. M. Warburg & Co. is a Hamburg private bank founded in 1798, and its head Max Warburg, who ran it from 1910 to 1938, moved between the bank and German state posts. He served as an expert at the 1919 Versailles peace talks, where his partner Carl Melchior became principal delegate for economic questions on his recommendation, and sat on the general council of the Reichsbank, Germany's central bank, from 1924. The Nazis forced him off the council because he was Jewish and 'Aryanised' the bank in 1938. In 2016 a €47 million cum-ex tax claim against the bank was dropped after its co-owner met Hamburg mayor Olaf Scholz.

orgs.d: BlackRock, the world's largest asset manager, was hired to run US public rescue programmes while its own executives moved into top government posts. The US Treasury retained it in 2009, and in March 2020 the Federal Reserve chose it to manage its $500 billion and other corporate bond-buying programmes. In 2021 Brian Deese, BlackRock's former global head of sustainable investing, became director of President Biden's National Economic Council, which coordinates economic policy. In Germany, Friedrich Merz chaired BlackRock's German arm from 2016 to 2020, returned to parliament in 2021 and was elected Chancellor in May 2025.

orgs.d: Banco Rural, a Brazilian bank owned by the Rabello family, supplied the cash used to pay members of Congress for their votes in the 'mensalão' (big monthly payment) scheme of 2005. Large withdrawals from its branches in Brasília and Belo Horizonte, made through firms of publicist Marcos Valério, went to deputies, their relatives or advisers so that they would back the Workers' Party government. In 2012 Brazil's Supreme Federal Court convicted the bank's president, Kátia Rabello, of money laundering and other crimes. The Central Bank of Brazil put the bank into liquidation in 2013.

orgs.d: The National Intelligence Service (NIS), formerly the KCIA, is South Korea's intelligence agency, and US prosecutors charged that it recruited a Washington foreign-policy expert to work for it. Sue Mi Terry, a former CIA analyst and fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, a leading US think tank, was indicted in July 2024 as an unregistered foreign agent acting for the NIS since 2013. Prosecutors said she passed notes from a 2022 private meeting with Secretary of State Antony Blinken and wrote op-eds at NIS request, in return for designer goods and over $37,000 for her programmes. NGOs with UN accreditation may speak at Council sessions. EU DisinfoLab exposed the network in 2019 and in December 2020 as 'Indian Chronicles': it revived dead NGOs, impersonated dead rights activists, ran hundreds of fake local news sites and also worked on the European Parliament. EU DisinfoLab did not show that the Indian government directed it.

Leaked ministry emails reported by Semafor and Iran International in September 2023 revealed it and said it was proposed by diplomat Saeed Khatibzadeh. Pentagon official Ariane Tabatabai was linked to it, and House Armed Services chairman Mike Rogers objected. The US sanctioned him for corruption on 21 December 2017. When the US asked for leader Christopher Coke's extradition, the government resisted for nine months and hired a Washington law firm to lobby against it. The 2010 police and army operation to arrest him killed at least 69 people. Coke pleaded guilty in New York in 2011, Golding resigned over the affair, and a 2016 commission found the operation unjustified in how it was carried out.

orgs.d: The Mong Tai Army was the private force of Khun Sa, the best-known opium warlord of the Golden Triangle, indicted in the US in 1990. Myanmar's military rulers made a secret deal with him: in return for surrendering the army in January 1996 he received government protection and no extradition. He moved to Yangon with a large fortune and became a businessman with investments in Yangon, Mandalay and Taunggyi, a ruby mine and a highway contract, under military intelligence watch, until his death in 2007.

Israel alleged in January 2024 that 12 UNRWA employees took part in the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023; UN internal investigators concluded that nine may have been involved and they were dismissed. orgs.d: The Houthi movement, a Zaydi Shia armed group from northern Yemen, took over the Yemeni state from inside its capital. Its fighters seized Sana'a's government buildings in September 2014, evicted oil company officials, blocked the Hodeidah port director and fired four provincial governors. After President Hadi resigned in January 2015 it declared parliament dissolved and put its Revolutionary Committee in charge, and in 2016 set up the Supreme Political Council, which appoints the cabinet in Sana'a. The UN called it a clear violation of Yemen's constitution.

In 2017 he used the force to take Darfur gold mines, and his firm al-Junaid became Sudan's biggest gold trader. After the 2019 coup he became deputy head of the ruling council; RSF forces killed about 100 protesters in Khartoum that June. In 2023 the RSF went to war with the army, and in 2025 the US found it had committed genocide.

Some police applications were filed after the 6 January 2021 attack on the Capitol. Founder Stewart Rhodes was convicted of seditious conspiracy in 2022; his sentence was commuted in 2025.

After the putsch failed, Salan and colonels such as Yves Godard and Antoine Argoud led the OAS, which killed Algiers police chief Roger Gavoury and tried to kill de Gaulle at Petit-Clamart in 1962.

Membership was secret and Chiang never acknowledged it. Its members spread through the army and the party, competing with the civilian CC Clique, and some joined the regime's espionage and assassination service, the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics. Membership peaked at about 10,000 in 1935, and in 1938 the new party youth corps was placed largely under its influence.

It placed members in the army, civil service, police, national assembly, schools and media, growing from about 10,000 members in 1955 to 1,386,757 in 1962. Historian Bernard Fall called it 'a state within a state'. It was banned and dissolved after the November 1963 coup in which Diệm and Nhu were killed.

orgs.d: The Black Dragon Society was a Japanese ultranationalist society founded in 1901 by Uchida Ryōhei, successor to Tōyama Mitsuru's Gen'yōsha, with the stated aim of keeping Russia north of the Amur River. Its members included cabinet ministers, senior army officers and intelligence operatives. The Imperial Japanese Army used its network for espionage, sabotage and assassination during the Russo-Japanese War, the annexation of Korea and the Siberian Intervention, and it organised Manchurian guerrillas against Russian forces. US occupation authorities ordered it disbanded in 1946.

orgs.n: Order of the Golden and Rosy Cross
orgs.d: The Order of the Golden and Rosy Cross was a secret Rosicrucian society of the German lands whose members reached the Prussian throne and cabinet. King Frederick William II was himself a member under the name Ormesus, alongside his favourite Johann Rudolph von Bischoffswerder. In 1788 the king made Johann Christoph von Wöllner, a supreme director of the order's circles, minister of justice and head of the office for worship, and Wöllner set up a commission to oversee religious activity across Prussia with powers to confiscate money and property.

orgs.d: The Portuguese Carbonária was a secret, anti-clerical revolutionary society refounded in 1896 and organised in a hierarchy of cells with military training. It took part in plots against the monarchy, including the conspiracy behind the assassination of King Carlos I and his heir on 1 February 1908. By 1910 it had about 40,000 members, and it played a key role in the revolution of 5 October 1910 that ended the monarchy and created the Portuguese Republic.

orgs.d: The Tongmenghui was a secret society and underground resistance movement founded in Tokyo in 1905 by Sun Yat-sen, Song Jiaoren and others, merging several revolutionary groups to overthrow China's Qing dynasty. Its members organised uprisings, and after the 1911 Xinhai Revolution Sun became Provisional President of the new Republic of China in January 1912. In August 1912 the Tongmenghui became the core of the Kuomintang, the Nationalist party that later ruled China and then Taiwan.

Evatt attacked the 'Groupers' for holding outsized influence in the party, and in 1955 Labor split: many were expelled or left, several unions went with them, and they formed what became the Democratic Labor Party, which helped keep Labor out of federal power for almost 30 years.

Its papers of 1981–1985 laid out the poll tax, a flat per-head local charge introduced in Scotland in 1989 and in England and Wales in 1990, then abolished after protests. Its 1987 paper The Right Lines proposed private train franchises on a separately owned network, which John Major's government enacted. Its Omega Project produced 19 papers, one for each government department.

orgs.d: The Fabian Society, founded in London in 1884 to move Britain gradually towards socialism by working through existing institutions, placed its members in Parliament and government. Sidney Webb wrote the constitution of the Labour Representation Committee, borrowing from the society's own documents, and at the 1945 election 229 Fabians were elected to the Commons, including Clement Attlee and Hugh Dalton. Its Colonial Bureau, set up in 1940 under Rita Hinden, strongly influenced the colonial policy of Attlee's government from 1945 to 1951.

After the 1973 coup Guzmán became a trusted adviser to General Pinochet without holding an official post and was legal adviser to the commission that drafted a new constitution. He is called the principal architect of the 1980 Constitution, approved in a plebiscite under the dictatorship, which governed Chile for four decades. He founded the UDI party in 1983 and was assassinated in 1991.

Its deputy commander Vadym Troyan was made Kyiv region police chief that October, then first deputy and acting head of the National Police, and deputy interior minister from 2017 to 2019. In the Yatsenyuk government formed in February 2014, Oleksandr Sych became deputy prime minister and party members took the agriculture and environment ministries; in March members were made governors of the Poltava, Ternopil and Rivne regions. Svoboda left the coalition that July, its ministers resigned in November and President Poroshenko dismissed the three governors.

orgs.d: The Gorakhnath Math, a Hindu monastery in Gorakhpur, has sent its successive heads (mahants) into elected office for decades, and its present head runs India's most populous state. Mahant Digvijay Nath won the Gorakhpur Lok Sabha seat in 1967; his successor Avaidyanath held it four times; and Yogi Adityanath won it five times from 1998. Adityanath became mahant in 2014 and Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh in 2017, keeping both roles, and won a second term in 2022.

orgs.d: Tablighi Jamaat, a worldwide Islamic missionary movement, had one of its members placed in charge of Pakistan's main spy agency. Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif made Lieutenant General Javed Nasir head of the ISI in March 1992, over the army chief's objections and despite his little intelligence experience. During his 13 months in the post the ISI covertly armed the Bosnian army against the UN embargo and helped set up an Afghan mujahideen government. He was retired early in 1993, which commentators linked to Arab states' pressure, and became a Tablighi missionary.

orgs.d: The Haghani Circle is a hardline school of thought centred on a Qom seminary founded in 1964 by clerics including Mohammad Beheshti and Mohammad Taghi Mesbah Yazdi, whose graduates have repeatedly run Iran's intelligence ministry, a post that by law must go to a qualified Islamic jurist. Ministers Mohammad Reyshahri, Ali Fallahian, Ali Younesi and Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei came from its circle. Mohseni-Ejei was intelligence minister from 2005 to 2009, then prosecutor-general, and became Chief Justice in 2021; the EU and US sanctioned him in 2011 over the torture of protesters.

orgs.d: Ennahda, the Islamist party that led Tunisia's government after 2011, is accused by prosecutors of running a 'secret apparatus' that infiltrated state institutions, spied, and was involved in the 2013 assassinations of leftist politicians Chokri Belaid and Mohamed Brahmi. Lawyers for the victims' families first presented documents in 2018. In June 2026 a Tunis court sentenced party leader Rached Ghannouchi to life plus 30 years and gave eleven others life terms. Ennahda called the charges political, and rights groups called the trial part of a crackdown on opponents.

orgs.d: Mali's High Islamic Council, the country's top Islamic body, had its demands written into national law after leading mass protests. The National Assembly adopted a family code in August 2009 that expanded women's rights; after marches of up to 50,000 people the president sent it back. The text adopted in December 2011, endorsed by the council, recognises religious marriage, states that a wife must obey her husband and the man heads the family, sets marriage at 16 for girls with exceptions from 15 and rolled back gains in inheritance. FIDH said the council's demands were met.

orgs.d: Hefazat-e-Islam, a coalition of Qawmi madrasa teachers and clerics whose 2013 charter demanded sharia law and a changed curriculum, got its demands written into Bangladesh's 2017 state school textbooks. Its members said the government made the 29 changes they had asked for, and its leader Shah Ahmad Shafi praised the authorities. Removed items included a poem by Humayun Azad, a Baul essay and a children's Ramayana excerpt, while essays on the Prophet and the early caliphs were added. The textbook board's chairman denied Hefazat's influence.

orgs.d: Sri Lanka's senior Buddhist monks of the Maha Sangha, led from the Malwatte and Asgiriya chapters in Kandy, were given formal seats in policy-making under President Gotabaya Rajapaksa. In April 2020 he set up a Buddhist Advisory Council of senior monks that met him monthly with ministry secretaries present and advised on archaeological sites, temple land, national security and education; the government reported acting on its proposals. In June 2020 monks were placed on a presidential task force to allocate land around archaeological sites in the Eastern Province, with no Tamil or Muslim member, though those communities are over 70% of its people.

orgs.d: Santi Asoke, an ascetic Thai Buddhist sect, placed its followers in elected office through the Palang Dharma party. Follower Chamlong Srimuang, a former general, won the Bangkok governorship in 1985 and founded the party in 1988; sect members gathered the signatures to register it and made up close to half its 1988 candidates. In 1990 the party won 49 of 55 seats on Bangkok's city council, and in 1992 it won up to 47 parliamentary seats and joined the government. Thaksin Shinawatra later led the party and served as a minister.

orgs.n: Church of the Word (Iglesia El Verbo)
orgs.d: The Church of the Word (Verbo), a Pentecostal-style church founded in Guatemala by the California mission Gospel Outreach, put its elders at the side of the head of state. When its member General Efraín Ríos Montt took power in the March 1982 coup, Verbo elders Francisco Bianchi and Álvaro Contreras became his personal secretaries and key advisers. His 17-month rule saw the worst of the army's massacres of Maya villagers, and in 2013 a Guatemalan court convicted him of genocide; the verdict was later annulled.

orgs.d: New Tribes Mission, now Ethnos360, a US evangelical group with a history of contacting and converting isolated peoples, saw a former missionary placed in charge of the Brazilian office that protects them. In February 2020 the government named pastor Ricardo Lopes Dias, ten years a New Tribes missionary, head of FUNAI's department for isolated peoples, giving him data on more than 100 registered groups. Federal prosecutors warned of possible genocide if missionaries gained that data, and in May 2020 a judge annulled the appointment over the conflict of interest.

orgs.d: Le Cercle, a private foreign-policy club founded in 1952–53 that brings politicians, intelligence figures and business people together in private, has been chaired by sitting British politicians. PoliticsHome reported in 2019 that two MPs on the Commons Foreign Affairs Committee, which scrutinises UK foreign policy, chaired it without declaring the role: Rory Stewart in 2013–14 and Nadhim Zahawi in 2015–18. Earlier UK chairs included Julian Amery, Jonathan Aitken, Norman Lamont and Michael Ancram.

orgs.d: The Group of Thirty is a private club whose 30 members include heads of large private banks alongside central bank governors from about 19 countries, giving bankers regular private contact with the officials who supervise them. European Central Bank president Mario Draghi was a member; in 2018 the European Ombudsman, Emily O'Reilly, asked him to leave, saying his membership could be seen as giving its banking members undue influence over the euro area's central bank and main bank supervisor. Two presidents of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York have also been members.

orgs.d: The Peruvian Corporation was a London company of holders of Peru's defaulted government bonds that took control of Peru's main state assets. Under the Grace Contract, ratified in 1890, it took over the bonds in exchange for its own shares and received the use of Peru's state railways, mainly the Southern and Central lines, for 66 years, plus up to 2 million tons of guano. Peru also agreed to pay it 33 annual payments of $400,000. A 1907 change extended the railway leases to 1973.

orgs.d: The League of Nations, through its Financial Committee, made rescue loans on condition that it supervise the borrower's economy. In October 1922 Austria accepted a League loan of 650 million gold Kronen, guaranteed by Britain, France, Italy and Czechoslovakia; Chancellor Ignaz Seipel accepted League oversight of the economy and promised Austria would not seek union with Germany for 20 years. League supervision of Austria's finances lasted until 1926, and the budget was balanced within two years.

orgs.n: Banca Popolare Italiana (Banca Popolare di Lodi)
orgs.d: Banca Popolare Italiana, led by Gianpiero Fiorani, had the governor of Italy's central bank working in its favour. In the 2005 contest to take over Banca Antonveneta, Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio, who was also the bank supervisor, backed Fiorani's bid against the Dutch bank ABN AMRO, as published wiretaps showed. Fiorani was arrested in December 2005 and Fazio resigned days later, replaced by Mario Draghi. In 2011 a court sentenced Fazio to four years for market rigging in the takeover.

orgs.n: Mellon family banks (Mellon National Bank, Union Trust)
orgs.d: The Mellon family's Pittsburgh banks, Mellon National Bank and Union Trust, which also backed Alcoa and Gulf Oil, put their head in charge of the US Treasury. Andrew Mellon was Treasury Secretary from 1921 to 1932 under three presidents and pushed tax cuts on top incomes, with the 1926 Revenue Act cutting the top rate to 25 percent. In 1932 Congressman Wright Patman began impeachment proceedings, charging that he broke conflict-of-interest laws by keeping company shares in office; President Hoover then moved him to ambassador to Britain.

orgs.d: Merrill Lynch, the US investment bank, supplied the man who ran Lebanon's central bank for 30 years. Riad Salameh, a Merrill Lynch employee from 1973 to 1993 who managed Rafic Hariri's personal portfolio, was appointed governor of Banque du Liban by Hariri as prime minister in 1993. From 2016 he ran 'financial engineering' swaps with commercial banks to hold the currency peg, which broke in 2019. France and Switzerland opened laundering inquiries, the US, UK and Canada sanctioned him in 2023, and he was arrested in 2024 on charges of embezzling $42 million.

Luis de Guindos advised Lehman in Europe from 2006 and directed its Spanish and Portuguese arm until the collapse. He became Spain's economy minister in December 2011, negotiated the EU's €100 billion rescue of Spain's failing savings banks, and in 2018 became Vice-President of the European Central Bank, a post he held until 2026.
